title: Arbitrage Risk and Post‐Earnings‐Announcement Drift
authors: Richard R. Mendenhall
key_findings: The magnitude of post earnings announcement drift is strongly related to the arbitrage risk measure (idiosyncratic volatility). | The effect of arbitrage risk is statistically and economically significant under a wide range of specifications. | The results suggest that drift represents an underreaction to earnings information. | Arbitrage risk impedes arbitrageurs from eliminating the drift (prices do not adjust immediately). | Citing papers note that the drift is concentrated in the smallest firms (based on Mendenhall 2004 findings referenced in 'What Drives Anomaly Returns?', 2020).
for_the_app: Add a 'Drift Probability' score to earnings news events: flag earnings surprises in stocks with high idiosyncratic volatility as high potential drift candidates, but warn that these stocks are riskier and may have lower liquidity.

title: Liquidity and the Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift
authors: Tarun Chordia, Ronnie Sadka, Amit Goyal et al.
key_findings: A long short strategy in the most illiquid stocks yields a gross monthly return of 2.43 percent, compared to only 0.04 percent in the most liquid stocks. | Transaction costs account for 70–100 percent of the gross profits from the long short strategy, depending on the cost model used. | Using the most comprehensive market impact cost estimates (Chen, Stanzl, and Watanabe), the net monthly return for the most illiquid long short portfolio is -0.65 percent. | For the most illiquid stocks, the net return of a long only high SUE portfolio is positive (e.g., 1.64 percent net of Keim and Madhavan costs) but the risk adjusted alpha is often zero or negative. | While gross returns for the drift have declined slightly over time, transaction costs have declined even more, yet for large positions, costs still exceed potential profits in the most illiquid stocks.
for_the_app: The app should flag 'Post Earnings Drift' stories in illiquid stocks as 'High Cost / Low Realizability' and warn users that the expected price move is likely consumed by bid ask spreads and market impact, especially if the strategy involves shorting.

themes: Events that make prices drift; Already priced in or not; Does it still work
title: Information Uncertainty and Post‐Earnings‐Announcement‐Drift
authors: Jennifer Francis, Ryan LaFond, Per Mikael Olsson et al.
key_findings: Unrestricted Post Earnings Announcement Drift (PEAD) earns 0.53% per month (abnormal return, 4-factor model) | High Information Uncertainty (IU) PEAD earns 0.95% to 1.07% per month (abnormal return) | Low Information Uncertainty (IU) PEAD earns -0.06% to 0.11% per month (abnormal return) | Drift concentrates in the two subsequent earnings announcements (quarters +1 and +2) | Information uncertainty explains why high idiosyncratic volatility stocks show stronger PEAD
for_the_app: Prioritize earnings news for stocks with high information uncertainty to flag potential drift storylines

themes: Events that make prices drift; News spreading to linked companies; Text and attention signals; Already priced in or not; From signal to trade
title: Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift: Delayed Price Response or Risk Premium?
authors: Victor L. Bernard, Jk Thomas
key_findings: A long position in the highest surprise decile and a short position in the lowest decile yielded an abnormal return of approximately 4.2% over the 60 days following the announcement (about 18% annualized) for the full sample (1974-1986). | For small firms (size deciles 1-4), the same strategy yielded an abnormal return of approximately 5.3% over the 60 days post announcement. | For large firms (size deciles 8-10), the same strategy yielded an abnormal return of approximately 2.8% over the 60 days post announcement. | Approximately 100% of the drift for small firms occurs within nine months, while for large firms it occurs within six months. | The drift is bounded: the abnormal return stops increasing once the difference in surprise between the top and bottom groups reaches a certain threshold, suggesting transaction costs may prevent traders from exploiting the full gap.
for_the_app: The app should flag stocks immediately after an earnings beat or miss and link this event to a 'drift storyline' that predicts continued movement in the same direction for the next 4-6 weeks, with a specific warning that the effect is stronger for smaller companies.

title: Post–earnings–announcement Drift in the UK
authors: Weimin Liu, Norman Charles Strong, Xinzhong Xu
key_findings: Using the price based measure (AR4D), the arbitrage portfolio (buying highest surprise, selling lowest) generated a 6-month raw return of 7.8% and a 12-month raw return of 10.4% (UK, 1992-1997). | Using the SUE measure, the 6-month raw return for the highest minus lowest decile was 5.2%, and the 12-month return was 10.8% (UK, 1992-1997). | Using the analyst forecast revision measure (REV6), the 6-month raw return for the highest minus lowest decile was 5.7%, and the 12-month return was 10.0% (UK, 1992-1997). | The price based measure (AR4D) produced the strongest drift, and its effect almost completely subsumed the drift found in the other two measures when tested together. | The drift persists for up to 12 months, with a significant portion of the return occurring around the date of the next earnings announcement.
for_the_app: The app should flag stocks immediately after an earnings announcement where the price reaction (4-day return) was extreme, then track these stocks for the next 6-12 months as a 'drift storyline' that is likely to continue until the next earnings report.

themes: Events that make prices drift; Already priced in or not; Does it still work
title: A review of the Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift
authors: Josef Fink
venue: Journal of Behavioral and Experimental Finance
key_findings: Bernard and Thomas (1989) found positive (negative) drift of around 2% over 60 trading days for good (bad) news stocks, amounting to about 4% (18%) in abnormal quarterly (annualized) excess returns | PEAD exists globally across developed and emerging markets, though magnitude is surprisingly stable | The drift is strongest in the quarter directly following the announcement but persists for two to three quarters | PEAD strength is inversely related to firm size - stronger in smaller firms | The magnitude of PEAD returns has been declining in recent years (Chordia et al., 2014; Martineau, 2019; Richardson et al., 2010)
for_the_app: Track earnings surprise magnitude (SUE) and flag stocks with extreme surprises for potential drift monitoring; warn users that drift has weakened and costs matter more for small stocks

title: Implications of Transaction Costs for the Post–Earnings Announcement Drift
authors: Jeffrey Ng, Tjomme O. Rusticus, Rodrigo S. Verdi
key_findings: Using seasonal random walk earnings surprises, the equal weighted 12-month hedge portfolio generated 11.92% abnormal returns, but after deducting transaction costs, profits were only 0.19% (using LDV costs) or negative (-3.18% to -6.88%) using other cost measures. | Firms with the highest transaction costs showed the largest abnormal returns (up to 14.61% for the top quintile), but after costs, the net profit was only 1.02% or negative, showing costs erase the edge. | Using analyst consensus earnings surprises, the 12-month equal weighted hedge portfolio generated 13.70% abnormal returns, but net profits after costs were 2.80% (LDV) or negative (-4.57% using effective spreads). | A strategy combining extreme revenue and earnings surprises generated 12.92% abnormal returns, but net profits were 1.73% (using effective spreads) or -2.55% (using LDV costs). | The paper notes that abnormal returns using analyst forecasts have declined over time and are converging toward the magnitude of transaction costs.
for_the_app: The app should filter out stocks with high estimated transaction costs (wide spreads or low liquidity) before suggesting a trade based on an earnings surprise, as the drift is likely to be eaten by costs.

themes: Events that make prices drift; Does it still work
title: Investor Trading and the Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift
authors: Benjamin C. Ayers, Oliver Zhen Li, P. Eric Yeung
key_findings: Small traders continue to trade in the direction of seasonal random walk based earnings surprises after announcements. | Large traders continue to trade in the direction of analyst based earnings surprises after announcements. | When small traders react more thoroughly to random walk surprises at the announcement, the random walk drift attenuates (weakens). | When large traders react more thoroughly to analyst based surprises at the announcement, the analyst based drift attenuates. | The analyst based drift has declined in recent years.
for_the_app: The app should categorize earnings surprises into 'simple' (random walk) and 'complex' (analyst based) types and track the subsequent trading volume of small vs. large investors to predict the likely duration and direction of the drift.

title: Momentum and post-earnings-announcement drift anomalies: The role of liquidity risk
authors: Ronnie Sadka
key_findings: Momentum 5-1 spread excess return: 0.68% per month (Table 6/7) | PEAD (SUE) 5-1 spread excess return: 0.84% per month (Table 6) | PEAD (SUE) combined with liquidity risk 5-1 spread excess return: 0.91% per month (Table 7) | Liquidity risk (variable component) is priced in these portfolios (t statistics > 2 in some models) | Introduction notes momentum/PEAD returns are short lived (first few months) and involve high turnover/costs
for_the_app: Filter earnings surprise signals by liquidity risk to improve reliability.

title: Rest in Peace Post-Earnings Announcement Drift
authors: Charles Martineau
key_findings: For large stocks (all but microcap), post earnings announcement drift (PEAD) has been non existent since 2006. | For microcap stocks (smallest 20% by market cap), PEAD has largely disappeared, with any remaining drift lasting no more than five days. | In the 2016-2019 period, the response coefficient (beta) for post announcement returns (days 2-60) is statistically zero for all but microcap stocks using analyst surprises. | Since 1996, there is no evidence of PEAD for the top four size quintiles when using random walk earnings surprises. | The price formation on the announcement date has become more efficient, with announcement day returns now capturing almost all the information (beta converges to 1.0) for large stocks.
for_the_app: The app should flag earnings announcements as 'fully priced' events and avoid generating 'drift' storylines for them, instead focusing on whether the market reaction was immediate or if there is a specific reason for a delay (e.g., low liquidity).

title: Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift: The Role of Revenue Surprises
authors: Narasimhan Jegadeesh, Joshua Livnat
key_findings: Drift is stronger when revenue surprises are in the same direction as earnings surprises (e.g., both positive or both negative). | Portfolios with extreme earnings and revenue surprises in the same direction earned significantly higher abnormal returns in the quarter after the announcement. | Using analyst forecasts for both earnings and revenue provided a better measure of surprise and resulted in higher performance than using historical time series data alone. | The result held across subperiods, including the extreme market fluctuations of 1998–2002. | The improvement in performance came at the cost of a smaller number of companies in the portfolio, though it remained sufficient for diversification.
for_the_app: Add a 'Signal Alignment' metric that flags earnings events where the revenue surprise sign matches the earnings surprise sign, and weight the confidence of the predicted price drift higher for these aligned events.

title: Earnings Volatility, Post–Earnings Announcement Drift, and Trading Frictions
authors: SEAN SHUN CAO, Ganapathi S. Narayanamoorthy
key_findings: Standard PEAD strategy (long high SUE, short low SUE) earns a 0.793% abnormal return over the 3-day window and 6.131% over the quarter long window (US, 1987-2008). | Firms with lower ex ante earnings volatility show significantly higher PEAD returns; the interaction between low volatility and high SUE drives the anomaly. | Contrary to typical friction based anomalies, the volatility driven PEAD is NOT concentrated in firms with high trading costs (high bid ask spreads); it is actually stronger in firms with lower spreads. | Using analyst forecast surprises (DSUEA) instead of time series surprises yields stronger PEAD returns, but the volatility effect remains robust. | The effect persists through 2008, and robustness tests truncating the sample in 2004 show 'virtually the same' results, suggesting the anomaly did not disappear over time.
for_the_app: Implement a 'Volatility Filter' for the PEAD storyline: when an earnings surprise is detected, check the company's 8-quarter earnings variance; if variance is low, flag the event as a high confidence 'drift' signal with a 60-day (quarter) target horizon.

title: Earnings Management and the Post‐earnings Announcement Drift
authors: Henock Louis, Amy X. Sun
key_findings: Firms with large positive earnings changes and large negative abnormal accruals (likely managing earnings downward) generated an average buy and hold abnormal return of 9.1% over the subsequent two quarters. | Firms with large negative earnings changes and large positive abnormal accruals (likely managing earnings upward) generated an average buy and hold abnormal return of -10.4% over the subsequent two quarters. | The combined hedge portfolio (long the downward managed positive surprises, short the upward managed negative surprises) yielded an average abnormal return of 19.5% over the two quarter holding period. | When using normal (nondiscretionary) accruals instead of abnormal accruals to sort firms, the hedge portfolio return dropped to 12.6% over the same period, indicating the drift is driven by the discretionary component. | The drift is smooth over the 120-day horizon, suggesting the market underreaction persists for about 4 months after the announcement.
for_the_app: The app should flag earnings announcements where the reported earnings change contradicts the cash flow or accrual patterns (e.g., high earnings but low cash flow), labeling these as 'High Drift Potential' storylines to be tracked for the next 120 days.

title: Post-Earnings Announcement Drift?
authors: Stephen J. Brown, Peter F. Pope
key_findings: Post announcement drift increases monotonically with SUE; the difference in abnormal returns between extreme SUE portfolios is approximately 5.4% over 60 days. | When using standardized announcement period returns as a proxy for unexpected earnings, the drift is weaker (approx. 2.6% difference between extremes) but remains statistically significant. | The magnitude of the drift is inversely related to firm size (smaller stocks drift more). | For firms with high ex ante bankruptcy risk, the difference in abnormal returns between high and low SUE portfolios is 5.78%, compared to 3.56% for low risk firms. | When controlling for financial distress and microstructure variables, the standalone explanatory power of SUE drops significantly, suggesting the drift is partly driven by survival bias and measurement errors rather than pure market inefficiency.
for_the_app: The app should flag earnings surprises but must filter out companies with high bankruptcy risk or low liquidity to avoid false signals caused by survivorship bias and bid ask spread artifacts.

title: Comparing the Post-Earnings Announcement Drift for Surprises Calculated from Analyst and Time Series Forecasts
authors: Joshua Livnat, Richard R. Mendenhall
key_findings: Using analyst forecasts (I/B/E/S), the drift (hedge return between top and bottom deciles) is 4.95% over the subsequent quarter. | Using time series forecasts (Compustat), the drift is 4.01% over the subsequent quarter. | The drift is approximately 30% larger when defined by analyst forecasts compared to time series models. | For the specific subsample of firms with analyst coverage, the drift using analyst forecasts is 4.72% versus 2.54% for time series forecasts over the subsequent quarter. | The drift pattern for analyst surprises does not show the negative reversal often seen in time series models around the fourth subsequent earnings announcement.
for_the_app: The app must integrate a paid data feed for analyst consensus estimates (I/B/E/S style) to calculate the 'Surprise' metric; it should flag stocks with large positive or negative surprises and suggest a holding period of one quarter to capture the drift.

title: Post-earnings announcement drift
authors: Ian D. Gow, Tongqing Ding
key_findings: Cumulative returns of 'good news' firms and 'bad news' firms drift apart even after earnings announcements. | This drift was originally considered an anomaly because efficient markets should quickly price in earnings information. | Later research confirmed the existence of post earnings announcement drift (PEAD) using more refined measures. | No specific return percentages, holding periods, or cost adjustments are provided in the abstract.
for_the_app: Feature: Flag stocks with large earnings surprises and track their price momentum for 4-8 weeks to confirm if the 'drift' story is playing out before suggesting a trade.

themes: Events that make prices drift; Does it still work
title: PEAD.txt: Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift Using Text
authors: Vitaly Meursault, Pierre Jinghong Liang, Bryan Routledge et al.
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
key_findings: SUE.txt generates a text based post earnings announcement drift (PEAD.txt) that is larger than the classic PEAD. | The magnitude of PEAD.txt is considerable even in recent years when the classic PEAD is close to 0. | The news content in the calls relates to details behind the earnings number and the fundamentals of the firm. | Citing papers note that these works evaluate at a multi day horizon where drift has largely disappeared (Fast Numbers, Slow Language, 2026). | The text based measure provides independent support for the distinction between fast numerical signals and slow language signals.
for_the_app: Implement a feature that parses earnings call transcripts to generate a 'Text Surprise' score (SUE.txt) and flag stocks where this score diverges significantly from the numerical earnings surprise, signaling a potential extended drift storyline.

themes: Events that make prices drift; Does it still work
title: Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift in Global Markets: Evidence from an Information Shock
authors: Mingyi Hung, Xi Li, Shiheng Wang
key_findings: The proportion of total market reaction to earnings surprises that occurs as drift (days +2 to +64) dropped from 58.99% in the pre shock period to 3.43% in the post shock period for treatment firms. | Cross listing on a U.S. exchange reduced quarterly abnormal returns (PEAD) by 3.99%. | Voluntary IFRS adoption reduced quarterly abnormal returns (PEAD) by 0.74%. | The reduction in PEAD was more pronounced for firms with fewer concurrent earnings announcements (less distraction) and lower transaction costs (lower Amihud illiquidity). | The reduction in PEAD was more pronounced for firms with lower arbitrage risks (lower idiosyncratic volatility) and higher institutional ownership.
for_the_app: Feature: Filter for 'High Distraction' events (e.g., earnings released on Fridays or during weeks with many other announcements) and 'High Friction' stocks (low liquidity, low institutional ownership) to prioritize storylines where the market is likely to underreact initially.

title: Jump on the Post–Earnings Announcement Drift (corrected)
authors: Haigang Zhou, John Qi Zhu
key_findings: Annualized abnormal return of 15.3% over the last four decades. | Annualized Sharpe ratio of 1.52 over the last four decades. | Conventional risk factors do not explain the abnormal return. | Common company characteristics do not explain the abnormal return. | Strategy involves long positions in positive jump stocks and short positions in negative jump stocks.
for_the_app: The app should flag stocks with significant price jumps immediately following earnings releases as potential 'storyline' starters, but must warn users that the full strategy requires short selling capabilities.

title: Volume, Opinion Divergence, and Returns: A Study of Post-Earnings Announcement Drift
authors: Jon A. Garfinkel, Jonathan S. Sokobin
key_findings: Post earnings announcement returns are strictly increasing in the component of volume unexplained by prior trading activity (Change in Market Adjusted Turnover coefficient: 0.24, significant at 1%). | Post earnings announcement returns are strictly increasing in Standardized Unexpected Volume (SUV) (coefficient: 0.14, significant at 1%). | Drift is positively correlated with earnings surprise (PEpf coefficient: 0.23, significant at 1%) and negatively correlated with firm size (MVpf coefficient: -0.36, significant at 1%). | Higher variability in analyst forecasts (SDF) is associated with more negative post earnings announcement returns (coefficient: -0.20, significant at 1%), which contradicts the volume based proxy results. | The positive relationship between unexpected volume and drift is significantly weaker or insignificant for firms with high analyst following compared to firms with low or no analyst following.
for_the_app: When an earnings event occurs, the app should calculate the 'unexpected volume' metric; if volume is high relative to the prior 50 days, the app should flag the stock as having a higher probability of a sustained drift in the direction of the earnings surprise.

themes: Events that make prices drift; From signal to trade
title: Do Individual Investors Cause Post-Earnings Announcement Drift? Direct Evidence from Personal Trades
authors: David A. Hirshleifer, James N. Myers, Linda A. Myers et al.
key_findings: individual investor trading fails to subsume any of the power of extreme earnings surprises to predict future abnormal returns | individuals are significant net buyers after both negative and positive extreme earnings surprises | no indication that trading by individuals explains the concentration of drift at subsequent earnings announcement dates | Abnormal returns are calculated as the buy and hold returns that begin on day +6 and end 3, 6, 9, or 12 months later | SUE coefficient 0.006 (t=4.68) for 3 Months and 0.014 (t=4.72) for 12 Months for actively trading investors
for_the_app: Flag earnings surprises (SUE) as potential drivers of multi month price drift; do not rely on retail flow data to predict this drift

title: Earnings Autocorrelation and the Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift: Experimental Evidence
authors: Josef Fink, Stefan Palan, Erik Theissen
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
key_findings: Prices of stocks with positive earnings news jump by 3.96 talers... continue to drift upward by another 3.80 talers in the 170 s following | prices drop by 2.10 talers... drift downward by another 7.88 talers | strategy... earns 11.71 talers (before transaction costs) | profits... ranging from 1.05% to 3.51% | earnings autocorrelation is not a necessary condition for PEAD
for_the_app: Flag earnings surprises as potential multi day drift opportunities, but warn about execution costs

title: Post-earnings announcement drift: Evidence from Turkey
authors: Aykut Ahlatcıoğlu, Nesrin Okay
key_findings: The difference in average cumulative abnormal return between the highest and lowest earnings surprise groups is 2.9% over the 60 days following the announcement when using time series or analyst forecast surprise measures. | When using the earnings announcement return (EAR) surprise measure, the drift difference between high and low surprise groups is 2.2% over the 60-day period. | Over the 21-day window, the drift is 1.18% (SUETF), 1.31% (SUEAF), and 0.76% (EAR). | Over the 41-day window, the drift is 2.19% (SUETF), 2.61% (SUEAF), and 1.21% (EAR). | Firm size significantly reduces the drift: a one standard deviation increase in firm size decreases the sensitivity of returns to earnings news by 50% (using SUETF) and 54% (using EAR).
for_the_app: The app should flag earnings surprises as 'under reaction' signals and suggest a 21-60 day holding window, while filtering out large cap stocks where the effect is weaker.

title: … and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns
authors: Campbell R. Harvey, Yan Liu, Caroline Zhu
key_findings: The long short portfolio (buying low CID sensitivity, selling high CID sensitivity) generates a monthly return of 49 basis points (0.49%) with a t statistic of 3.19 (US, 1963-2018). | The abnormal return (alpha) of this strategy relative to the Fama French 5-factor model augmented with momentum and short term reversal is 29 to 60 basis points per month, depending on the specific factor model used. | Stocks with high sensitivity to CID (high beta) have lower average returns (0.30% monthly) compared to stocks with low sensitivity (0.79% monthly) in value weighted portfolios. | The return spread is not explained by other uncertainty measures like VIX, financial uncertainty, or common idiosyncratic volatility, as CID subsumes much of their predictive power. | High CID sensitivity stocks tend to be larger, more liquid, have higher momentum, and lower book to market ratios, consistent with them being 'winners' in sectoral shifts.
for_the_app: The app should flag stocks with high sensitivity to sectoral dispersion as potential 'overvalued' or 'crowded' trades to avoid, and highlight low sensitivity stocks as potential value opportunities, while warning users that these are contrarian signals against recent momentum.

themes: Events that make prices drift; Already priced in or not; News spreading to linked companies; Text and attention signals; Does it still work; From signal to trade
title: Investor Inattention and Friday Earnings Announcements
authors: Stefano DellaVigna, Joshua Matthew Pollet
key_findings: Friday earnings announcements have a 15% lower immediate price response compared to non Friday announcements. | The delayed price response (drift) for Friday announcements is 70% higher than for non Friday announcements. | A portfolio that buys the Friday drift and sells the non Friday drift earns an abnormal return of approximately 3.84% per month (net of the risk free rate, before transaction costs). | The differential drift between Friday and non Friday announcements becomes most apparent approximately 30 trading days after the announcement and continues to increase over the next 60 trading days. | Trading volume around Friday announcements is 8% lower than around non Friday announcements, supporting the theory of limited investor attention.
for_the_app: The app should flag earnings announcements released on Fridays as 'high drift potential' events, suggesting a longer holding period (30-75 days) to capture the delayed market reaction, while warning that immediate price moves may be muted.

themes: Events that make prices drift; News spreading to linked companies; Text and attention signals; Already priced in or not; Does it still work; From signal to trade
title: Driven to Distraction: Extraneous Events and Underreaction to Earnings News
authors: David A. Hirshleifer, Sonya S. Lim, Siew Hong Teoh
key_findings: On days with high competing news (top decile), the 'good minus bad' earnings surprise hedge portfolio earned a 3-factor alpha of 1.64% per month (significant at 1% level). | On days with low competing news (bottom decile), the same hedge portfolio earned an insignificant alpha of 0.77% per month. | The immediate 2-day price reaction to earnings news was 20% weaker on high news days compared to low news days. | The 60-day post announcement drift spread between extreme earnings surprise deciles was 7.41% on high news days versus only 2.81% on low news days. | The distraction effect was stronger for positive earnings surprises than for negative ones; competing news significantly muted the immediate reaction to good news but had little effect on the immediate reaction to bad news.
for_the_app: The app should flag earnings announcements occurring on 'high distraction' days (many other firms reporting) and suggest a delayed entry strategy (e.g., wait 1-2 days) to capture the stronger post earnings drift, rather than trading on the announcement day itself.

themes: Events that make prices drift; News spreading to linked companies; Text and attention signals; Already priced in or not; Does it still work; From signal to trade
title: Economic Links and Predictable Returns
authors: Lauren H. Cohen, Andrea Frazzini
key_findings: The long short customer momentum strategy yields Fama French 3-factor abnormal returns of 1.45% per month (t statistic = 3.61), or approximately 18.4% per year. | After adjusting for the stock's own momentum (Carhart 4-factor), the strategy still earns 1.37% per month (t statistic = 3.12). | Supplier stock prices underreact to customer news by roughly 40%; they immediately react to about 60% of the shock and drift to close the remaining gap over the next 6 months. | The predictable positive returns persist for about a year (12 months) and then fade away. | The effect is asymmetric: the returns are largely driven by the slow diffusion of negative news (bad customer news leads to larger subsequent underperformance of suppliers).
for_the_app: The app should automatically map customer supplier relationships (using 10-K/10-Q filings) and flag suppliers when a major customer's stock moves significantly, predicting a delayed move in the supplier's price over the next 6-12 months.

title: Stock price reaction to news and no-news: drift and reversal after headlines
authors: Wesley S. Chan
key_findings: Stocks with bad public news (losers) show a negative drift of -2.68% cumulative size and B/M adjusted return over 12 months (t statistic -2.73), while similar stocks with no news reverse and gain +1.21% over the same period. | The long short strategy (buying news losers, shorting no news losers) generates a cumulative abnormal return of 3.93% over 12 months (t statistic 3.93) for the full 1980–2000 period. | Drift is strongest in small, illiquid stocks: the 12-month cumulative abnormal return for the news strategy in the smallest size quintile is 4.01% (t statistic 3.28), compared to 0.58% (t statistic 0.39) for the largest quintile. | The drift after bad news persists even when excluding stocks that had earnings announcements in the formation month, with a 12-month cumulative return of -3.3% for news losers (t statistic -2.8). | The effect weakened in the 1991–2000 subperiod compared to 1980–1990, but a statistically significant 12-month abnormal return of 3.33% (t statistic 2.22) remained for the news strategy in the later decade.
for_the_app: Feature: When the app detects a negative news headline for a small cap stock, it should flag a 'slow drift' storyline and suggest holding the position for 3–12 months rather than selling immediately; Warning: Do not short stocks that rose on no news, as the reversal is short term and liquidity costs may erase profits.

title: Global Pricing of Carbon‐Transition Risk
authors: Patrick G M Bolton, Marcin T. Kacperczyk
key_findings: Higher stock returns associated with higher levels and growth rates of carbon emissions in all sectors and most countries. | US: 0.071 coefficient for LOGS1TOT, annualized value 0.95% per one standard deviation change. | China: 0.069 coefficient, annualized value 1.18% per one standard deviation change. | Sample: 14,400 listed companies in 77 countries from 2005 to 2018. | Carbon premium rose significantly following the COP21 meeting (Paris Agreement 2015).
for_the_app: Include carbon emission levels and growth as risk factors in the storyline engine to flag high emission stocks as higher risk/reward.

title: Tests of Analysts' Overreaction/Underreaction to Earnings Information as an Explanation for Anomalous Stock Price Behavior
authors: Jeffery S. Abarbanell, Victor L. Bernard
key_findings: Analysts' forecasts underreact to recent earnings, but this underreaction is at most only about half as large as necessary to explain the magnitude of the stock price drift. | The 'extreme' analysts' forecasts studied by DeBondt and Thaler (1990) cannot be viewed as overreactions to earnings. | Extreme analyst forecasts are not clearly linked to the stock price overreactions discussed in DeBondt and Thaler (1985, 1987) and Chopra, Lakonishok, and Ritter. | Security analysts' behavior is at best only a partial explanation for stock price underreaction to earnings. | Analysts' behavior may be unrelated to stock price overreactions.
for_the_app: The app should flag earnings surprises where the consensus analyst forecast has barely moved, as the market may still have a significant drift ahead that analysts have not fully priced in.

themes: Events that make prices drift; Does it still work
title: Analyzing the Analysts: When Do Recommendations Add Value?
authors: Narasimhan Jegadeesh, Joonghyuk Kim, Susan D. Krische et al.
key_findings: Consensus recommendation levels (CONS) only predict positive returns when the stock has favorable quantitative characteristics (High QScore); in low QScore groups, high consensus recommendations lead to negative returns. | The return difference between High QScore/High Consensus and Low QScore/Low Consensus stocks (Agreement strategy) is 9.28% to 11.86% over six months. | Changes in consensus recommendations (CHGCONS) are a robust predictor of returns across all quantitative groups, generating positive excess returns even when the absolute level of the recommendation is not useful. | When signals disagree (High QScore but Low Consensus), the quantitative score dominates, and the return differential is -9.51% (meaning the low consensus stock outperforms the high consensus stock). | Earnings forecast revisions (FREV) and Total Accruals (TA) are the most significant individual predictors in multivariate tests, with positive coefficients in 48 and 52 out of 56 quarters respectively.
for_the_app: Implement a 'Consensus Filter' feature: only surface analyst upgrades if the stock's underlying quantitative score (momentum/earnings revisions) is also positive; flag upgrades on weak stocks as potential traps.

themes: Events that make prices drift; Already priced in or not
title: Price Reactions to Dividend Initiations and Omissions: Overreaction or Drift?
authors: Roni Michaely, Richard H. Thaler, Kent L. Womack
key_findings: Short run (3-day) reaction: Omissions -7.0%, Initiations +3.4% (Abstract) | 1-year excess return: Initiations +7.5%, Omissions -11.0% (Page 14) | 3-year excess return: Initiations +24.8%, Omissions -15.3% (Page 14) | Trading rule (1 year): Positive returns in 22 out of 25 years, average 9.7% (Page 21) | Stock dividend replacements (3-year): -31.3% excess return (Page 14)
for_the_app: Flag dividend initiations and omissions as high confidence drift signals in the storyline tracker; warn users about shorting constraints for omissions

title: Analyst Forecast Revisions and Market Price Discovery
authors: Cristi A. Gleason, Charles M.C. Lee
key_findings: The market fails to distinguish between 'high innovation' revisions and 'low innovation' revisions, leading to delayed price adjustment for the former. | Price adjustment is faster and more complete for 'celebrity' analysts (Institutional Investor All Stars) than for obscure but highly accurate analysts. | Firms with greater analyst coverage experience faster and more complete price adjustment processes. | A substantial portion of the delayed price adjustment occurs specifically around subsequent earnings announcement dates. | A substantial portion of the delayed price adjustment occurs around subsequent forecast revision dates.
for_the_app: The app should flag 'high innovation' forecast revisions as high priority storylines and track the 'All Star' status of the analyst issuing the revision to predict how quickly the price might adjust.

title: Does Meeting Earnings Expectations Matter? Evidence from Analyst Forecast Revisions and Share Prices
authors: Ron Kasznik, Maureen F. McNichols
key_findings: 56.9% of firm year observations met expectations in the current year (Table 1) | Firms meeting expectations have significantly higher abnormal annual returns (Abstract) | Firms meeting expectations in one year have an incremental market reward of $0.37 per share (Section 6.3) | Firms meeting expectations in three consecutive years have an incremental market reward of $1.57 per share (Section 6.3) | Sample firms are larger than average, in the 2nd or 3rd largest NYSE deciles, with a median of 7 analysts (Section 4)
for_the_app: Track the streak of earnings beats over multiple years to identify firms with a consistent market premium

title: Short-Sale Strategies and Return Predictability
authors: Karl B. Diether, Kuan‐Hui Lee, Ingrid M. Werner
key_findings: Short sales represent 24% of NYSE and 31% of Nasdaq share volume in 2005. | A 10% increase in short selling activity is associated with a future decline in returns by 0.94% per month on the NYSE and 0.72% per month on Nasdaq. | A long low/short high strategy generated an average abnormal return of 0.063% per day (1.39% per month) for NYSE stocks over a 1-day holding period. | The same strategy generated 0.064% per day (1.41% per month) for Nasdaq stocks over a 1-day holding period. | Extending the holding period to 4 days reduced the daily abnormal return to 0.042% (0.92% per month) for NYSE and 0.055% (1.21% per month) for Nasdaq.
for_the_app: The app should flag stocks with sudden spikes in short selling activity as potential 'overreaction' signals for a bearish storyline, but must warn the user that the profit window is very short (1-4 days) and costs are high.

title: Perspectives on Behavioral Finance: Does "Irrationality" Disappear with Wealth? Evidence from Expectations and Actions
authors: Annette Vissing‐Jørgensen
key_findings: Wealthy investors (net worth >$1M) are more likely to trade frequently: 35.7% traded more than 10 times in 1998, compared to only 1.2% of those with net worth <$10K. | Individual investors in a discount brokerage sample underperformed the S&P 500 by 1.5% per year after costs, with the top 20% of traders underperforming by 5.5% per year after costs. | Median annual stock market participation costs sufficient to explain non participation were estimated at around $350 (real 1982-1984 dollars) for 1994, $500 for 1989, and $800 for 1984. | Even among the wealthiest households, not all hold stocks, suggesting participation costs are not the sole reason for non participation among the rich. | Investor beliefs depend on their own past portfolio performance (law of small numbers) and are asymmetric (biased self attribution), even for wealthy investors.
for_the_app: The app should flag high activity portfolios as potential 'overconfidence' risks regardless of the user's wealth level, and include a 'cost of inaction' metric to explain why some investors stay out of the market.

themes: Text and attention signals; Does it still work
title: Can Twitter Help Predict Firm-Level Earnings and Stock Returns?
authors: Eli Bartov, Lucile Faurel, Partha S. Mohanram
key_findings: Aggregate tweet opinion predicts quarterly earnings and announcement returns (2009-2012) | OPI_BAYES difference (25th to 75th percentile) = 9.4 basis points per 3 trading days (8.2% annualized) | OPI_VOCAB difference (25th to 75th percentile) = 30.4 basis points per 3 trading days (29.0% annualized) | Results hold after controlling for traditional media and SeekingAlpha coverage | Predictive power is stronger for firms in weak information environments
for_the_app: Add a feature to aggregate tweet sentiment in the 9 days before earnings and flag divergence from traditional media

themes: Events that make prices drift; News spreading to linked companies; Already priced in or not; Does it still work; From signal to trade
title: Industry Information Diffusion and the Lead-lag Effect in Stock Returns
authors: Kewei Hou
read_from: full text (your PDF, working paper version)
key_findings: Within an industry, last week's returns of big firms predict this week's returns of small firms, but not the other way round: sum of four weekly lag coefficients 0.2304 (significant at 1%) against 0.0294 (not significant) for big firms of other industries (Intra- versus Inter-Industry Lead-Lag Effects panel) | The effect is driven by bad news: small firms' response to big firm returns is 0.2841 after negative weeks and 0.1283 after positive weeks (Good News versus Bad News panel) | The signal is in small stocks at a weekly horizon, and is stronger in small, volatile, less competitive and neglected industries; leaders lead followers, value firms lead growth firms, and low volatility firms lead high volatility peers | The intra industry lead lag drives industry momentum. The 25, 18 and 22 basis points per week (1, 6 and 12 month formation periods) are industry momentum profits, not returns of this signal | The paper trades no strategy: it reports regression coefficients only, with no returns after costs and no data after 2001
for_the_app: Feature: Prioritize news on industry leaders; link to followers with a delay warning.

themes: Does it still work; Skill or luck
title: Maxing Out: Stocks as Lotteries and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns
authors: Turan G. Bali, Nusret Cakici, Robert Whitelaw
key_findings: Value weighted average raw return difference between low MAX and high MAX deciles is -1.03% per month (t statistic -2.83). | Value weighted 4-factor alpha difference between low MAX and high MAX deciles is -1.18% per month (t statistic -4.71). | Equal weighted average raw return difference between low MAX and high MAX deciles is -1.11% per month after controlling for size, book to market, momentum, short term reversal, and liquidity. | Equal weighted average risk adjusted return difference is -1.06% per month after controls. | The effect is driven by the top deciles (8, 9, 10) where average returns drop from 1.00% to -0.02% per month, while lower deciles remain stable around 1.00% to 1.16%.
for_the_app: Add a 'Lottery Risk' filter that flags stocks with a maximum daily gain >10% in the last 21 days and suggests a 'Sell' or 'Avoid' signal, explaining that these stocks often underperform in the following month due to investor overpayment for lottery like payoffs.

title: Can ChatGPT forecast stock price movements? Return predictability and large language models
authors: Alejandro Lopez-Lira, Yuehua Tang
key_findings: A long short strategy based on GPT-4 scores for overnight news earns 34 basis points per day before transaction costs (2021m10 to 2024m5). | Without transaction costs, the cumulative return of the long short overnight strategy is around 700% from October 2021 to May 2024. | With a 5 basis point round trip transaction cost, the equal weighted 100% rebalancing strategy maintains a Sharpe ratio of 2.13 and a cumulative return over 300%. | With a 10 basis point round trip transaction cost, the equal weighted 100% rebalancing strategy's Sharpe ratio falls to 1.29, while the 25% rebalancing strategy maintains a Sharpe ratio of 1.34. | The strategy becomes unprofitable at 20 basis points round trip transaction costs for equal weighted 100% rebalancing (Sharpe ratio -0.394) and for all value weighted strategies even at 5 basis points.
for_the_app: The app should implement a 'partial rebalancing' logic for its trading signals to reduce turnover and transaction costs, and prioritize equal weighted portfolios over value weighted ones for better risk adjusted returns.

title: Caught on tape: Institutional trading, stock returns, and earnings announcements
authors: Prof Tarun Ramadorai
venue: Oxford University Research Archive (ORA) (University of Oxford)
key_findings: Cumulative institutional flows over 60 days before earnings predict earnings surprise (coefficient 0.018, t stat 4.509, Table 9) | Cumulative institutional flows predict post earnings announcement drift over [+1,+60] days (coefficient 0.385, t stat 2.674, Table 10) | Institutional trades generate short term losses but longer term profits (Abstract) | Daily institutional trades are highly persistent and respond positively to recent daily returns (Abstract) | Extreme earnings surprise deciles show cumulative abnormal returns diverging by approximately 4-5% over 60 days (Figure 3)
for_the_app: Feature: Flag stocks with high pre earnings institutional flow to confirm earnings storylines

title: Stock Price Reaction to News: The Joint Effect of Tone and Attention on Momentum
authors: Thanh Huynh, Daniel R. Smith
key_findings: Stocks having important and positive news exhibit stronger return continuation. | The market's underreaction to good news is a driver of weekly momentum returns. | Investors in international markets (US, Europe, Japan, Asia Pacific) show similar underreaction to the same news characteristics. | News appearance frequency is used to quantify news influence on market movements.
for_the_app: The app should weight news signals by both 'tone' (positive/negative) and 'attention' (frequency/repetition) to predict which stocks are likely to drift upward after a good news event.

themes: Events that make prices drift; Text and attention signals; Already priced in or not; From signal to trade
title: The Disposition Effect and Under-Reaction to News
authors: Andrea Frazzini
key_findings: Monthly alphas of over 200 basis points (Abstract) | Net monthly alphas of 0.885% and 1.062% (Table VIII, 3 and 6 month holding) | Semiannual buy and hold returns between 1.7% and 6% (Page 2038) | None of the alphas of the negative overhang spread portfolios is significantly different from zero (Page 2037) | Overhang spread portfolio displays price drift following analysts’ recommendation changes (Page 2044)
for_the_app: Add a 'Cost Basis Overhang' metric to news alerts

themes: Events that make prices drift; Text and attention signals; Already priced in or not
title: Which News Moves Stock Prices? A Textual Analysis
authors: Jacob Boudoukh A, Ronen Feldman, Shimon Kogan et al.
key_findings: Identified news days show continuation (0.7% positive autocorrelation), no news days show reversal (-3.7%). | No news reversal strategy earns 15.6bp per day (alpha 0.16%). | Identified news continuation strategy earns 19.6bp per day (alpha 0.20%). | Positive sentiment filter on continuation strategy increases alpha to 34bp per day. | Unidentified news days show no significant alpha (indistinguishable from zero).
for_the_app: Classify news as "identified event" vs "noise" and flag sentiment to filter continuation signals; warn users that daily holding incurs high costs.

title: Daily market news sentiment and stock prices
authors: David E. Allen, Michael J. McAleer, Abhay Kumar Singh
key_findings: Using 2 features (Sentiment_Weighted, Sentiment_MA) with a 34/66 data split, K Nearest Neighbors achieved 1.29% cumulative return, while Buy and Hold lost 2.00%. | Using 3 features (Sentiment_Weighted, Sentiment_MA, Tweet Volume) with a 34/66 data split, K Nearest Neighbors achieved 1.374% cumulative return, while Buy and Hold lost 2.00%. | Using 3 features with a 66/34 data split, K Nearest Neighbors achieved 0.638% cumulative return, while Buy and Hold lost 0.636%. | Across both data splits, the K Nearest Neighbor classifier outperformed the Random Forest classifier in cumulative returns, with an average return of 0.915% compared to the market's average loss of 1.32%. | The models showed higher accuracy in detecting negative returns (down markets) than positive returns, with the 3-feature model achieving 51.0% accuracy in the 34/66 split.
for_the_app: The app should treat tweet sentiment as a short term (1-day) signal that is more reliable for identifying downside risk (shorting) than upside potential, but must warn users that this signal degrades quickly and requires real time data processing.

title: Feverish Stock Price Reactions to COVID-19*
authors: Stefano Ramelli, Alexander F. Wagner
venue: The Review of Corporate Finance Studies
key_findings: In the 'Outbreak' period, a one standard deviation higher exposure to China was associated with 1.36% lower cumulative returns. | In the 'Fever' period, a one standard deviation higher cash holding (25.80%) was associated with approximately 2.99% higher cumulative returns. | In the 'Fever' period, high leverage was associated with significantly lower returns (coefficient -0.135), while high cash was associated with higher returns (coefficient +0.112). | Firms that discussed COVID-19 on conference calls had, on average, lower cumulative returns over the whole period compared to those that did not. | The negative impact of leverage and positive impact of cash reversed briefly (March 23-25) after Fed intervention but resumed their original direction by April 3, 2020.
for_the_app: The app should flag stocks with high 'China exposure' or 'foreign revenue' as high risk during global health alerts, and prioritize 'high cash/low debt' firms as defensive holdings; it should also monitor conference call transcripts for increased negativity as a confirmation signal of distress.

themes: Text and attention signals; Does it still work; Skill or luck
title: In Search of Attention
authors: Zhi Da, JOSEPH ENGELBERG, Pengjie Gao
key_findings: An increase in ASVI predicts a positive abnormal return of 18.7 basis points in week 1 and 14.9 basis points in week 2 for Russell 3000 stocks (US, 2004-2008). | The predictive effect disappears by week 3 and turns negative in week 4 (-1.6 basis points), indicating a price reversal within the year. | For IPOs, a one standard deviation increase in pre IPO ASVI leads to a 3.18% higher first day return (US, 2004-2007). | IPOs with high pre IPO ASVI and high first day returns show significant long run underperformance (reversal) over the 4 to 12 months following the IPO. | ASVI captures retail investor attention specifically, as shown by correlations with small order sizes in SEC Dash-5 data.
for_the_app: Implement a 'Hype Alert' feature: flag stocks with a sharp rise in search volume (ASVI) as potential short term buys with a strict 2-week exit rule, and flag high search IPOs as potential short candidates for the 4-12 month period.

title: Corporate Sustainability: First Evidence on Materiality
authors: Mozaffar Khan, George Serafeim, Aaron S. Yoon
key_findings: Top material portfolio alpha ranges from about 3% to about 8% annualized (significant) | Immaterial portfolio high vs low difference is -1.49% (equal weighted) or 0.71% (value weighted), not significant | Material investment firms (good material, bad immaterial) alpha is 6.01%, Immaterial investment firms (bad material, good immaterial) alpha is 0.60%, difference is 5.41% annually | No investment firms have an estimated alpha of -2.90% | Firms with better material performance have more positive changes in profitability margins up to three years in the future
for_the_app: Add a filter to weight news by industry materiality (e.g., water usage matters more for beverage companies than tech firms)

themes: Events that make prices drift; From signal to trade
title: Do Brokerage Analysts' Recommendations Have Investment Value?
authors: Kent L. Womack
key_findings: For stocks added to buy lists, the mean size adjusted return in the first month after the event (starting 2 days post announcement) is +2.4%. | For stocks added to sell lists, the mean size adjusted return over the 6-month period after the event is -9.1%. | The total market impact (event return plus drift) for stocks added to buy lists is +5.4% over the event plus one month. | The total market impact for stocks added to sell lists is -13.7% over the event plus six months. | The market reaction to sell recommendations is significantly larger and longer lasting than for buy recommendations; buy drift is short lived (1 month) while sell drift extends for 6 months.
for_the_app: The app should flag 'Added to Sell' recommendations as high confidence, long duration (6-month) bearish signals, while treating 'Added to Buy' signals as short term (1-month) bullish opportunities that may fade quickly.

title: Firm-Level Political Risk: Measurement and Effects*
authors: Tarek A. Hassan, Stephan Hollander, Laurence van Lent et al.
key_findings: Firms with higher PRisk scores significantly increase lobbying and political donations in the following quarter, while non political risk measures do not predict these actions. | Firms with higher PRisk scores retrench (reduce) hiring and investment, indicating real economic consequences of the measured risk. | The measure correlates strongly (0.82) with aggregate Economic Policy Uncertainty (EPU) indices, validating it captures broad political uncertainty. | About two thirds of the variation in political risk is idiosyncratic (firm level) rather than driven by sector or aggregate economic factors. | The paper does not report specific stock return figures, holding periods, or trading costs for a strategy based on this signal.
for_the_app: The app should include a 'Political Risk Score' derived from earnings call transcripts as a fundamental risk metric to flag companies likely to reduce investment or face regulatory headwinds, rather than as a direct buy/sell trigger.

title: Input Specificity and the Propagation of Idiosyncratic Shocks in Production Networks *
authors: Jean-Noël Barrot, Julien Sauvagnat
key_findings: Customer firms experience a cumulative abnormal return (CAAR) drop of 1.13% over the 51-day window [-10, +40] when a supplier is hit by a disaster (Table IX). | Directly hit suppliers experience a CAAR drop of 2.46% over the same 51-day window [-10, +40] (Table IX). | The drop in customer stock prices is significantly larger (-2.37%) when the disrupted supplier produces specific inputs compared to non specific inputs, where the effect is statistically insignificant (0.58%) (Table X). | Most of the price drop for customers occurs within the first 21 days (window [-10, +10]), with a CAAR of -0.85% (sum of -0.49% and -0.36% from Table IX), suggesting rapid market reaction. | Related suppliers (those sharing a customer with the disrupted firm) see a 3.8 percentage point decrease in sales growth, indicating negative spillovers rather than substitution benefits (Table XI).
for_the_app: The app should flag customers of suppliers located in disaster prone areas if those suppliers produce 'specific' (hard to replace) inputs, and alert users that the market reaction is likely to be front loaded (happening within 2 weeks).

title: Ratings Changes, Ratings Levels, and the Predictive Value of Analysts’ Recommendations
authors: Brad M. Barber, Reuven Lehavy, Brett Trueman
key_findings: Combined levels- and changes based hedge strategy of purchasing single upgrades to buy or strong buy and shorting single downgrades to sell or strong sell generates a significant average daily abnormal return of 5.5 basis points | Combined levels- and changes based strategy of purchasing double upgrades to buy or strong buy and shorting double downgrades to sell or strong sell yields a significant average daily abnormal return of 5.2 basis points | Levels only based hedge strategy of purchasing all buys and strong buys and shorting all sells and strong sells generates an average daily abnormal return of 3.5 basis points | Changes only based hedge strategy of purchasing all single upgrades and shorting all single downgrades earns an average daily abnormal return of 2.5 basis points | Upgrades are associated with an average daily abnormal return of 1.9 basis points versus -1.0 for downgrades
for_the_app: Add analyst rating changes as a trigger event and weight them by the current rating level to confirm storylines

title: The Value of Client Access to Analyst Recommendations
authors: T. Clifton Green
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
key_findings: After controlling for transaction costs, purchasing quickly following upgrades results in an average two day return of 1.02%. | Selling short following downgrades produces an average two day return of 1.50%. | Short term profit opportunities persist for roughly two hours following the pre market release of new recommendations. | A calendar based strategy (buying upgrades, selling downgrades) produces positive abnormal daily returns of over 10 basis points, roughly 30% annualized. | Approximately one quarter of the total price impact of an upgrade occurs over the following two trading days, with the rest happening immediately or over the next month.
for_the_app: The app should flag analyst recommendation changes as high priority events but warn users that the immediate price jump often happens before public release; the app should focus on tracking the 'drift' that continues for 2 days to 1 month rather than trying to catch the initial spike.

title: Can Investors Profit from the Prophets? Security Analyst Recommendations and Stock Returns
authors: Brad M. Barber, Reuven Lehavy, Maureen F. McNichols et al.
key_findings: Most favorable stocks earn 4.13% annual abnormal gross return (1986-1996) | Least favorable stocks earn -4.91% annual abnormal gross return (1986-1996) | Daily rebalancing is crucial for positive returns on most favorable stocks | Transaction costs (0.727% to 4.12% round trip) eliminate abnormal net returns | Shorting least favorable stocks yields up to 3% annual net return but not reliably significant
for_the_app: Track consensus changes as events, but warn users that frequent trading costs may erase gains

title: Do Earnings Estimates Add Value to Sell-Side Analysts’ Investment Recommendations?
authors: Ambrus Kecskés, Roni Michaely, Kent L. Womack
key_findings: Earnings based upgrades have a 65% larger initial price reaction (+3.64% vs +2.21%) and a 166% larger one month drift (+1.62% vs +0.61%) compared to non earnings based upgrades. | Earnings based downgrades have a 186% larger initial price reaction (-5.06% vs -1.77%) and a 53% larger one month drift (-1.04% vs -0.68%) compared to non earnings based downgrades. | A trading strategy buying earnings based upgrades and selling earnings based downgrades earns a risk adjusted return (alpha) of 3.11% per month for a one month holding period. | The unconditional strategy (buying all upgrades and selling all downgrades regardless of earnings estimates) earns an alpha of 1.80% per month for a one month holding period. | The profitability of the earnings based strategy persisted throughout the 1994-2010 sample period, with similar performance at the beginning and end of the sample.
for_the_app: The app should filter analyst recommendation news to flag only those accompanied by earnings estimate revisions (up or down) and prioritize these as high confidence triggers for the 'drift' storyline, while deprioritizing recommendations without estimate changes.

title: Analysts’ Earnings Forecast, Recommendation,and Target Price Revisions
authors: Ronen Feldman, Joshua Livnat, Yuan Zhang
key_findings: Revisions in earnings forecasts are positively and significantly associated with short term market returns around the revisions. | Short term market returns around target price revisions and recommendation changes are even stronger than those for earnings forecast revisions. | Portfolios using information from all three types of revisions (earnings, target price, recommendations) show superior future performance (return drift) compared to portfolios using only one type of revision. | Citing papers note the study uses 'short event windows' and '1-month hedge return analysis' to measure these effects. | Citing papers confirm that each of the three signals conveys incremental information, but target price and recommendation revisions trigger stronger investor responses than earnings estimates.
for_the_app: The app should weight 'target price revisions' and 'recommendation changes' higher than 'earnings forecast revisions' when calculating the strength of a storyline, and flag cases where all three signals move in the same direction as high confidence events.

title: The Cross Section of Analyst Recommendations
authors: Sorin M. Sorescu, Avanidhar Subrahmanyam
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
key_findings: Long term returns following recommendation changes by highly experienced analysts outperform those of low experience analysts | Investors appear to overreact to dramatic upgrades of low ability analysts | Investors appear to underreact to small upgrades by high ability analysts | Results are consistent with behavioral theory that agents emphasize signal strength over analyst ability | The study analyzes both short term and long term price reactions
for_the_app: Filter analyst signals by experience level and magnitude of change to flag potential overreactions or underreactions in storylines

title: What Motivates Buy-Side Analysts to Share Recommendations Online?
authors: Steve Crawford, Wesley R. Gray, Bryan R. Johnson et al.
key_findings: Analyst recommendations posted on SumZero generate significant returns, and prices drift in the direction of the recommendation. | Long window returns are particularly strong for contrarian buy recommendations. | Long window returns are particularly strong for most sell recommendations. | Analysts who share ideas are more likely to change jobs, and this likelihood is positively related to peer ratings of their recommendations. | Analysts with strong incentives to build a reputation (those not from top 10 universities or employed at small funds) are significantly more likely to share recommendations.
for_the_app: The app should prioritize ingesting data from professional only networks (if accessible) or filter for 'contrarian' signals where buy side consensus differs from sell side consensus, as these show the strongest drift.

themes: From signal to trade; Skill or luck
title: Trading Is Hazardous to Your Wealth: The Common Stock Investment Performance of Individual Investors
authors: Brad M. Barber, Terrance Odean B
key_findings: Most active traders (top turnover quintile) earned a net annualized geometric mean return of 11.4%, while the market returned 17.9% (US, 1991-1996). | Average households earned a net annual return of 16.4%, underperforming the market's 17.9% by 1.5 percentage points annually. | Trading costs for the average household were high: a round trip trade over $1,000 cost 3% in commissions and 1% in bid ask spread. | Stocks bought by individual investors underperformed the market index by 47 basis points in the month following purchase, while stocks sold outperformed the index by 2 basis points. | High turnover households underperformed low turnover households by 80 basis points per month (9.6% per year) based on Fama French risk adjusted returns.
for_the_app: The app should include a 'Trading Cost & Turnover Warning' feature that calculates the estimated drag on returns based on a user's current turnover rate and explicitly shows the performance gap between their active trades and a passive benchmark.

themes: Events that make prices drift; Text and attention signals; Already priced in or not; From signal to trade
title: Market underreaction to open market share repurchases
authors: David L. Ikenberry, Josef Lakonishok, Theo Vermaelen
key_findings: The average market reaction on the announcement day was only 3.54 percent. | Using a buy and hold strategy, the average excess return (above the benchmark) over four years was 12.6 percent. | For 'value' stocks (high book to market ratio), the average excess return over four years was 45 percent. | For the bottom two quintiles of stocks (low book to market), the four year excess return was close to zero or slightly negative. | The positive drift mostly occurred between year 1 and year 3, with returns flattening out after year 3.
for_the_app: The app should flag companies announcing open market buybacks, specifically highlighting those with high book to market ratios, and set a 'storyline' alert to monitor the stock for a 3-4 year period to confirm the drift.

title: Share Issuance and Cross‐sectional Returns
authors: Jeffrey Pontiff, Artemiza Woodgate
key_findings: Post-1970, a one standard deviation increase in annual share issuance is associated with a 0.33% decrease in the monthly cross sectional return (slope -2.23, t stat -7.08). | Post-1970, a one standard deviation increase in 5-year share issuance is associated with a 0.23% decrease in the monthly cross sectional return (slope -0.71). | The predictive power of annual share issuance is statistically stronger than size, book to market, and momentum for all holding periods from 1 month to 3 years. | Pre-1970, annual share issuance was only statistically significant in 1 out of 40 specifications, and 5-year issuance was insignificant for most holding periods, suggesting the effect is specific to the post-1970 era. | The negative return effect persists even when removing firms that had seasoned equity offerings (SEOs), share repurchases, or stock mergers in the recent past, indicating a broader 'issuance effect'.
for_the_app: Add a 'Share Issuance Trend' metric to the app that flags companies with a significant increase in shares outstanding over the last 12 months or 5 years as a negative signal in the storyline, warning users that historical data suggests these stocks drift downward.

title: The Timing and Source of Long-Run Returns Following Repurchases
authors: Leonce L. Bargeron, Alice A. Bonaimé, Shawn Thomas
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
key_findings: Returns between program authorization and completion announcements are indistinguishable from 0. | Postcompletion period monthly alphas: 0.6682% (12 months) to 0.2849% (48 months). | Full sample monthly alphas: 0.2082% (12 months) to 0.1465% (48 months). | Subsequent repurchase authorizations drive returns: 0.2886% (12 months) to 0.4054% (48 months). | Firms with no subsequent events show insignificant returns after 24 months (0.0928% to -0.0406%).
for_the_app: Track completion dates and flag subsequent authorization or takeover news as confirmation signals.

title: Asymmetric Information, Financial Reporting, and Open-Market Share Repurchases
authors: Matthew T. Billett, Miaomiao Yu
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
key_findings: Opaque firms experience positive abnormal returns of twice the magnitude of those of transparent firms around the repurchase announcement. | Significant positive long run post announcement returns are documented for opaque firms. | No significant long run post announcement returns are documented for transparent firms. | Takeover activity and premiums rise with repurchase activity by opaque firms, which may explain some of the wealth effects. | Asymmetric information plays an important role in the wealth effects around open market share repurchases.
for_the_app: Add a 'Reporting Quality' filter to repurchase alerts: flag repurchase announcements from 'opaque' firms (high accrual variation) as high potential storylines for a drift strategy, while deprioritizing similar announcements from 'transparent' firms.

themes: Already priced in or not; From signal to trade
title: The long-run performance of stock returns following debt offerings
authors: D. Katherine Spiess, J. F. Affleck‐Graves
key_findings: Median seasoned debt issuing firms underperformed matched control firms by 18.7% over the post issue period (cited in 2000 paper). | Underperformance is more severe for smaller, younger, and NASDAQ listed firms, and for firms issuing speculative grade debt. | Underperformance is limited to periods with a high volume of debt issues; it does not appear in low volume periods. | Contrary to earlier studies, the market underreacts at the announcement, meaning the full negative impact is realized over the long run, not on day one. | Mean abnormal performance following debt issues is statistically insignificant, but the median performance is significantly negative, indicating a few large failures drive the result.
for_the_app: Add a 'Debt Issuance Watchlist' feature: when a company announces a debt offering, flag it as a 'slow burn sell' signal for a 3-5 year horizon, with higher severity scores if the firm is small, young, or has low credit ratings, and if the current month's total debt issuance volume is above the historical median.

title: Underperformance in long-run stock returns following seasoned equity offerings
authors: D. Katherine Spiess, J. F. Affleck‐Graves
key_findings: Firms making seasoned equity offerings substantially underperformed matched non issuing firms during 1975–1989. | The underperformance persists after controlling for trading system, offer size, firm age, and book to market ratio. | A citing paper (Predicting Secondary Equity Offerings Using Machine Learning, 2018) reports that issuing firms underperform by 31.2% over a five year horizon compared to matched firms. | Another citing paper (Bank regulation, financial crisis, and the announcement effects of seasoned equity offerings of US commercial banks, 2016) states equity issuers have 7% lower annual returns for the five years following each SEO. | The underperformance is similar to that previously documented for initial public offerings (IPOs).
for_the_app: Add a 'Seasoned Equity Offering' event trigger that flags a stock for a 'sell' or 'avoid' signal for the next 3–5 years, linking the news of the share sale to a predicted long term underperformance storyline.

themes: Events that make prices drift; Already priced in or not
title: An Examination of Long‐Term Abnormal Stock Returns and Operating Performance Following R&D Increases
authors: Allan C. Eberhart, William F. Maxwell, Akhtar R. Siddique
key_findings: Firms that unexpectedly increase R&D experience significantly positive abnormal stock returns for 5 years following the increase. | In the 1974 to 2001 period, value weighted abnormal returns were at least 25.2 basis points per month (approx. 3% per year) using the Carhart four factor model. | Equal weighted abnormal returns were higher, reaching up to 56 basis points per month (approx. 6.7% per year) in the 1974 to 2001 period. | High tech firms showed significantly higher abnormal returns than low tech firms, but low tech firms also showed positive (though smaller) abnormal returns. | Operating performance (profit margins) also improved significantly for these firms over the same 5-year period, confirming the investment was beneficial.
for_the_app: The app should scan annual or quarterly filings to detect when a company's R&D to sales ratio jumps significantly compared to its own history, flag these as 'long term growth story' candidates, and alert the user to hold for 3-5 years rather than selling on short term volatility.

title: The Long-Term Effects of Hedge Fund Activism
authors: Lucian A. Bebchuk, Alon P. Brav, Wei Jiang
key_findings: Value weighted buy and hold abnormal returns were positive at 2.58% over 36 months and 5.81% over 60 months, but these were not statistically significant. | Equal weighted buy and hold abnormal returns were 7.17% over 36 months but dropped to -0.29% over 60 months, with neither being statistically significant. | After an activist exits, equal weighted buy and hold abnormal returns were 19.06% over 36 months, and value weighted were 14.90%, but the paper notes these are not statistically significant in the main text despite positive alphas in regression tables. | Calendar time portfolio regressions show a monthly alpha of 0.37% (equal weight) and 0.31% (value weight) for the 3-year period after activist exit, which are statistically significant at 5% and 10% levels respectively. | The study finds no evidence of 'pump and dump' patterns where prices fall after the activist leaves; instead, returns remain positive or flat.
for_the_app: Add a 'Post Activist Exit' storyline tracker that flags companies where an activist has recently sold their stake, warning users that a 3-year drift might occur but emphasizing the long holding period required.

themes: Does it still work; Skill or luck
title: Anomalies and Market Efficiency
authors: G. William Schwert
key_findings: Size effect alpha 0.2% per month (1982-2002), t stat 0.67 (not reliable) | Value effect (B/M) alpha -0.2% per month (1994-2002), t stat -0.59 (not reliable) | Momentum effect alpha 1% per month (1990-2001), t stat 2.7 to 7.0 (reliable) | Weekend effect disappeared since 1978 (alpha not reliably different from zero) | IPO stocks yield below normal returns in 36 months following IPO (Ritter 1991)
for_the_app: Prioritize momentum and event driven underperformance (IPO); avoid static size/value rules as they likely disappeared

title: Estimating the Returns to Insider Trading: A Performance-Evaluation Perspective
authors: Leslie A. Jeng, Andrew Metrick, Richard Zeckhauser
venue: The Review of Economics and Statistics
key_findings: Insider purchase portfolios earn abnormal returns of roughly 40 basis points (0.40%) per month (about 4.8% per year) after adjusting for size, value, and momentum risks. | Insider sale portfolios show no significant abnormal returns; insiders do not profit from selling their stock after adjusting for risk factors. | Approximately one sixth of the abnormal return on insider purchases occurs within the first 5 trading days. | Approximately one third of the abnormal return on insider purchases occurs within the first month (21 trading days). | Three quarters of the abnormal return on insider purchases occurs within the first 6 months.
for_the_app: Feature: 'Insider Buy Confidence Score' that flags stocks where insiders have bought in the last 30 days, with a recommendation to hold for at least 6 months to capture the full drift; Warning: Do not trigger immediate buy/sell alerts based solely on the first 5 days of data.

title: Some Insider Sales Are Positive Signals
authors: James Scott, Peter Xu
key_findings: Large insider sales that accounted for large percentages of insiders' holdings predicted significantly negative future abnormal returns (US, 1987-2002). | Small insider sales that accounted for small percentages of shares owned did not predict poor performance and were correlated with significantly positive abnormal returns (US, 1987-2002). | The percentage of shares owned by insiders is useful for predicting future returns following insider purchases (US, 1987-2002). | Not all insider sales are the same; the study distinguishes between information driven sales and those driven by liquidity or risk reduction needs (US, 1987-2002).
for_the_app: Add a filter to the insider trading module that flags 'Large Sales' (e.g., >10% of insider's holdings) as a negative storyline trigger and 'Small Sales' as neutral or slightly positive, rather than treating all sales as bad news.

title: The Profits to Insider Trading: A Performance-Evaluation Perspective
authors: Leslie A. Jeng, Andrew Metrick, Richard Zeckhauser
key_findings: Insider purchase portfolios earned abnormal returns of about 40 basis points (0.40%) per month. | Approximately one sixth of the abnormal returns from purchases occurred within the first 5 days after the transaction. | Approximately one third of the abnormal returns from purchases occurred within the first month. | The insider sale portfolio did not earn abnormal returns. | Abnormal returns for insider trades in small firms were not significantly different from those in large firms.
for_the_app: Flag insider buying events as high confidence 'buy' storylines with a 1-month confirmation window, but ignore insider selling as a 'sell' signal.

title: Streaks in Earnings Surprises and the Cross-Section of Stock Returns
authors: Roger K. Loh, Mitch Warachka
key_findings: Stocks with positive earnings surprise streaks earned a four factor alpha of 0.322% per month, while those with negative streaks lost 0.280% per month, creating a spread of 0.603% per month. | Stocks with earnings surprise reversals showed negligible drift, with a spread of -0.001% per month. | When controlling for the magnitude of the surprise (SURP quintiles), the spread between positive and negative streaks was 0.838% per month. | A 'streak factor' constructed from these strategies explains 70% of the Post Earnings Announcement Drift (PEAD) anomaly. | Longer streaks (6-9 quarters) produced the highest spread of 1.186% per month, though predictability weakened for very long streaks (10+) in high uncertainty stocks.
for_the_app: Implement a 'Streak Tracker' feature that flags stocks with 2+ consecutive positive or negative earnings surprises and visualizes the expected 6-month drift direction, while warning users that this signal is weaker for highly volatile companies.

title: Double Surprise into Higher Future Returns
authors: Alina Lerman, Joshua Livnat, Richard R. Mendenhall
key_findings: Using analyst forecasts to measure earnings surprise results in a significantly larger post earnings announcement drift than using historical time series data alone. | Combining the two models (analyst forecasts and historical data) predicts future stock returns better than using either model alone. | A hedge portfolio based on the combined model (top quintile long, bottom quintile short) generates a 2% return (specific time period for this 2% is not reported in the citing text). | The study suggests that the magnitude of the drift depends heavily on how the earnings surprise is measured. | The combined approach captures information that neither model captures individually.
for_the_app: Implement a dual calculation engine for earnings surprises: one based on analyst consensus and one based on the company's own historical seasonal patterns, then flag stocks where both models agree on a large surprise.

themes: Events that make prices drift; Already priced in or not
title: Investor and (Value Line) Analyst Underreaction to Information about Future Earnings: The Corrective Role of Non‐Earnings‐Surprise Information
authors: Philip B. Shane, Peter A. Brous
key_findings: Approximately 18% of a quarter's unexpected earnings predictably reappears in the next quarter's forecast error (coefficient 0.178), indicating underreaction. | Using the standard return window (from after the last earnings announcement to the next), controlling for the current quarter's earnings surprise explains 23.68% of the drift. | Adding analyst forecast revisions (which reflect non earnings information) to the model increases the explained portion of the drift to 31.95% over the standard window. | When the return window is extended to match the analyst forecast revision period (from after the last earnings announcement to the next forecast revision date), the explained portion of the drift rises to 45.65%. | The market underreacts to information contained in analyst forecast revisions, with a drift coefficient of 0.0449 (t statistic 4.64) that remains significant even after controlling for earnings surprises.
for_the_app: The app should not just track the initial earnings surprise or forecast revision; it must actively monitor and link 'non earnings' events (like management commentary or interim sales data) that occur between announcements, as these are the triggers that correct the initial underreaction and drive the price drift.

title: Herding on Earnings News: The Role of Institutional Investors in Post–Earnings-Announcement Drift
