authors: Linda H. Chen, Wei Huang, George J. Jiang
key_findings: Institutional herding on earnings news does not eliminate market underreaction; PEAD remains significant. | PEAD is significant only in the subsample of stocks where institutions herd in the same direction as earnings surprises. | Institutional herding is positively related to next quarter earnings announcement returns. | Transient institutions (those with short holding periods) have a stronger tendency to herd on earnings information than non transient institutions. | When institutions herd on earnings surprises, trading represents a gradual process of incorporating information into prices; when they herd against surprises, price discovery slows down.
for_the_app: The app should flag earnings events where institutional flow data confirms the direction of the surprise, prioritizing these stories for 'drift' prediction over events where institutions trade against the news.

themes: Events that make prices drift; Already priced in or not
title: Do Individual Investors Drive Post-Earnings Announcement Drift? Direct Evidence from Personal Trades
authors: David A. Hirshleifer, James N. Myers, Linda A. Myers et al.
key_findings: Individuals are significant net buyers after both negative and positive earnings surprises. | Post announcement individual net buying is a significant negative predictor of stock returns over the next three quarters. | Individual investor trading fails to subsume any of the power of extreme earnings surprises to predict future abnormal returns. | PEAD is the tendency for stocks to earn high positive average abnormal returns in the three quarters subsequent to extreme positive earnings surprises. | Drift is concentrated around the three subsequent quarterly earnings announcements.
for_the_app: Include earnings surprise magnitude as a primary signal for drift prediction, but do not rely on individual investor flow data to explain the drift.

title: Topic tones of analyst reports and stock returns: A deep learning approach
authors: Hitoshi Iwasaki, Ying Chen, Jun Tu
key_findings: Incorporating detailed topic tones increased the adjusted R squared of predicting cumulative abnormal returns from 6.1% to 17.9%. | The 'Conclusion' topic (Topic 4) was the most informative single signal, with high vs. low tercile portfolios showing cumulative abnormal return differences ranging from 2.1% to 4.5% over a two day window. | The DNN based overall tone (Tone_DNN) had a coefficient of 0.012 in out of sample tests, significantly outperforming the Naïve Bayes overall tone (coefficient 0.002). | The predictive power of the DNN tone remained significant in the out of sample period (Jan June 2018), whereas the Naïve Bayes tone's significance attenuated in longer term growth predictions. | The signal is strongest when there is a contradiction between the analyst's numerical recommendation and the report's textual tone, or when there is high variance in tones among different analysts.
for_the_app: The app should prioritize extracting and scoring the 'Conclusion' section of analyst reports separately from the rest of the text, and flag reports where the conclusion tone contradicts the numerical rating.

themes: Events that make prices drift; Already priced in or not
title: The Role of Anchoring Bias in the Equity Market: Evidence from Analysts’ Earnings Forecasts and Stock Returns
authors: Ling Cen, Gilles Hilary, K.C. John Wei
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
key_findings: The hedge portfolio (long high CAF, short low CAF) generates an abnormal return (Alpha) of 0.76% per month, or 9.12% per year, with a t statistic of 4.75 (US, 1983-2005). | The effect is stronger for smaller stocks: the smallest size quintile shows a monthly Alpha difference of 1.42% (t stat 7.12), while the largest quintile shows 0.35% (t stat 2.37). | Cumulative raw returns for the hedge portfolio grow consistently for at least 12 months, with a mean 12-month return of 9.3% before costs (US, 1983-2005). | Estimated transaction costs for the 12-month hedge strategy average 3.7% (ranging from 1.2% for large stocks to 6.3% for small stocks), leaving a net profit. | The strategy captures 0.37% in abnormal returns over the three day window surrounding subsequent earnings announcements, accounting for roughly 16% of the total annual return.
for_the_app: The app should flag stocks where the consensus EPS forecast is significantly higher than the industry median as a 'positive drift' signal, and track these stocks for a 3-to-12-month horizon, updating the signal strength as the next earnings date approaches.

title: Investors’ Reactions to Analysts’ Forecast Revisions and Information Uncertainty
authors: Tony Chieh‐Tse Hou, Weifeng Hung, Simon S. Gao
key_findings: Stocks with upward earnings revisions experience positive returns, while stocks with downward revisions have negative returns (Australia, 1992-2009). | The price drift effect is more prominent in stocks with high information uncertainty. | Results remain robust after controlling for market conditions, seasonality, and risks. | Investors underweight public information like forecast revisions, causing a conservative bias and subsequent return continuation. | The study provides evidence supporting the violation of the efficient market hypothesis in this context.
for_the_app: When the app detects an analyst forecast revision, it should flag the stock as a potential 'drift' candidate and highlight the company's 'information uncertainty' level to estimate the strength of the expected move.

title: Dispersion in Analyst Forecasts and the Profitability of Earnings Momentum Strategies
authors: Andreas Dische
key_findings: A strategy buying stocks with the most upward revisions and shorting those with the most downward revisions (P1-P5) generated a cumulative abnormal return of 6.64% over a 6-month holding period (1987-2000). | For stocks with low dispersion in forecasts, the same momentum strategy (P1-P5) yielded a cumulative abnormal return of 1.74% per month, compared to only 0.80% per month for high dispersion stocks. | The incremental return gained by filtering for low dispersion was 0.95% per month (1.74% minus 0.80%), which was statistically significant with a t statistic of 3.31. | The bulk of the price drift occurred within the first six months after the revision, making this the optimal holding period. | The dispersion effect (outperformance of low disagreement stocks) was present in all sub periods but declined over time, dropping from 1.70% per month in 1987-1991 to an insignificant 0.51% per month in 1995-2000.
for_the_app: The app should weight news storylines by 'analyst consensus strength' (low dispersion) to prioritize signals; when a news event triggers a forecast revision, the app should flag the trade as high confidence only if the dispersion metric is low.

title: Local information advantage and stock returns: Evidence from social media
authors: Yuqin Huang, Feng Li, Tong Li et al.
key_findings: An equal weighted long short portfolio (buying the top 20% of stocks by ARP, selling the bottom 20%) earned an excess return of 0.24% per week (equivalent to 12.5% per annum) with a t statistic of 5.72. | The Carhart four factor alpha for the long short portfolio was 0.24% per week (t=5.55), and the Fama French five factor alpha was also 0.24% per week (t=5.35). | The predictive power is stronger for small firms (0.42% weekly excess return for the long short portfolio) compared to large firms (0.13% weekly excess return). | Abnormal relative postings from peer firms in the same city also predict returns, with a long short portfolio earning a Carhart four factor alpha of 0.19% per week (t=3.09). | The strategy generates positive returns across all 31 provincial administrative divisions in China, with higher profits in underdeveloped inland regions compared to developed coastal regions.
for_the_app: The app should include a feature that tracks the 'Local vs. Non Local' posting ratio for stocks in the user's watchlist and flags significant spikes as a potential short term bullish signal, especially for small cap stocks.

title: CEO turnover, sequential disclosure, and stock returns
authors: Jiayin Hu, Laura Xiaolei Liu, Chloe Yue Liu et al.
key_findings: Firms experience large negative stock returns during the first informational events after forced CEO turnovers. | Firms experience positive stock returns following those initial negative events. | The V shaped return pattern is driven by incoming CEOs strategically releasing bad news first to manage expectations, followed by favorable long term news. | The pattern is stronger when firms had higher pre turnover returns and higher valuation uncertainty. | Investors appear to make a costly mistake by failing to understand the incentives behind the managers' disclosure sequence.
for_the_app: The app should flag a 'forced CEO turnover' event and link it to a 'short term pessimism / long term optimism' storyline, warning users that the initial negative news might be a strategic low ball rather than a fundamental collapse.

title: Differences of Opinion and the Cross Section of Stock Returns
authors: Karl B. Diether, Christopher J. Malloy, Anna D. Scherbina
key_findings: A portfolio of stocks in the highest dispersion quintile underperforms the lowest dispersion quintile by 9.48 percent per year (US, 1983 to 2000). | The effect is strongest in small stocks, where the monthly return differential between low and high dispersion quintiles is 1.37% (t stat 5.98) over the full sample. | The return differential was significant in the 1983-1991 period (1.16% monthly for all stocks) but became statistically insignificant in the 1992-2000 period (0.41% monthly, t stat 0.86). | If the lag between forecast measurement and portfolio formation exceeds five months, the return difference is no longer statistically significant. | The negative relationship between dispersion and returns remains significant even after controlling for size, book to market, momentum, and turnover.
for_the_app: The app should flag stocks with high forecast dispersion as potential 'overvalued' candidates for a bearish storyline, but must warn users that this signal has historically decayed over time and may not be reliable in current markets.

title: Analysts’ Forecasts and Asset Pricing: A Survey
authors: S.P. Kothari, Eric C. So, Rodrigo S. Verdi
key_findings: Firms with upward consensus forecast revisions earn higher abnormal returns over the next 3–12 months than firms with downward revisions (Stickel 1991). | Prices drift in the direction of the revision, indicating an incomplete reaction (Figure 1). | Market prices fail to incorporate predictable biases in analyst forecasts (So 2013; Hughes, Liu & Su 2008 mixed). | Bias in analysts' forecasts of future earnings growth explains over half of the returns to contrarian investment strategies (Dechow & Sloan 1997). | Analysts' forecast dispersion is negatively associated with future returns (Diether, Malloy & Scherbina 2002).
for_the_app: Flag analyst forecast revisions as key events and track consensus changes to identify potential drift opportunities.

title: Regression Discontinuity and the Price Effects of Stock Market Indexing
authors: Yen‐Cheng Chang, Harrison G. Hong, Inessa Liskovich
key_findings: Stocks added to the Russell 2000 (crossing the 1000 rank cutoff) show a price jump of approximately 5.6% in June compared to those just missing the cutoff (t statistic 2.65). | Stocks deleted from the Russell 2000 (crossing the 1000 rank cutoff out of the index) show a price drop of approximately 5.4% in June compared to those just staying in (t statistic 3.0). | All price adjustments for the 1000 cutoff occur in the month immediately following the addition (June), with no significant effects detected in subsequent months (July, August, etc.). | For the lower 3000 cutoff, no significant immediate price effect was found in June for additions or deletions, likely due to data limitations and smaller sample sizes. | Following the 3000 cutoff, significant effects appeared later: excess returns of around 5.5% in July and September, but a large, insignificant reversal of -5.4% in August.
for_the_app: The app should flag stocks approaching the 1000 rank cutoff in late May as high probability short term movers, but must warn users that the event is a one time 'jump' in June with no follow through drift, making it a poor candidate for multi week storylines.

title: Economic Links and Cross-Predictability of Stock Returns: Evidence from Characteristic-Based “Styles”
authors: Sebastian Müller
key_findings: An equal weighted long short strategy based on the Style based Earnings Surprise Measure (SESM) generated 167 basis points per month. | A value weighted long short strategy based on SESM generated 101 basis points per month. | The return predictability is not explained by industry spillovers, traditional post earnings announcement drift, unconditional abnormal style returns, or risk. | Earnings surprises contain information about future returns of other firms that share similar characteristics ('similar style' firms). | Characteristics are useful to identify economic links between firms.
for_the_app: The app should link news events (earnings surprises) not just to direct supply chain partners, but also to a 'style peer' network of companies sharing key financial characteristics, and flag potential delayed reactions in those peers.

title: Geographic links and predictable returns
authors: Zuben Jin, Frank Weikai Li
key_findings: A long short strategy based on 1-month lagged geographic peer returns yields a value weighted monthly alpha of approximately 60 basis points (about 6.5% per year) after adjusting for standard risk factors. | The predictive power of geographic peer returns is significant for 1-month, 6-month, and 12-month lags, but the effect is strongest at the 1-month horizon and loses significance at 24 months. | The effect is stronger for firms with lower investor attention, higher trading costs (low liquidity, high bid ask spreads), and during periods of high market sentiment. | The return spread generated by this strategy is 166% higher on days surrounding earnings announcements, suggesting the profit comes from correcting investor underreaction to news rather than exposure to hidden risks. | Sell side analysts also underreact, as forecast revisions of geographic peers predict future forecast revisions of the focal firm, confirming a delay in information processing.
for_the_app: The app should build a 'Geographic Peer' graph using establishment data (or a proxy like local economic news) and trigger a 'buy' signal for a company when its geographically linked peers show strong positive returns, with a holding period of 1 month.

title: R&D Spillover and Predictable Returns
authors: Yi Jiang, Yiming Qian, Tong Yao
key_findings: Firms with low R&D growth but high exposure to industry R&D spillovers experience positive abnormal returns and improved operating performance. | The positive abnormal returns are concentrated in peer firms that receive low investor attention. | Exogenous industry shocks to demand or productivity do not explain the results. | The level of spillover exposure positively predicts subsequent stock returns (confirmed by citing papers summarizing the finding).
for_the_app: Feature: When the app detects a surge in R&D news for a specific company, it should automatically flag its industry peers (especially those with low analyst coverage) as potential 'follow on' buys for a multi week hold.

title: Regional Economic Activity and Stock Returns
authors: Esad Smajlbegovic
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
key_findings: Regional economic activity forecasts for company relevant states positively predict cross sectional stock returns. | Information from all relevant states is more important for predicting returns than information from the company's headquarters state alone. | These forecasts predict future firm performance and earnings surprises, indicating returns come from actual cash flow improvements. | Regional information takes longer to be incorporated into prices for 'difficult to arbitrage' stocks (e.g., small, illiquid, or hard to short stocks). | The study does not provide specific return percentages or holding periods in the available text.
for_the_app: Feature: Build a 'Regional Exposure Map' for every stock in the app. When a major economic event (e.g., a state level recession or boom) is detected in the news, the app should flag all companies with high text based exposure to that specific state as potential 'slow movers' to watch for a delayed price reaction.

title: Cross-predictability of stock returns: A study of the limited-information model
authors: Oliver Nilsson
key_findings: Previous month supplier industry returns cross predict stock- and industry level returns. | Previous month customer industry returns exhibit only weak cross predictability effects, particularly in the Eurozone. | Self financing trading strategies based on return cross predictability are able to generate mean annual abnormal returns of up to 9.7%. | In Eurozone, composite sort mean excess return over next month is –2.5% for high portfolio and –11.2% for low portfolio. | In EU27, supplier sort yields highest Sharpe ratio (0.46).
for_the_app: Add a feature to map supplier and customer industry news to target stocks and track their lagged returns to confirm storylines.

themes: Already priced in or not; Does it still work
title: A Flow-Based Explanation for Return Predictability
authors: Dong Lou
key_findings: The spread between top and bottom deciles of fund returns sorted by E[FIPP*] is 4.80% in the year following portfolio formation, followed by a -4.62% reversal in quarters six to twelve. | After controlling for E[FIPP], the predictive power of past stock returns (momentum) drops by 25% to 50% depending on the horizon and sample. | E[FIPP] accounts for more than 39% of stock price momentum in the post-1993 period, compared to only 16% in the pre-1993 period. | Among large cap stocks, E[FIPP] explains close to 50% of the momentum effect, rendering past stock returns statistically insignificant in the regression. | The spread between the four factor alpha of top and bottom deciles of mutual funds sorted by past performance is 1.17% in the subsequent quarter and 4.44% in the subsequent year, but this is fully explained by E[FIPP*].
for_the_app: The app should flag stocks where recent price gains are heavily correlated with inflows into mutual funds that hold them, warning the user that this 'momentum' may be artificial and prone to a reversal once flows stop.

title: Measuring Economic Policy Uncertainty*
authors: Scott Baker, Nicholas Bloom, Steven J. Davis
key_findings: A 1% increase in the EPU index is associated with a roughly 0.4% increase in firm level 30-day implied stock price volatility (US, 1996-2012). | For a firm with 50% of revenue from government purchases, a 1% rise in the EPU index leads to a 0.11% increase in stock volatility (US, 1996-2012). | Policy uncertainty innovations foreshadow declines in investment, output, and employment in the US and 12 other major economies over a 36-month horizon. | The EPU index rose by 131% from 2005-06 to 2011-12, which the authors estimate implies a 44% upward shift in average firm level implied volatility. | Firms in defense, healthcare, and finance sectors show specific sensitivity to policy uncertainty related to their respective industries (e.g., National Security EPU affects defense firms).
for_the_app: Implement a 'Policy Uncertainty Monitor' that tracks the EPU index and flags sectors (Defense, Healthcare, Finance) with high exposure to government spending, warning users of likely volatility spikes and potential investment slowdowns rather than specific buy/sell targets.

title: Can Mutual Fund “Stars” Really Pick Stocks? New Evidence from a Bootstrap Analysis
authors: Robert L. Kosowski, Allan Timmermann, Russ R. Wermers et al.
key_findings: Among funds with an alpha exceeding 7% per year over a five year period, about half have genuine stock picking talent sufficient to cover costs, while the other half are simply lucky. | About $1.2 billion per year in wealth is generated (net of expenses and trading costs) by skilled managers in the top tail of the distribution during the 1975-2002 period. | Truly underperforming funds in the bottom tail destroy a total of $1.5 billion per year by failing to compensate for fees and trading costs. | Standard t tests incorrectly suggest that superior performance is about twice as prevalent as it actually is; the bootstrap shows that only the top decile (10%) of funds exhibits significant skill net of costs. | Performance persistence is strong for growth oriented funds (top decile), but there is no evidence of skill among managers of income oriented funds.
for_the_app: The app should implement a 'luck adjusted' scoring system that penalizes short term outliers and requires a minimum track record (e.g., 3-5 years) to confirm a storyline, preventing users from chasing funds or stocks that performed well purely by chance.

title: Predictability of Supplier Returns After Large Customer Price Changes
key_findings: Supplier stock prices experience significantly positive cumulative abnormal returns for up to 20 days after a large positive customer price change. | Supplier stock prices experience significantly negative cumulative abnormal returns for up to 20 days after a large negative customer price change. | The majority of these returns occur within the first 5 days after the customer event. | This return predictability is not observed for the largest stocks. | This return predictability is not observed in the most recent time period of the sample.
for_the_app: The app should flag supplier links when a customer has a large move but must warn that the opportunity window is short (under 5 days) and likely limited to small cap stocks.

title: The Economics and Finance of Customer–Supplier Relationships
authors: Ling Cen, Sudipto Dasgupta
venue: Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Economics and Finance
key_findings: Changes in disruption risk (e.g., bankruptcy, takeovers) have spillover effects along the supply chain. | The correlation of economic fundamentals and co attention from market participants translates to return predictability. | Smaller supplier firms benefit from relationships with large customers through knowledge sharing and reputation, but face risks from customer concentration. | Information diffusion occurs along the supply chain, affecting the stock price informativeness of partners. | Customer bargaining power and relationship specificity influence financing decisions and trade credit provision.
for_the_app: The app should flag 'co attention' events where a news story about a major customer or supplier appears, predicting a delayed price move in the linked firm, and track the time lag between the initial shock and the partner's reaction.

title: Institutional ownership and return predictability across economically unrelated stocks
authors: George P. Gao, Pamela C. Moulton, David T. Ng
key_findings: Industry neutral long short hedge portfolio earns an average of over 19 basis points per week (1980-2010). | Pairs with significant common institutional owners show 19.8 basis points per week excess return difference. | Pairs without significant common institutional owners show less than five basis points per week. | Abnormal returns dissipate quickly and are reversed in the following weeks, leading to cumulative average weekly returns near zero. | Annual return is positive in all but three years of the sample period.
for_the_app: Flag when unrelated stocks share major institutional owners; predict short term moves but warn of reversal after one week.

title: Technology and return predictability
authors: Jiaping, Qiu, Wang, Jin, Zhou, Yi et al.
key_findings: Long short equity strategy sorted on lagged returns of technology linked firms yields monthly alphas of around 105 basis points. | A strategy of holding firms with relatively high returns in the previous month and shorting technologically similar firms with low returns generates abnormal returns in the subsequent month in excess of 12% a year. | The findings are robust to specifications and are not driven by industry predictability, customer supplier relationships, or strategic alliances. | Investors' limited attention to technological linkages contributes to the return predictability. | The market appears to under react to value relevant information about technologically similar firms, causing price impacts to manifest slowly over time.
for_the_app: Add a 'Tech Peer Momentum' feature that flags when a company's stock moves significantly while its top 5 patent cited peers have not, suggesting a delayed reaction story.

themes: News spreading to linked companies; Does it still work
title: Market Segmentation and Cross‐predictability of Returns
authors: Lior Menzly, Oguzhan Ozbas
key_findings: Supplier industry returns predict target industry returns: 7.3% annualized premium (High Low) | Customer industry returns predict target industry returns: 7.0% annualized premium (High Low) | Composite supplier and customer returns predict target industry returns: 8.7% annualized premium (High Low) | Cross predictability effects continue for up to 12 months (1/12 strategy yield 2.1% annualized) | Effect is weaker for stocks with high analyst coverage or institutional ownership
for_the_app: Add a supply chain link module to news feed that flags when a supplier or customer has a major price move

title: Return Predictability: Evidence from the US–China Supply Chain
authors: Rui Chen, Zhennan Gao, Xueyong Zhang
key_findings: Chinese customer returns can predict US supplier future returns at the firm level. | A long short portfolio strategy based on this relationship yields significant abnormal monthly returns of 2.179% (equal weighted portfolio) using the Fama French five factor model. | The results hold when using Fama MacBeth regression analysis. | The results hold when using propensity score matching on a matched sample. | The findings support the hypothesis that value relevant information diffuses gradually due to limited investor attention.
for_the_app: The app should flag US suppliers with significant Chinese customers and monitor news for those customers, setting an alert to trade the supplier stock a few days after the customer's news breaks.

title: Return Predictability along the Supply Chain: The International Evidence
authors: Husayn K. Shahrur, Ying L. Becker, Didier Rosenfeld
key_findings: Equity returns of customer industries led the returns of supplier industries across 22 developed countries. | The effect is consistent with a slow diffusion of value relevant information. | The strategy is fairly orthogonal to well known risk factors (based on citing papers).
for_the_app: Feature: When a news event impacts a 'customer' company, automatically flag its 'supplier' companies as potential lagging trades to watch for entry over the next few days.

title: Whose Attention Matters? Evidence From Return Predictability Between Economic Linked Firms
authors: Xinyao Zhou
key_findings: Return predictability between customer supplier firms does not exist when retail investors pay high abnormal attention. | Retail investor limited attention drives the return predictability between linked firms. | Institutional investor attention has no significant impact on return predictability after controlling for retail attention. | Return predictability varies based on the attention paid by local retail investors compared to nonlocal retail investors. | Local retail attention facilitates the incorporation of information into asset prices.
for_the_app: Add a 'Retail Attention Filter' to the storyline engine: if news triggers high retail attention on the source company, suppress the 'expected follow on move' signal for the linked company.

title: Detecting lead–lag relationships in stock returns and portfolio strategies
authors: Álvaro Cartea, Mihai Cucuringu, Qi Jin
key_findings: Using CRSP data from 1963–2022 on large cap stocks, the signature strategy achieves about 20% annualized returns. | The strategy achieves a Sharpe ratio above 3. | The signals discovered are only weakly explainable by previously discovered lead–lag relationships and Fama–French factors. | The method outperforms standard benchmarks and benchmarks from the literature. | The trading horizon tested is daily.
for_the_app: nothing

themes: Text and attention signals; Does it still work; From signal to trade; Skill or luck
title: Investor Sentiment and the Cross‐Section of Stock Returns
authors: Malcolm P. Baker, Jeffrey A. Wurgler
key_findings: When sentiment is low, subsequent returns are relatively high on smaller stocks, high volatility stocks, unprofitable stocks, non dividend paying stocks, extreme growth stocks, and distressed stocks | When sentiment is high, on the other hand, these patterns attenuate or fully reverse | When SENTIMENT is negative, returns average 2.33 percent per month for the bottom ME decile and 0.91 for the top decile | future returns on stocks with characteristics of either extreme growth or distress are negatively related to sentiment proxies | The cross sectional effects of book to market, external finance, and sales growth do not have a strong monotonic relationship with sentiment... U shaped conditional effects
for_the_app: Add a sentiment metric to weight expectations for small/growth stocks

title: Cointegration, information transmission, and the lead‐lag effect between industry portfolios and the stock market
authors: Victor Troster, José Penalva, Abderrahim Taamouti et al.
key_findings: 6 out of 30 industry cumulative returns are cointegrated with the market cumulative return at the 5% significance level | equilibrium error... has strong predictive power for future excess industry portfolio returns | Sharpe ratio of 74.6% compared with 46.5% for the OWP strategy based on the historical average returns over the period Aug.1995-Aug.2005 | Sharpe ratio of 51.4% for the period Sep.2005-Dec.2015, compared with 42.3% for the OWP strategy based on the historical average returns | effects of imposing transaction costs on the SP and OWP strategies are negligible
for_the_app: Feature to track industry vs market divergence (equilibrium error) as a signal for medium term rotation.

themes: From signal to trade; Skill or luck
title: Empirical Asset Pricing via Machine Learning
authors: Shihao Gu, Bryan Kelly, Dacheng Xiu
key_findings: Neural network model NN4 (long short decile spread, value weighted) earned an annualized return of 27.1% with a Sharpe ratio of 1.35. | Neural network model NN4 (long short decile spread, equal weighted) earned an annualized Sharpe ratio of 2.45. | Market timing the S&P 500 using NN3 forecasts achieved an annualized Sharpe ratio of 0.77, compared to 0.51 for a buy and hold strategy. | Tree based models (GBRT, RF) and linear models (OLS, PLS) generally underperformed neural networks in predicting stock level returns, though they still outperformed naive benchmarks. | Turnover for neural network strategies was consistently between 110% and 130% per month, significantly higher than size based strategies (22.9%) but lower than short term reversal strategies (172.6%).
for_the_app: The app should prioritize neural network style non linear models for generating signals, but must include a 'turnover cost' warning or simulation feature, as the high turnover (110-130%/month) is a critical constraint for retail execution.

title: Information, analysts, and stock return comovement
authors: Allaudeen Hameed, Randall Mørck, Jianfeng Shen et al.
key_findings: Stocks followed by few analysts co move significantly with firm specific fluctuations in the prices of highly followed stocks in the same industry. | The reverse is not observed: highly followed stocks do not co move with firm specific fluctuations in neglected stocks. | The spillover effect is more prominent in industries where analysts follow fewer stocks overall. | Earnings forecast revisions for highly followed stocks cause price changes in little followed stocks. | The reverse causality is not observed: forecast revisions for little followed stocks do not cause price changes in highly followed stocks.
for_the_app: The app should prioritize tracking analyst forecast revisions and firm specific news for 'prominent' stocks and automatically flag 'neglected' peers in the same industry as potential follow on trades, while warning that the delay length and profit size are not specified in this study.

title: Analyst Following Along the Supply Chain
authors: M.H. Franco Wong, Yuyan Guan, Zhang, Yue
key_findings: Analysts are more likely to cover a supplier's customer if that customer represents a larger share of the supplier's sales (18% vs 16% average sales share in the covered group). | Analysts who follow a supplier's customer provide more accurate earnings forecasts for the supplier than those who do not, with an effect size comparable to following industry peers. | Both types of analysts (those who follow the customer and those who don't) revise their forecasts in response to customer earnings news, but there is no evidence that those who follow the customer react more strongly or faster. | Analysts who follow the customer pair show a greater *improvement* in forecast accuracy after the customer's earnings announcement compared to those who do not, suggesting they use the news more efficiently. | The likelihood of an analyst adding a customer to their portfolio decreased by 42.1% after the implementation of Regulation FD (post-2000).
for_the_app: Feature: When a customer releases earnings, flag the supplier as a 'high confidence' event for the app's storyline engine, but warn that the market reaction may be immediate rather than delayed, requiring fast execution or a focus on forecast revision quality rather than price drift.

title: Analyst Disagreement, Mispricing, and Liquidity*
authors: Ronnie Sadka, Anna D. Scherbina
key_findings: High disagreement stocks underperform with negative risk adjusted returns (alphas) of -0.98% per month for the highest disagreement quintile (equal weighted, 1-month holding) before costs. | Trading costs (effective spread) increase with analyst disagreement, reaching 0.68% per month for the highest disagreement quintile. | After accounting for transaction costs, the net alpha for the highest disagreement portfolio is -0.33% per month (value weighted), which is not statistically significant. | Price convergence to fundamentals for high disagreement stocks occurs within 6 months of the disagreement being detected. | Illiquid high disagreement stocks show larger pre cost underperformance but also higher trading costs, making the strategy less profitable after costs compared to liquid high disagreement stocks.
for_the_app: The app should flag high analyst disagreement as a potential 'overpriced' signal but must overlay a 'liquidity check' to warn users if the trading costs (spread) are too high to capture the expected return, effectively filtering out the most illiquid candidates.

title: Evidence on the Information Content of Text in Analyst Reports
authors: Allen Huang, Amy Y. Zang, Rong Zheng
key_findings: A one standard deviation increase in textual opinion (more positive text) increases the two day abnormal return by 41 basis points (0.41%). | For firms with a 'SELL' recommendation, if the text is in the top three quintiles (positive), the market reaction is positive, meaning investors ignore the 'SELL' label and follow the text. | For firms with a 'BUY' recommendation, if the text is in the bottom two quintiles (negative), the market reaction is negative, meaning investors ignore the 'BUY' label and follow the text. | The difference in returns between the most positive and most negative text within a 'BUY' recommendation group is 1.77% over two days. | Textual opinion is more useful (triggers stronger reactions) when the report discusses non financial topics, is written assertively/concisely, or when the quantitative signals (like the recommendation) are perceived as less valid.
for_the_app: Feature: When an analyst report is released, the app must parse the full text to generate a 'Text Sentiment Score' and flag cases where this score contradicts the 'Buy/Sell' rating, as these are high probability trade setups.

title: Complicated firms
authors: Lauren Cohen, Dong Lou
venue: London School of Economics and Political Science Research Online (London School of Economics and Political Science)
key_findings: value weighted returns of 95 basis points (t=3.18) in the following month | equal weighted portfolio, the returns are 118 basis points per month (t=5.51) | For a $10 million portfolio... net returns to our strategy are roughly 84 basis points per month | At a size of $50 million... value weighted net returns drop... to 49 basis points per month | Extending the horizon to 12 (or 24) months produces largely the same results... no sign of any return reversal
for_the_app: Flag conglomerates that haven't moved after peer news

title: Does Foreign Information Predict the Returns of Multinational Firms Worldwide?
authors: Christian Finke, Florian Weigert
key_findings: Global long short portfolio yields an average monthly return spread of 0.85% (10.20% per annum) based on value weighted sorts. | The effect is significant across regions: Asia Pacific (0.80% monthly), North America (0.82% monthly), but not statistically significant in Europe for value weighted sorts (0.38% monthly). | After adjusting for risk using the global Carhart four factor model, the strategy earns a statistically significant alpha of 0.89% per month (10.68% per annum). | The effect is stronger during economic recessions, with the return spread being 0.46% per month higher in downturns than in expansions. | The effect is robust to controls for firm size, book to market, momentum, turnover, and idiosyncratic volatility, and is not driven by exchange rate effects.
for_the_app: Feature: Calculate a 'Foreign Shock Score' for each stock by weighting its foreign sales regions by the recent industry performance in those specific countries; alert users when a stock's score diverges significantly from its peers, suggesting a delayed price reaction.

title: Cosearch Attention and Stock Return Predictability in Supply Chains
authors: Ashish Agarwal, Alvin Chung Man Leung, Prabhudev Konana et al.
key_findings: Cosearch intensity across supply chain partners determines cross return predictability: low intensity (low attention) leads to higher predictability, while high intensity leads to lower predictability. | A simulated trading strategy using returns of supply chain partners with low co search attention generates a significant and positive return above market returns. | The strategy using low co attention pairs performs better than a strategy using returns of all supply chain partners regardless of attention levels. | When investors pay less attention to a focal stock's supply chain partners, lagged partner returns can predict the focal stock's future return. | When investors' co attention to focal and partner stocks is high, the predictability of returns is low.
for_the_app: Implement a 'Co Attention Filter' that ranks supply chain links by search volume correlation; only trigger alerts for price movements in partners when the co search intensity with the focal stock is below a specific threshold.

title: The spillover effects of supply chain corruption practices on stock returns
authors: Geng Wang, Yangchun Xiong, Cheng Yang et al.
venue: International Journal of Operations & Production Management
key_findings: SCCPs have negative effects on the stock returns of corrupt firms' bystander supply chain partners. | Negative effects are more pronounced for bystander buyers than for bystander suppliers. | SCCPs do not have a significant impact on the stock returns of corrupt firms' industry peers. | SCCPs are more likely to affect the stock returns of domestic rather than overseas bystander supply chain partners.
for_the_app: When a corruption event is detected for a company, automatically flag its direct buyers as high risk for a short term drop, while deprioritizing its industry peers and overseas partners in the alert system.

title: Do Countries Matter for Information Diffusion in Financial Markets? Evidence from Global Supply-Chain Networks.
authors: Craig Doidge, Ling Cen, Christopher M. Schiller
key_findings: Information diffusion from international customers to US suppliers is not uniform; it is significantly slower when the customer's country has lower market operational efficiency (high liquidity frictions, high zero return days). | Market operational efficiency is the predominant factor explaining cross country variation in diffusion speed, outweighing market capacity, legal risks, and political stability. | More than 75% of the information diffusion from customers to suppliers occurs within the first 4 weeks (28 trading days). | In countries with higher market liquidity (lower Amihud illiquidity), information diffuses faster, with the coefficient on Amihud liquidity being positive and significant at the 1% level. | When short selling restrictions were lifted in Japan (2008), South Korea (2010), and Taiwan (2010), the speed of information diffusion increased significantly, confirming that regulatory frictions slow down price adjustment.
for_the_app: The app should calculate a 'Country Efficiency Score' for every international customer in a supply chain; when news hits a customer in a low efficiency country, the app should flag the linked US supplier as a 'slow diffusion' candidate and suggest a longer holding period (e.g., 10-20 days) to capture the delayed reaction.

title: Stock Price Responses to Firm-Level News in Supply Chain Networks
authors: Hiroyasu Inoue, Yasuyuki Todo
key_findings: Own firm stock prices are higher by an additional 0.6% after positive news disclosure (1-day window, global sample). | Supplier stock price reaction to client news is 0.033 (coefficient difference) at 1 day, dropping to 0.004 by 5 days (global sample). | Client stock price reaction to supplier news is 0.028 (coefficient difference) at 1 day (global sample). | For Japanese firms, post disclosure associations for suppliers and clients are smaller than pre disclosure associations (unlike global pattern). | Significant price associations exist before news disclosure for both own firms and supply chain partners.
for_the_app: Feature: Automatically link news to supply chain partners and flag potential price moves within 1–5 days of the event.

title: When suppliers engage in sustainable supply chain management: how does the stock market react?
authors: Jason X. Wang, Tsan‐Ming Choi, Lincoln Christopher Wood et al.
venue: International Journal of Operations & Production Management
key_findings: Mean CAR (-1,1) is -0.38% (significant at 1% level) | Median CAR (-1,1) is -0.32% (significant at 1% level) | 55% of suppliers had negative CAR | 1,977 supplier observations from 1990 to 2016 | High buyer dependence marginally reduces negative reaction (β=0.0027, p<0.1)
for_the_app: Flag supplier stocks when buyers announce SSCM mandates, but warn that the price drop often happens immediately

title: Intra-industry information transfers associated with earnings releases
authors: GEORGE J. FOSTER
key_findings: Earnings announcements by one firm significantly impact the stock prices of non announcing industry peers. | The information transfer is primarily positive, meaning good news for one firm often leads to positive returns for peers, though negative transfers can occur due to competition. | The transfer is linked to the same 4-Digit SIC industry classification, suggesting peers share similar economic shocks. | Investors' assessment of a firm's value is impacted by information in the financial reports of its peer firms. | The magnitude of the stock price reaction is generally greater for early announcing firms than for late announcing firms.
for_the_app: Feature: 'Peer Earnings Watch' - When a bellwether company in a sector announces earnings, automatically flag all other companies in the same 4-digit SIC code for potential immediate price movement.

title: Intra-industry information transfers associated with management earnings forecasts
authors: Stephen P. Baginski
venue: Illinois Digital Environment for Access to Learning and Scholarship (University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign)
key_findings: Empirical tests failed to reject the null hypothesis that information transfers exist between disclosing and non disclosing firms in the same industry. | At the 4-digit SIC code level, the magnitude of information transfer is positively related to the sign and magnitude of changes in earnings expectations. | The magnitude of information transfer is inversely related to the relative diversification of industry co members. | Market share variability was not supported as a determinant of the magnitude of information transfers.
for_the_app: nothing

themes: News spreading to linked companies; Already priced in or not
title: Overreaction to Intra‐industry Information Transfers?
authors: Jacob K. Kandathil Thomas, Frank Zhang
key_findings: The hedge portfolio (buying stocks with the lowest initial reaction to peer news and shorting those with the highest) earned an average return of 1.16% over the late announcer's 3-day earnings announcement window (1973–2005). | The negative correlation between the initial reaction to peer news and the subsequent own earnings reaction is statistically significant (t statistic 4.25), indicating systematic overreaction. | The overreaction effect is stronger in later periods: the hedge return was 0.48% in the 1970s (insignificant) but rose to 1.55% in the 1990s and 1.52% in the 2000s. | Even after controlling for bid ask bounce (using midpoint prices), the hedge return remains significant at 1.35% (t=6.56), suggesting the effect is not purely a microstructure artifact. | The effect exists across all firm sizes, with the largest firms (Size 5) still generating a significant hedge return of 0.54%.
for_the_app: Add a 'Correction Risk' metric: when a stock moves significantly due to a peer's news, flag it as a potential overreaction that may reverse upon the stock's own earnings release, advising the user to wait for the actual report before acting on the peer news.

title: Industry classification and the efficiency of intra-industry information transfers
authors: Dennis Y. Chung, Karel Hrazdil, Kim Trottier
key_findings: Confirmed the original overreaction anomaly exists when using the older SIC industry classification system. | The overreaction anomaly disappears during recent years (period characterized by markedly higher trading activity) when using the GICS classification system. | The study demonstrates that the anomaly is sensitive to the industry classification method used (SIC vs GICS).
for_the_app: When building storylines linking companies by industry, use GICS (or newer) classifications rather than SIC, and flag that 'overreaction' patterns in these groups are likely no longer profitable in the current market.

title: Explain Overreaction in Intra-Industry Information Transfer
authors: Yue Hu
key_findings: Evidence supports that overreaction decreases as the industry has more firms (H1). | Evidence supports that overreaction decreases as the early announcer's earnings are more informative about industry wide earnings (H3). | Evidence contradicts the hypothesis that overreaction decreases as more firms announce before the early announcer; instead, the magnitude of overreaction increases (opposite to H2). | The unexpected increase in overreaction is attributed to investors' slow reaction to early announcers' earnings announcements.
for_the_app: Feature: When an early announcer in a sector releases earnings, flag linked 'late announcers' as potential candidates for a delayed reaction trade, specifically warning that the reaction might be stronger if fewer firms have announced so far (contrary to simple logic).

title: The Role of Analysts in Intra-Industry Information Transfer
authors: Gilles Hilary, Rui Shen
key_findings: Analysts with experience covering the firm that issued a management forecast reduce their forecasting error for peer firms by 12.92% for every one standard deviation increase in experience (US, 1996-2006). | The mean time for analysts to revise forecasts after a management forecast is 10.5 days, with a median of 8 days (US, 1996-2006). | Investors react more strongly to forecast revisions made by analysts with MF experience; the 3-day size adjusted abnormal return (CAR) around the revision is 0.360% higher for MF analysts than non MF analysts (US, 1996-2006). | The benefit of MF experience is stronger when the peer firm is opaque (less transparent) than when it is transparent (US, 1996-2006). | The market reaction to revisions by experienced analysts is significantly stronger in firms with high institutional ownership compared to those with low institutional ownership (US, 1996-2006).
for_the_app: The app should flag 'linked' companies when a peer issues a forecast and specifically monitor for earnings forecast revisions from analysts who cover both the issuer and the peer, treating these revisions as high confidence confirmation events for the storyline.

title: Dividend Changes, Abnormal Returns, and Intra-Industry Firm Valuations
authors: Michael A. Firth
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
key_findings: Some small positive information transfer exists: good news for one firm leads to price increases for rivals. | The size of the transfer depends on the 'dividend surprise' (how unexpected the change was), the recent dividend history of the peers, and how closely their stock returns move together. | Dividend decreases or omissions have a 'contagion effect,' causing negative returns for rivals (cited as -0.60% abnormal return for rivals in one citing paper). | Cross border transfers (US to UK) exist but are weaker than domestic transfers; US announcers have a larger impact on UK peers than vice versa. | Analysts revise earnings estimates for peer firms after the dividend news, which drives the price changes.
for_the_app: Feature: When a dividend change is detected, automatically flag industry peers (based on SIC code or return correlation) and check if the change is a 'surprise' (vs. previous dividend) to predict short term moves in those peers.

title: Product Market Competition and Overreaction to Intra-Industry Information Transfers
authors: Norio Kitagawa
key_findings: Investors overreact more to information transfers in industries with higher product market competition. | In competitive environments, investors overreact more to negative information transfers than to positive ones. | Overreaction is less observed when the announcing firm is a 'bellwether' (a leading indicator for the industry) or when the industry has high sales growth. | The results are robust when using an alternative measure of product market competition. | The study finds no specific return percentages or holding periods, only the existence and direction of overreaction.
for_the_app: Add a 'Competition Intensity' filter to the news linkage engine: when linking news from a peer firm, weight the expected price impact higher if the target firm operates in a highly competitive sector, and flag potential overreactions to negative news in these sectors for reversal monitoring.

title: Business Strategy and Intra-Industry Information Transfers
authors: Peng Wei Guo
key_findings: coefficient of 0.026 on CAR (T stat. = 37.713) | coefficient on CAR x STRATEGY is -0.001 (T stat. = -2.074) | coefficient on CAR x STRATEGYPEER is -0.001 (T stat. = -1.925) | Results unchanged using 4-digit NAICS codes | General finding is positive information transfers between industry peers
for_the_app: Classify companies as prospectors or defenders to adjust the weight of news signals from industry peers

title: The Influence of Analysts, Institutional Investors, and Insiders on the Incorporation of Market, Industry, and Firm-Specific Information into Stock Prices
authors: Joseph D. Piotroski, Darren T. Roulstone
key_findings: Analyst forecasting activity is positively associated with stock return synchronicity, meaning analysts help spread industry level information across companies. | Insider trades are inversely related to stock return synchronicity, meaning insiders convey firm specific information that makes a stock move independently of the market. | Insider and institutional trading accelerate the incorporation of the firm specific component of future earnings news into prices. | Analyst forecasting activity accelerates the incorporation of both the industry and firm specific components of future earnings news. | The type of information conveyed depends on the participant's relative information advantage: analysts focus on industry/market, while insiders focus on the specific firm.
for_the_app: Use this logic to weight news sources: prioritize analyst reports for identifying industry wide storylines that will affect multiple linked companies, and prioritize insider filings for identifying unique, company specific events that may not yet be priced in.

title: Positive and Negative Information Transfers from Management Forecasts
authors: Yongtae Kim, Michael J. Lacina, Myung Seok Park
key_findings: negative (positive) information transfers between forecasting firms and non forecasting rival (non rival) firms | negative intra industry information transfers from revenue forecasts are more evident than those from earnings forecasts | information transfers account for less than two percent of the three day abnormal returns of non forecasters | median value of non forecasting firms' abnormal returns is -0.13% while the corresponding median value for forecasting firms is 2.88% (when good news) | coefficient sum on UMRF... is negative and significant (t value = -2.01) for bad news revenue forecasts to rivals
for_the_app: Flag rival relationships when bad revenue news hits a peer to predict competitor weakness

title: Intra‐Industry Reactions to Stock Split Announcements
authors: Oranee Tawatnuntachai, Ranjan D’Mello
key_findings: Non splitting firms experienced a mean cumulative abnormal return of 0.34% over the 5-day window (-2 to +2 days) around the split announcement, which was statistically significant at the 10% level. | Splitting firms themselves saw a significant average cumulative abnormal return of 3.82% over the same 5-day window. | Non splitting firms with higher book to market (B/M) ratios earned significantly higher abnormal returns (coefficient 2.337 to 2.400, significant at 5% level), suggesting undervalued firms benefit more. | Non splitting firms with higher return variance (proxy for asymmetric information) earned significantly higher abnormal returns (coefficient 0.043 to 0.048, significant at 5% level). | Non splitting firms in industries with lower concentration (lower HHI) earned higher abnormal returns, as the HHI coefficient was negative and significant (-0.556 to -0.769).
for_the_app: The app should flag non splitting peers when a split is announced, but must filter for high book to market, high return variance, and low industry concentration to find the strongest potential signals; it should warn users that the raw return is small and short lived.

title: The Dark Side of Low Financial Reporting Frequency: Investors' Reliance on Alternative Sources of Earnings News and Excessive Information Spillovers
authors: Salman Arif, Emmanuel T. De George
key_findings: Returns of semi annual earnings announcers are almost twice as sensitive to the earnings announcement returns of U.S. industry bellwether peers for non reporting periods compared to reporting periods. | Heightened spillovers from peer news are followed by return reversals when investors finally observe own firm earnings at the subsequent semi annual earnings announcement. | Price volatility and trading volume are elevated around earnings announcements for non reporting periods, consistent with investor overconfidence.
for_the_app: Flag stocks with low reporting frequency (e.g., semi annual) as high risk for 'false storylines' when peer news drives their price; the app should predict a reversal event triggered by the company's own upcoming earnings date.

title: Spillover Effects in Disclosure-Related Securities Litigation
authors: Dain C. Donelson, Rachel W. Flam, Christopher G. Yust
key_findings: Peer firms experienced negative and significant abnormal returns of -0.33% in the 9 trading days before the lawsuit filing ([-10, -2]), which annualizes to approximately -9%. | Abnormal returns remained negative and significant for up to 60 days after the filing ([+11, +60]). | For cases that eventually settle, peers saw a -0.60% return before filing and a -4.21% return after filing, collectively annualizing to approximately -16%. | There was no significant negative return for peers when the focal firm's lawsuit was dismissed. | The negative reaction is concentrated in growth firms and firms in industries with low litigation frequency.
for_the_app: The app should flag 'industry litigation risk' as a storyline trigger: when a lawsuit is filed against a high risk firm, automatically check if the case is likely to settle (based on early signals) and alert users to potential downside in peer stocks over the next 60 days.

title: Law enforcement spillover effects in the financial sector
authors: Shivam Agarwal, Cal B. Muckley
key_findings: Recipient firms suffered a -1.58% abnormal return over the 3-day window (-1, 1) around the announcement (2009–2019). | Peer firms matched by 4-digit SIC code suffered a -0.46% abnormal return over the 3-day window (-1, 1) (2009–2019). | Peer firms matched by Propensity Score (similar risk characteristics) suffered a -1.03% abnormal return over the 3-day window (-1, 1) (2009–2019). | No significant price reaction was found for peer firms matched only by broad industry codes (1-digit or 2-digit SIC), indicating the effect is specific to close peers. | The price drop for peers occurred immediately around the announcement (Day 0 to Day 1) with no significant reversal or further drift observed in the extended window (-10, 10).
for_the_app: Feature: 'Peer Risk Alert'. When a regulatory sanction is announced for a bank, the app should instantly flag its 4-digit SIC peers and Propensity Score matches as high risk for immediate short term downside, rather than suggesting a multi week hold.

title: Disclosure spillover from going‐private activity
authors: Lisa A. Hinson, Jeffery Piao
key_findings: After a peer goes private, analyst forecast errors for remaining public firms increase by 5.44% and forecast dispersion increases by 7.02% within a 6-month window. | Stock liquidity for peer firms declines immediately after a going private event, with illiquidity increasing significantly (coefficient 0.152, p < 0.01) for the average firm. | In response to the lost information, peer firms increase their own disclosure quality, adding 1 to 3 financial statement line items and increasing MD&A text modifications by 18.6% for a one standard deviation increase in going private activity. | The negative impact on peers is stronger when the firm that went private previously had high quality disclosure (interaction coefficient 0.035 for forecast errors, p < 0.01). | Peers with lower competitive concerns are more likely to increase their disclosure quality after a rival goes private, while firms with high competitive pressure do not significantly change their disclosure.
for_the_app: Add a 'Peer Information Shock' alert: when a major industry player goes private, flag its public competitors as having temporarily degraded information quality and potential upcoming increases in their own disclosure filings.

title: Spreading the Misery? Sources of Bankruptcy Spillover in the Supply Chain
authors: Madhuparna Kolay, Michael L. Lemmon, Elizabeth Tashjian
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
key_findings: The CAR for the 5-day distress announcement period is a statistically significant −12.3% for economically distressed firms | Suppliers to firms with reorganization probabilities below 40% lose an average of 19% of their market cap at our announcement date | The overall customer sample has significant negative returns (–1.4%, significant at the 1% level) around the distress announcement date | The high probability group has a return of –0.8% (not statistically significant) | Suppliers experience increased selling, general, and administrative (SG&A) expenses and lower margins in the year following the bankruptcy
for_the_app: Flag supply chain partners of distressed firms and show reorg probability

title: Enforcement Waves and Spillovers
authors: Hae Mi Choi, Jonathan M. Karpoff, Xiaoxia Lou et al.
key_findings: The first firm targeted in an enforcement wave sees an average abnormal stock return of -19.3% on the day misconduct is revealed. | Industry peers of the first target experience an immediate average abnormal return of -0.30% on the same day. | Peer firms of targets revealed later in a wave experience smaller immediate drops, but cumulative spillover losses over the preceding year are significant (e.g., -3.33% over 126 days for uncaught peers in early waves). | Late wave targets experience 64% of their total share price loss via information spillovers from earlier peers before their own misconduct is revealed, compared to only 36% for early wave targets. | There is no price reversal for uncaught peer firms; their cumulative abnormal return remains negative (-0.68%) over the 126 days following the initial peer revelation.
for_the_app: The app should flag an industry as 'high risk' for fraud contagion when the first enforcement action occurs, then track the cumulative decline of peer stocks over the next 6-12 months as a confirmation of the 'wave' storyline, warning users that prices may drift down slowly rather than crash instantly.

title: News-Induced Dynamic Networks for Market Signaling: Understanding the Impact of News on Firm Equity Value
authors: Kun Chen, Xin Li, Peng Luo et al.
key_findings: Extracted dynamic networks provide additional value in predicting firm equity value over current adopted supply chain and coindustry networks. | Predictive value holds after controlling for market activities and traditional news indicators like volume, sentiment, and co mentions. | Cobenefit/counter benefit networks provide good buy and sell signals. | These networks enrich known indicators and support more complex trading strategies. | The analysis helps understand economic structure and assess firm/industry changes in a timelier fashion.
for_the_app: Implement a feature that dynamically maps 'cobenefit' and 'counter benefit' links between companies based on real time news events to flag potential delayed price movements in linked firms.

title: The Effect of Innovation Similarity on Asset Prices: Evidence from Patents’ Big Data
authors: Ron Bekkerman, Eliezer M. Fich, Natalya V. Khimich
venue: The Review of Asset Pricing Studies
key_findings: Buying shares of technological peers that had high returns in the previous month and shorting those with low returns yields a 1.29% monthly return. | Investors do not immediately and fully incorporate information about technological connectedness into prices. | Return predictability is stronger when patents are complex or when firms disclose less technology information. | Return predictability is weaker when firms have better information transparency. | The text based return predictability remains active even when simpler, class based technological links do not show the same effect.
for_the_app: The app should calculate a 'tech similarity score' between companies and flag a stock for a potential buy if a highly similar peer had a strong positive return in the last 20 trading days, while warning that this signal weakens if the target company is very transparent.

title: Language Tone in Financial News Media and the Cross-Section of Stock Returns
authors: Mikael Bask, Lars Forsberg, Andreas Östling
key_findings: A strategy that longs stocks with the most negative news and shorts stocks with the least negative news is not profitable. | The sentiment factor derived from news tone is not a priced risk factor in the cross section of stock returns. | The sentiment factor is statistically significant for two thirds of the individual stocks when added to well known factor models.
for_the_app: Do not use news tone negativity as a standalone trigger to buy or sell; the app should treat tone as a context variable rather than a direct signal.

themes: Text and attention signals; Already priced in or not
title: Media Content and Stock Returns: The Predictive Power of Press
authors: Nicky J. Ferguson, Dennis Philip, Herbert Y. T. Lam et al.
key_findings: Both tone and volume of news media content significantly predict next period abnormal returns. | The impact of news volume is more pronounced than the impact of tone. | The predictive power of tone is stronger among lower visibility (smaller) firms. | High media coverage creates an attention grabbing effect, mainly seen among larger firms. | A simple news based trading strategy produced statistically significant risk adjusted returns of 14.2 to 19 basis points per period in the 2003–2010 sample.
for_the_app: Prioritize 'news volume' spikes over 'tone' when generating alerts, and weight signals from low visibility firms more heavily for tone based predictions.

title: Social Media Sentiment in International Stock Returns and Trading Activity
authors: Selin Düz Tan, Oktay Taş
key_findings: Twitter activity and sentiment are associated with trading volume and returns, and predict subsequent day trading volume. | Firm specific Twitter sentiment contains information for predicting stock returns, remaining significant after controlling for news sentiment. | The positive tone of Twitter sentiment is more pronounced in small and emerging market firms. | Small firms are hard to value and emerging market firms contain high information asymmetry, making them more sensitive to social media signals. | From a practical perspective, investors could potentially use social media sentiment in trading strategies.
for_the_app: Integrate a 'Social Sentiment Strength' metric that weights positive sentiment higher for small cap and emerging market stocks, and flag these as high volatility storyline triggers.

title: Media sentiment and stock returns
authors: Mikael Bask, Lars Forsberg, Andreas Östling
venue: The Quarterly Review of Economics and Finance
key_findings: Negative media sentiment is a priced factor in five of nine asset pricing models | Sentiment factor yearly returns were 0.89% (2005–09), 6.30% (2010–18), and 4.40% (2005–18) | Factor spanning regressions confirm the sentiment factor contributes to explaining mean excess returns in 2005–09 and 2005–18 (p=0.05) | Cross sectional regression shows a negative premium for the sentiment factor (e.g., -0.0535 in 2005–09) | Jensen’s alpha for the sentiment factor is positive in factor spanning regressions for 2005–09 and 2005–18
for_the_app: Track negative tone in news for large cap stocks and flag when it deviates from the norm, but do not rely on it alone for timing

title: Media abnormal tone, earnings announcements, and the stock market
authors: David Ardia, Keven Bluteau, Kris Boudt
key_findings: An increase of one standard deviation in RCAT during the event window (-1 to +1 days) is associated with an abnormal return of 0.84% at the time of the event. | An increase of one standard deviation in RCAT is associated with an abnormal return of -0.36% over the next 19 trading days (days 2 to 20), indicating a partial price reversal. | The immediate positive reaction and subsequent reversal are stronger for negative earnings surprises than for positive ones. | Both newswires (professional audience) and newspapers/web publications (retail audience) show similar patterns of immediate reaction and reversal, though the reversal is slightly larger for newswires. | Higher absolute RCAT values correlate with higher abnormal trading volume, supporting the theory that investors overreact to the media's incremental information.
for_the_app: The app should flag 'overreaction risk' when RCAT is extreme, suggesting a potential reversal trade rather than a trend following trade, and highlight the difference between the initial tone and the underlying earnings facts.

title: Media Coverage and the Stock Market Valuation of TARP Participating Banks‡
authors: Jeffrey Ng, Florin P. Vasvari, Regina Wittenberg Moerman
key_findings: Negative media sentiment decreased valuation of CPP banks relative to non CPP banks. | Difference in size adjusted returns between CPP and non CPP banks around negative article dates was -0.393%. | Within CPP banks, size adjusted returns on negative sentiment days were -0.345% lower than on non negative days. | Effect was stronger for larger banks. | CPP banks had 0.005 higher ROA and 0.018 lower non performing loan ratio than non CPP banks.
for_the_app: Flag when news tone turns negative on government backed entities but fundamentals remain strong, as a potential contrarian signal for sentiment driven drops.

title: Pollution news, media sentiment and stock returns
authors: Oliver Budras, Maik Dierkes
key_findings: Stocks in the highest pollution news beta quintile earn significantly higher returns than those in the lowest quintile. | The outperformance of high beta stocks survives risk adjustment (returns remain higher even after accounting for standard market risks). | Betas related to other environmental topics (non pollution) are not consistently priced (do not predict returns). | A positive pollution news premium only exists when media sentiment is above its median value. | No specific return percentage or basis points are provided in the abstract.
for_the_app: Add a 'Sentiment Filter' to the storyline logic: only flag 'pollution news' storylines as buy signals if the overall media sentiment score for that event is above the historical median.

title: Stock market returns and the content of annual report narratives
authors: Tomasz Piotr Wisniewski, Liafisu Sina Yekini
key_findings: Activity and Realism indicators predict subsequent price increases (Page 3) | Holding period is about one year (250 trading days) (Page 18) | Estimates are in excess of typical transaction costs (Page 21) | Adjusted R squared is slightly below 4% (Page 21) | Linguistic variables are negatively related to risk (Page 3)
for_the_app: Add a feature to score annual report narratives for 'Activity' and 'Realism' as annual signals

title: Does News Tone from Large Language Models (LLMs) Predict Stock Returns? Evidence from Korea
authors: Cheol‐Won Yang
key_findings: The BERT based long short portfolio achieved a daily raw return of 0.242% (5.324% per month) with a t value of 3.772. | Other LLMs showed significant daily returns for long short portfolios: RoBERTa (0.146%), ELECTRA (0.134%), and Llama3 (0.060%), while DistilBERT was not statistically significant (0.065%). | The strategy is most effective for smaller firms, those with low analyst coverage, and low foreign ownership, indicating higher value in high information asymmetry. | When transaction costs (0.23% round trip) are applied to the daily rebalancing strategy, the net return drops to roughly 0.012% per day, potentially eliminating profitability. | Using a value weighted portfolio instead of equal weighted significantly reduces returns; only the BERT model remained significant (0.168% daily), while others turned negative or insignificant.
for_the_app: The app should flag stocks with extreme LLM sentiment shifts as potential short term movers but must warn users that holding periods shorter than a few days are likely unprofitable after costs; it should prioritize smaller, less covered stocks where the signal is strongest.

themes: Text and attention signals; From signal to trade
title: Firm‐Level Climate Change Exposure
authors: Zacharias Sautner, Laurence van Lent, Grigory Vilkov et al.
key_findings: Measures predict green tech job creation and green patenting | Stocks with higher exposure have probability mass shifted to the tails (crash protection and upside potential relatively more expensive) | CCEXPOSURE factor risk premium is positive, on average (3.7% p.a.) | Effect magnitudes are modest and hardly tradeable after transaction costs | Risk premium is not constant over time
for_the_app: Feature to track climate exposure scores from earnings calls to warn about tail risk or long term transition risks

title: Predicting Returns With Text Data
authors: Zheng Tracy Ke, Bryan Kelly, Dacheng Xiu
key_findings: The equal weighted SESTM long short strategy (buying day +1) achieved an annualized Sharpe ratio of 4.29 and an average daily return of 33 basis points (Table 2). | The SESTM signal is fully incorporated into prices by the start of Day +3, with the long leg incorporating within two days and the short leg within three days (Figure 8). | The SESTM strategy outperformed RavenPack (Sharpe 3.24) and Loughran McDonald (Sharpe 1.71) on an equal weighted basis, with SESTM remaining stable post-2014 while RavenPack performance flattened (Figure 12, Table 4). | After applying a 10 basis point daily transaction cost assumption, the net Sharpe ratio for the SESTM strategy peaked at 2.30 when using a turnover constraint (gamma=0.5), which extends the effective holding period (Table 5). | The 'Day 0' strategy (same day reaction) showed an infeasible annualized Sharpe ratio of 10.78, indicating that much of the news is stale or already priced in before the article is published (Table 3).
for_the_app: Implement a 'decay' feature where news sentiment scores for a stock automatically decrease in weight over 3-4 days unless reinforced by new news, preventing the app from over trading on stale signals.

title: Is Positive Sentiment in Corporate Annual Reports Informative? Evidence from Deep Learning
authors: Mehran Azimi, Anup Agrawal
venue: The Review of Asset Pricing Studies
key_findings: A one standard deviation increase in negative sentiment predicts a -0.13% change in cumulative abnormal return over days 0 to +3, while a one standard deviation increase in positive sentiment predicts a +0.07% change (US, 1994-2017). | Negative sentiment predicts higher abnormal returns in the weeks following the filing (up to +26 days), suggesting the market overreacts to bad news initially, while positive sentiment predicts continued higher returns, suggesting underreaction to good news. | Standard word list methods (Loughran McDonald) and Naïve Bayes classifiers failed to find a significant link between positive sentiment and filing day returns, unlike the deep learning method. | Changes in positive sentiment from the previous year predict positive abnormal returns around the filing date, but changes in negative sentiment do not show a significant relationship. | A yearly rebalanced portfolio strategy (longing high positive/low negative sentiment stocks and shorting the opposite) produced statistically insignificant alpha after controlling for Fama French factors and momentum.
for_the_app: Implement a deep learning sentiment scorer for 10-Ks that separates positive and negative scores rather than using a net score; flag stocks where positive sentiment is high but the price has not yet moved (potential underreaction) or where negative sentiment is high but price has already dropped (potential overreaction).

title: Trading Volume and Cross‐Autocorrelations in Stock Returns
authors: Tarun Chordia, Bhaskaran Swaminathan
key_findings: Daily returns on high volume portfolios lead returns on low volume portfolios, even after controlling for firm size (e.g., in the largest size quartile, the coefficient for lagged high volume returns predicting low volume returns is 0.1286, significant at 1%). | Weekly returns show similar lead lag patterns, with high volume portfolios leading low volume portfolios (e.g., in the largest size quartile, the coefficient is 0.0372, significant at 10%). | Stocks that contribute most to these cross autocorrelations (slow adjusters) have 30% to 50% lower raw trading volume than those that contribute least (fast adjusters). | Low volume stocks respond more slowly to marketwide information, while high volume stocks adjust rapidly, confirming the 'speed of adjustment' hypothesis. | The paper states that transaction costs are likely to overwhelm potential profits from trading these short horizon patterns, suggesting they may not be arbitraged away due to costs rather than market efficiency.
for_the_app: Add a 'Speed of Adjustment' metric to the app: when news hits a high volume leader, flag linked low volume stocks as 'lagging' and predict a delayed move over the next few days rather than an immediate reaction.

title: Textual Analysis in Finance
authors: Tim Loughran B, Bill McDonald
key_findings: On FOMC meeting dates, a one standard deviation increase in lagged tweet sentiment is associated with 0.62% higher returns (Azar & Lo 2016, 2009–2014). | A trading portfolio going long on 'nonchangers' and short on 'changers' generates large abnormal returns (up to 188 basis points in monthly alphas) based on 10-K disclosure changes (Cohen et al. 2020). | A corpus specific lexicon for StockTwits is 32% better than the Loughran & McDonald (2011) lexicon for classification (Chen et al. 2019). | Firms with abnormal vocabulary in 10-K MD&A have a significantly higher probability of ex post accounting misstatements (Hoberg & Lewis 2017, out of sample 2002–2010). | Higher News Implied Volatility (NVIX) from WSJ articles is associated with higher subsequent market stock returns (Manela & Moreira 2017, exact return not reported in text).
for_the_app: Prioritize free SEC filing data (10-K) for fraud and complexity signals; warn users when signals rely on paid news or social media data that may be noisy or inaccessible.

title: Sentiment trading with large language models
authors: Kemal Kirtac, Guido Germano
key_findings: The OPT model achieved 74.4% accuracy in predicting the direction of 3-day stock returns, outperforming BERT (72.5%), FinBERT (72.2%), and the Loughran McDonald dictionary (50.1%). | The long short OPT strategy yielded a Sharpe ratio of 3.05 after accounting for 10 basis points in transaction costs. | From August 2021 to July 2023, the long short OPT strategy generated a 355% gain, compared to 235% for BERT, 165% for FinBERT, and only 0.91% for the Loughran McDonald dictionary strategy. | The long only OPT strategy had a Sharpe ratio of 1.81 and a mean daily return of 0.32%. | The short only OPT strategy had a Sharpe ratio of 1.42 and a mean daily return of 0.25%.
for_the_app: The app should prioritize integrating LLM based sentiment analysis (like OPT or FinBERT) over simple dictionary lookups to generate storylines, and warn users that the signal is strongest when combined with a shorting mechanism and daily updates.

title: ControversyBERT: Detecting Social Controversies and Their Impact on Stock Returns
authors: Harald Lohre, Sandra Nolte, Ananthalakshmi Ranganathan et al.
venue: The Journal of Impact and ESG Investing
