key_findings: Companies linked to social controversies experience an average drop in returns of more than 200 basis points in the days surrounding the outbreak of controversial news. | Controversies regarding product safety, labour standards, and consumer data safety/privacy breaches significantly affect firm returns. | The negative stock price reaction occurs in all considered geographic regions. | The effect is largely driven by small to medium market capitalization companies where information diffusion is slowest. | Timely divesting upon detection can help avoid about 30% of the overall negative price effect.
for_the_app: Implement a 'Controversy Alert' feature that flags small cap holdings when ControversyBERT detects news in high impact categories (safety, labor, data), suggesting an immediate review for potential divestment to limit losses.

title: Chronologically consistent large language models
authors: Songrun He, Linying Lv, Asaf Manela et al.
key_findings: The long short portfolio (top decile minus bottom decile) using ChronoBERT Realtime achieved an annualized Sharpe ratio of 4.80 from 2008 to 2023. | The long short portfolio using ChronoGPT Realtime achieved an annualized Sharpe ratio of 4.92 from 2008 to 2023. | These chronologically consistent models performed comparably to the much larger Llama 3.1 model (Sharpe ratio 4.90), suggesting lookahead bias in news based return prediction is modest. | Predictive power decays rapidly: most of the return is captured on Day 0 (the first trading day after news), with performance converging to zero by Days 3-6. | Using a model trained on future data (e.g., 2024 knowledge) to interpret past news (e.g., 2020) actually reduced performance compared to using a model trained only on data available at that time, due to temporal misalignment of language meanings.
for_the_app: The app should prioritize 'freshness' over 'depth': it must process and act on news within the same trading day, as the signal decays significantly after 24 hours; it should also use language models trained or fine tuned on data from the specific era of the news to avoid misinterpreting period specific slang or context.

title: News as sources of jumps in stock returns: Evidence from 21 million news articles for 9000 companies
authors: Yoontae Jeon, Thomas H. McCurdy, Xiaofei Zhao
key_findings: The probability of a stock price jump increases significantly with the number of news articles and the absolute value of the news tone (regardless of whether the tone is positive or negative). | The link between news and price jumps has grown stronger over time; the coefficient on news count rose from 0.1–0.2 in the 1980s to over 0.5 by 2012. | The sensitivity of jump probability to news is higher for firms with greater media visibility, analyst coverage, and institutional ownership. | Specific news categories like 'Earnings and Revenues' and 'Analyst Ratings' show the strongest statistical association with daily jumps (odds ratios of 1.190 and 1.098 respectively for news count). | Even when excluding news around earnings announcement dates, the relationship between news flow and jump probability remains statistically robust, though slightly weaker.
for_the_app: The app should flag stocks with sudden spikes in news volume or high 'tone volatility' (rapid shifts in sentiment) as high probability candidates for sudden price jumps, warning the user to expect high volatility rather than predicting a specific direction.

title: News vs. Sentiment: Predicting Stock Returns from News Stories
authors: Steven L. Heston, Nitish Ranjan Sinha
key_findings: Daily news predicts stock returns for only one to two days. | Weekly news predicts stock returns for one quarter. | Positive news stories increase stock returns quickly. | Negative stories receive a long delayed reaction. | Much of the delayed response to negative news occurs around the subsequent earnings announcement.
for_the_app: The app should link negative news events to the upcoming earnings announcement date as a 'delayed reaction' storyline, while treating positive news as a short term trigger.

title: News versus Sentiment: Predicting Stock Returns from News Stories
authors: Steven L. Heston, Nitish Ranjan Sinha
key_findings: Daily news predicts returns for only 1 to 2 days (Day 0 excess return 1.99%, Day 1 0.17%, Day 2 0.04%). | Weekly news predicts returns for one quarter (13 weeks); announcement week spread 3.75%, Week 13 return 0.21%. | Negative news predicts low returns for up to 13 weeks (significant at lags 1-6 and 10), while positive news reacts quickly and fades. | Firms with neutral news outperform firms with no news (no news intercept -1 to -6 basis points per week). | Delayed reaction to news mostly occurs around subsequent earnings announcements (5.57% excess return over 13 weeks in earnings week).
for_the_app: Aggregate news sentiment over a week rather than a day; flag earnings announcements as key confirmation points for news storylines.

title: Four-Fold News Sentiment and Stock Returns
authors: Ming Deng, Miha Kebe, Patrick Matei Lucescu et al.
key_findings: Stocks with more positive news sentiment have higher expected returns. | The relationship is strongest when using the aggregate measure from all four providers compared to individual datasets. | The effect is more pronounced for stocks with lower investor attention. | The effect is more pronounced for stocks with higher arbitrage constraints. | Positive sentiment signals better future earnings and lower risk.
for_the_app: Implement a 'Sentiment Consensus' metric that only triggers a signal when at least three of four major news providers agree on the tone, and flag these signals as higher confidence for low attention stocks.

title: News sentiment indicators and the cross-section of stock returns in the European stock market
authors: Luca Gambarelli, Silvia Muzzioli
key_findings: Value weighted long short portfolio (1-month hold) returned 1.04% monthly average and 0.58% monthly FF5 alpha (6.14% annualized). | Equal weighted long short portfolio (1-month hold) returned 1.31% monthly average and 0.80% monthly FF5 alpha. | Value weighted long short strategy profitability becomes weak or insignificant at 2-month and 3-month horizons after adjusting for risk factors. | Equal weighted long short strategy remains statistically significant with positive alphas for 2-month (0.56% FF5 alpha) and 3-month (0.73% FF5 alpha) horizons. | Positive news (high sentiment) incorporates into prices more slowly than negative news, with high sentiment stocks showing rising returns over 3 months while low sentiment stocks drop quickly within 30 days.
for_the_app: Feature: Implement a 'Sentiment Momentum' signal that triggers a buy when a stock enters the top sentiment quintile, with a dynamic holding period recommendation (1 month for large caps, 2-3 months for small caps) and a warning that negative sentiment resolves faster than positive sentiment.

title: Reuters Sentiment and Stock Returns
authors: Matthias Uhl
key_findings: Negative sentiment predicts stock returns better than positive or combined sentiment. | The effect of sentiment on stock returns lasts for months, with the strongest response occurring after one month. | Sentiment explains 15-20% of the forecast error variance in stock returns, while macroeconomic factors explain only about 5%. | A long short strategy based on negative sentiment forecasts in 2010 produced an annual return of over 10% (implied by the text stating it 'produces high returns' and 'outperforms the benchmark' which was ~8%), whereas the strategy using combined sentiment underperformed the benchmark by over 4%. | Positive sentiment signals were not statistically significant in predicting returns in the lagged endogenous terms of the model.
for_the_app: Implement a 'Sentiment Drift' feature that tracks negative news intensity over a 30-day window and flags it as a high probability signal for a market decline, rather than reacting to daily spikes.

title: Trading Strategies to Exploit Blog and News Sentiment
authors: Wenbin Zhang, Steven Skiena
venue: Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media
key_findings: correlation coefficients between logged normalized article counts and logged stock trading volume are more than 0.4 | today's news almost have no predictive power for the return of tomorrow or later days (for Dailies news) | Twitter polarity has some correlationship with tomorrow's or the day after tomorrow's return | market neutral strategy gives consistently favorable returns with low volatility over a long period (ignoring costs) | worst sentiment strategy always produces negative returns
for_the_app: Use sentiment as a same day signal rather than a multi week hold signal for news sources

title: The Predictive Value of Abnormal Positive Tone in Earnings Conference Calls
authors: André Holmström, Haris Kovacevic
venue: Gothenburg University Publications Electronic Archive (Gothenburg University)
key_findings: Abnormal positive tone in the preparation remarks predicts positive abnormal returns in the initial market reaction window. | Abnormal positive tone in the preparation remarks predicts positive abnormal returns in the 60-day delayed market reaction window. | The predictive value of abnormal positive tone is considerably stronger for firms with high earnings information uncertainty (biotech and pharma) compared to traditional industries.
for_the_app: Add a feature to flag 'abnormal positive tone' in earnings call transcripts (specifically preparation remarks) and link it to a potential 60-day storyline, with a stronger weight for biotech/pharma stocks.

title: Tone Distance: Managerial Tone Divergence and Market Reaction to Earnings Announcements
authors: Ben Angelo, Mitchell Johnston, Atul Kumar Singh et al.
key_findings: A one interquartile increase in Tone Distance is associated with a lower 1-day cumulative abnormal return of 0.21%. | A one interquartile increase in Tone Distance is associated with a lower 5-day cumulative abnormal return of 0.23%. | Higher Tone Distance is a positive predictor of monthly stock returns in the 3 months following the earnings announcement (coefficient 0.2282, significant at 1%). | Higher Tone Distance is positively associated with future stock volatility and operational risk, suggesting the initial price drop reflects genuine uncertainty. | The negative reaction to high Tone Distance persists even after adjusting for analyst tone and using alternative weighting methods (e.g., weighting by words spoken).
for_the_app: Feature: Add a 'Managerial Consistency Score' to earnings call analysis. If the score is low (high Tone Distance), flag the stock as 'High Risk/Short Candidate' for the immediate days and 'Potential Long Reversal' for the 3-month horizon, linking this event to a storyline of 'Internal Disagreement leading to future volatility'.

title: An Investigation of Analysts' Praise of Management During Earnings Conference Calls
authors: Jonathan A. Milian, Antoinette L. Smith
key_findings: Analysts praise management in over half of all earnings conference calls. | The amount of praise is strongly associated with the earnings surprise and even more strongly with the stock return on the announcement day. | Tracking analyst flattery predicts abnormal stock returns over the following quarter. | The study examined 16,609 conference calls from S&P 500 companies. | The predictive power of praise is incremental to prior research on general call tone.
for_the_app: Implement a 'Praise to Surprise Ratio' metric: flag calls where analyst praise is high relative to the actual earnings beat, as this specific combination predicts the next quarter's abnormal returns.

title: Linguistic Passiveness in Earnings Calls and Stock Returns
authors: Lynn Tao, Yuntao Wu, Charles Martineau et al.
key_findings: Among firms with positive earnings surprises, announcement day returns fall from 4.38% to 2.74% as passiveness moves from the lowest to the highest quintile. | The announcement day discount for positive surprise firms with high passiveness fully reverses over the subsequent quarter (61 trading days). | For firms with negative earnings surprises, passiveness has no effect on announcement day returns but predicts negative long run returns over the next 61 days. | A one standard deviation increase in passiveness predicts a 0.20% return over the 61-day window for positive surprise firms (reversing the initial drop). | A one standard deviation increase in passiveness predicts approximately a -0.41% return over the 61-day window for negative surprise firms.
for_the_app: Add a 'Passiveness Score' to the app's event analysis: flag positive earnings calls with high passiveness as 'Overheated/Reversal Risk' and negative calls with high passiveness as 'Continued Downside Risk' to help users avoid emotional overreaction to the headline number.

title: Credibility Signals from Soft Information: Evidence from Investor Reactions to Tone in Earnings Conference Calls
authors: Jan Christoph Hennig, Sebastian Firk, Michael Wolff
key_findings: Investor reactions to tone are stronger when sender and message credibility are high. | The credibility effect is stronger in weaker information environments. | Sender and message credibility strongly attenuate (reduce) the negative post conference call drift in investor reaction to tone.
for_the_app: Add a 'Credibility Score' metric to earnings call analysis that combines speaker personality traits and message structure; use this score to weight the 'tone' signal, reducing the signal strength if credibility is low.

title: When Managers Change Their Tone, Analysts and Investors Change Their Tune
authors: Marina Druz, Ivan Petzev, Alexander F. Wagner et al.
key_findings: Increases in negativity ('bleak tone changes') in presentations strongly predict lower future earnings and greater uncertainty, while decreases in negativity ('bright tone changes') only weakly predict the opposite. | Bleak tone changes in presentations predict a significant drift in stock prices: the 59-day cumulative abnormal return (CAR[2,60]) is negatively associated with the tone change, indicating under reaction by the market. | For presentations, bleak tone changes drive the total effect (initial reaction + drift), whereas for answers, bleak changes explain the total effect but do not predict significant drift on their own. | The profitability of the negativity based strategy is concentrated in smaller stocks and those with lower institutional ownership or analyst coverage, suggesting the effect is stronger where information processing is less efficient. | The study explicitly states that trading costs were not considered in the reported returns, noting that significant costs may deplete profits, especially for smaller stocks where the profits are concentrated.
for_the_app: The app should flag 'Bleak Tone Changes' in presentation scripts as a high confidence negative signal for a 2-month hold, while treating similar changes in Q&A answers as less predictive of future drift.

title: Investor Attention and Stock Returns
authors: Jian Chen, Guohao Tang, Jiaquan Yao et al.
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
key_findings: The composite investor attention index predicts the stock market risk premium significantly, both in sample and out of sample. | Every individual attention proxy used to build the index has little predictive power on its own. | The index delivers sizable economic gains for mean variance investors in asset allocation. | The predictive power primarily stems from the reversal of temporary price pressure. | The index has stronger forecasting ability for high variance stocks.
for_the_app: Build a feature that aggregates multiple attention signals (search, news, social) into a single 'Attention Pressure' score; when this score spikes for high volatility stocks, flag a potential short term reversal opportunity rather than a trend.

title: Investor Attention and Global Stock Returns
authors: Tao Chen
key_findings: A significant decrease in index returns follows an increase in investor attention (measured by Google search volume). | The negative effect of attention is strengthened in markets with positive sentiment and weakened in markets with negative sentiment. | The effect is primarily driven by local and U.S. investors. | The study covers 67 countries including both developed and developing markets. | The results support the investor recognition hypothesis, suggesting high attention leads to lower future returns.
for_the_app: Add a 'Search Volume Spike' alert that flags when Google search volume for a specific index rises sharply, warning the user of a potential short term reversal in that market.

title: Investor Attention and Stock Returns: International Evidence
authors: Liyan Han, Ziying Li, Libo Yin
key_findings: The predictive power of investor attention is described as 'short lived'. | Attention weakens the autocorrelation (the tendency of returns to follow previous returns) within stock returns. | When accounting for business cycles, the predictability of attention endures with volatility. | The effect is asymmetric: 'underlying pessimism' (negative attention) functions better at predicting returns than optimism. | The effects of attention differ across three levels of market efficiency: semi strong, stronger than semi strong, and weak.
for_the_app: Implement a 'Pessimism Weighting' feature that boosts the signal strength of negative news events during recessions, and set a very short default holding window (e.g., 1-3 days) for attention based triggers.

title: Investor Attention, Divergence of Opinions, and Stock Returns
authors: Zhen Cao, Osman Kilic, Xuewu Wang
key_findings: There is a positive relationship between divergence of opinions and future stock returns, supporting the risk hypothesis rather than the overvaluation hypothesis. | The predictive power of divergence of opinions is more pronounced in stocks with lower investor attention. | A portfolio that goes long on stocks with low investor attention and the highest divergence of opinions, and short on stocks with low attention and the lowest divergence of opinions, generates a Fama French 5-factor monthly alpha of 1.14%.
for_the_app: The app should flag stocks with high analyst disagreement (divergence) but low search volume or news coverage (low attention) as potential 'high risk/high reward' storyline candidates to watch for confirmation.

title: Local investor attention and stock returns
authors: L. Vincent Raj Kumar
key_findings: Firms attracting unusual local investor attention experience significant future price reversals. | Firms with considerably higher local attention than non local attention experience monotonic declines in future returns. | The 'Google Top State' (state with highest search interest) is often different from the company's headquarters state. | Investor attention from the headquarters state has no predictive power for future returns. | The Google Top State is proposed as a superior benchmark for testing local bias theories compared to the headquarters state.
for_the_app: Add a 'Local Attention Spike' warning metric that flags stocks with abnormal Google search volume from specific states, suggesting a potential short term reversal (sell signal) rather than a breakout.

title: Investor attention using the Google search volume index – impact on stock returns
authors: Vighneswara Swamy P.M., M. Dharani
key_findings: High Google search volumes predict positive and significant returns in the subsequent fourth and fifth weeks. | The GSVI performs as a useful predictor of both the direction and magnitude of excess returns. | Higher quantiles (levels) of the GSVI correspond to higher excess returns. | Domestic investor searches are more strongly correlated with higher excess returns than worldwide investor searches. | The study supports the 'price pressure hypothesis' for the Indian market, where attention drives temporary price increases.
for_the_app: Implement a 'Delayed Momentum' feature: when search volume for a stock spikes, flag it as a potential buy signal but set a reminder to check the trade status in 4-5 weeks to confirm the expected return materializes.

title: Attracting Investor Attention through Advertising
authors: Dong Lou
key_findings: The spread in four factor alpha between the top and bottom deciles of advertising growth is 12.8% (t=4.83) in the formation year. | In the first year after formation, the return spread reverses to -9.2% (t=-3.73). | In the second year after formation, the return spread is -6.6% (t=-2.04). | Doubling a firm's advertising spending in a year leads to a lower stock return of 0.24% per month in the subsequent year. | The reversal effect is stronger for consumer goods firms (-11.64% in year one) than for non consumer goods firms (-6.36%).
for_the_app: Add a 'Warning' flag for stocks with a sudden year over year spike in advertising spend, linking it to a predicted short term price pump followed by a long term decline.

title: Asymmetric Attention and Stock Returns
authors: Péter Cziráki, Jordi Mondria, Thomas Yen Hon Wu
key_findings: A portfolio going long on stocks with high asymmetric local attention and short on stocks with low asymmetric local attention earns an alpha of 32 basis points per month. | The results are stronger for stocks with a greater degree of information friction (harder to get information about). | The measure allows inferring the arrival of unobservable private information by observing investor attention behavior.
for_the_app: Integrate a 'Local vs. Global Search Ratio' metric for each stock to flag potential private information events; use this as a trigger to start a storyline tracking the stock's price reaction.

title: Internet Search Intensity and Its Relation with Trading Activity and Stock Returns*
authors: Daniel Chai, Mengjia Dai, Philip Gharghori et al.
key_findings: High minus low ASVI portfolio generated an average monthly return of 4.38% (t=11.92) over a 1-month holding period. | The return premium declines as the holding period extends, dropping to 0.38% (t=3.84) over a 12-month holding period. | Over 3 to 12 months, the strategy reverses: high ASVI stocks underperform low ASVI stocks in the long run, with the reversal being statistically significant. | The attention effect is strongest in stocks with high limits to arbitrage; the ASVI coefficient is significantly larger in the high LTA group compared to the low LTA group. | In the high limits to arbitrage group, the high minus low ASVI return difference is 1.29% (t=3.62) over 3 months and 0.65% (t=2.47) over 6 months, but turns negative or insignificant at 12 months.
for_the_app: Implement a 'Search Spike' alert that triggers a buy signal when ASVI spikes, with a hard automatic sell signal 21 trading days later to capture the reversal risk.

title: Investor Inattention, Firm Reaction, and Friday Earnings Announcements
authors: Stefano DellaVigna, Joshua Matthew Pollet
key_findings: Friday announcements have a delayed response that makes up 60 percent of the total reaction, compared to 40 percent for other weekdays. | Abnormal trading volume on the day after a Friday announcement is 40 percent lower than for other weekdays. | In a homogeneous sample, the post announcement drift for Friday announcements is 5.27 percentage points larger than for non Friday announcements, which is 124.6 percent larger. | Firms are 45 percent more likely to release a negative earnings surprise on a Friday compared to other days. | Friday announcements are associated with an abnormal stock return that is 50 basis points (0.50%) lower than other days. | Over the full 75-day window, there is no significant difference in total returns between Friday and non Friday announcements; the initial underreaction is fully corrected later.
for_the_app: Feature: When a stock has a major earnings surprise on a Friday, flag it as a 'High Delay' candidate and extend the expected storyline confirmation window from 1 day to 2-4 weeks.

title: Asymmetric Trading Costs Prior to Earnings Announcements: Implications for Price Discovery and Returns
authors: Travis L. Johnson, Eric C. So
key_findings: Preannouncement returns are positive and significant, peaking at 0.180% on day t-1 (US, 1993-2012) | Asymmetric Liquidity Provision (ALP) increases before announcements, with losers earning 0.325% and winners -0.168% at t-10 (Table 1) | Preannouncement returns decreased over time, from 0.138% (1993-1999) to 0.002% (2007-2012) (Table 4 Panel B) | Bad news is incorporated on the announcement date, not before, while good news is incorporated preannouncement (Figure 3) | Preannouncement abnormal turnover has a significant positive relation with returns (coefficient 1.213) and predicts positive earnings surprises (Table 3)
for_the_app: Flag pre earnings price rises as potential liquidity bias rather than fundamental news

title: Limited attention and the earnings announcement returns of past stock market winners
authors: David Aboody, Reuven Lehavy, Brett Trueman
key_findings: Top 1% past winners gained an average market adjusted return of 1.58% in the 5 days before earnings announcements (1971–2005). | Top 1% past winners lost an average market adjusted return of -1.86% in the 5 days after earnings announcements (1971–2005). | For stocks announcing earnings after market close, the pre announcement gain was 3.09% and the post announcement loss was -3.05%. | Small and medium sized traders (under $100k trade value) showed significant buying pressure before announcements, while large traders did not. | The pre announcement return pattern was stronger in the 1990–2005 period (1.69%) than in the 1971–1989 period (0.74%), suggesting it grew as individual investors gained easier market access.
for_the_app: The app should flag 'past winners' (top 12-month performers) as high risk for a 'sell on the fact' reversal immediately after their earnings release, and potentially suggest avoiding new entries in the 5 days prior to the announcement.

title: Investor Inattention and the Market Reaction to Merger Announcements
authors: Henock Louis, Amy X. Sun
key_findings: Market reaction to Friday stock swap announcements is muted, with lower abnormal trading volumes for acquirers. | Acquirers' merger announcement abnormal stock returns are less pronounced for Friday announcements compared to other days. | The effect is consistent with the hypothesis that investors are less attentive to Friday announcements. | Citing papers note that for stock swaps involving privately owned targets, the Friday effect results in less positive returns, while for publicly owned targets, it results in less negative returns. | The study covers the period 1994-2006.
for_the_app: Flag merger announcements made on Fridays as 'potential underreaction' and trigger a follow up alert 1-3 days later to check if the price drifts in the direction of the initial news.

title: Visuals and attention to earnings news on twitter
authors: Alexander Nekrasov, Siew Hong Teoh, Shijia Wu
key_findings: Using visuals in earnings tweets increases the immediate market reaction (CAR(-1,+1)) by 0.020 for a full decile increase in earnings surprise, which is a 25% increase over the average earnings response coefficient of 0.080. | The immediate reaction is significantly stronger on days with high investor distraction (many other firms announcing earnings), where the coefficient rises to 0.042 to 0.050. | Visuals are associated with a lower post announcement response (CAR(-1,+1) for the next quarter), with a coefficient of -0.019 to -0.021, indicating a price reversal. | Firms are more likely to use visuals when earnings are good but less persistent, suggesting opportunistic behavior rather than improved information clarity. | The effect of visuals on immediate reaction is more pronounced for stocks with high individual investor interest (high Google search volume).
for_the_app: The app should flag earnings tweets containing visuals as a potential signal of 'overreaction risk' and suggest a shorter holding period or a contrarian strategy (selling after the initial spike) if the earnings persistence is low.

title: Time Will Tell: Information in the Timing of Scheduled Earnings News
authors: Travis L. Johnson, Eric C. So
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
key_findings: Firms that schedule later than expected announcement dates subsequently announce worse news than those scheduling earlier than expected dates. | Equity markets fail to reflect the information in scheduling disclosures until the actual earnings announcement day, despite the schedule being observable weeks in advance. | Option markets respond efficiently to the 'volatility timing' information embedded in the scheduling disclosures, unlike the equity market. | Citing papers confirm that early announcers tend to announce better news than late announcers. | Citing papers note that expected announcement dates are highly accurate and rarely off by more than one day.
for_the_app: The app should flag any change in a company's scheduled earnings date relative to its historical pattern as a predictive signal for the upcoming earnings quality, even if the stock price does not move immediately.

title: Firm–specific information processing and the delayed discovery of macroeconomic news: evidence from earnings announcement returns
authors: Jing Pan, Edward Sul, Sean Wang
key_findings: For firms with extreme earnings surprises, approximately 23.2% of the aggregate market return on the announcement day is incorporated into the firm's price over the subsequent three trading days. | The predictability of the market return for extreme announcers becomes statistically insignificant between days four and seven, indicating the delay is short lived. | For firms with very small or zero earnings surprises, the market return on the announcement day is fully priced immediately and shows no correlation with post announcement returns. | The delay effect is stronger for firms with high retail trading activity and smaller market capitalization, where investor attention is more constrained. | The magnitude of the delay has decreased over time, with the average 3-day return spread for extreme announcers dropping from 1.56% in 1998–2002 to 0.61% in 2018–2022.
for_the_app: The app should flag stocks with 'Extreme Earnings Surprises' on announcement day and monitor their correlation with the broader market index; if the stock moves less than the market on that day, the app should predict a 'catch up' move in the same direction over the next 3 days.

title: How Does Post-Earnings Announcement Sentiment Affect Firms’ Dynamics? New Evidence from Causal Machine Learning
authors: Francesco Audrino, Jonathan Chassot, Chen Huang et al.
key_findings: Positive sentiment yields a 0.76% higher average return over one week compared to negative sentiment (statistically significant at 0.2% p value). | Negative sentiment causes a larger immediate price jump (up to 75 basis points) and higher volatility/turnover than positive sentiment on the day after the announcement. | The difference in returns between positive and negative sentiment is 0.76% over a week, while the difference in volatility is a reduction of 0.16% (16 basis points) for positive vs. negative sentiment over the same period. | Effects are significantly larger during recessions: the volatility reduction for positive vs. negative sentiment is 0.93% during recessions compared to only 0.12% during expansions. | Investors underreact to news, as abnormal returns and volatility levels revert to average values only after several days, consistent with the limited attention hypothesis.
for_the_app: The app should flag earnings announcements with strong positive sentiment as potential 'buy' candidates but advise holding for 3-5 days to capture the underreaction drift, while warning that volatility will be higher immediately after negative news.

title: Casting Conference Calls
authors: Lauren H. Cohen, Dong Lou, Christopher J. Malloy
key_findings: A long short portfolio (short casting, long non casting) earns abnormal returns of 129 to 149 basis points per month (t=2.59 to 2.64), which is roughly 15% to 18% per year (US sample, 2003-2015). | The return shock occurs primarily at the *subsequent* earnings announcement (about 3 months after the call), not on the day of the call, indicating the market is initially fooled by the optimistic tone. | A one standard deviation increase in the 'casting' measure predicts a 39% lower cumulative abnormal return (CAR) at the next earnings announcement and a 20% lower earnings surprise relative to the interquartile range. | Casting behavior predicts a 32% increase in the likelihood of future earnings restatements (accounting irregularities). | The effect is global: in an international sample (UK, Canada, France, Japan), a one standard deviation move in casting predicts a 32 basis point lower earnings announcement return in the next quarter.
for_the_app: Add a 'Casting Risk' metric to the app that flags companies where the ratio of bullish to bearish analysts on the call is skewed, and link this event to a predicted negative price movement at the next earnings date.

title: Front‐Page News: The Effect of News Positioning on Financial Markets
authors: Anastassia Fedyk
key_findings: Front page articles see 240% higher trading volume and 176% larger absolute excess returns in the first 10 minutes compared to non front page articles. | Information in front page articles is fully incorporated into prices within one hour of publication. | Non front page information takes more than two days to be fully reflected, with a statistically significant gap of 34 basis points remaining after two days. | The price gap between front page and non front page news shrinks to 8 basis points (statistically indiscernible) after 15 days. | Finance professionals in a survey could not distinguish the importance of front page vs. non front page 'Secondary Important' news (48.24% chose front page as more impactful, not different from 50%).
for_the_app: The app should flag 'under reacted' news events that have not yet been confirmed by price movement, specifically looking for stories that lack immediate high volume confirmation, as these may drift over the next 1-2 weeks.

themes: Already priced in or not; Does it still work
title: Local Bias in Google Search and the Market Response around Earnings Announcements
authors: Sabrina S. Chi, Devin M. Shanthikumar
key_findings: Firms with high local bias experience post earnings announcement drift (PEAD) that is 11.9% stronger (relative to the baseline drift) than firms with low local bias over a 60-trading day window. | In the week before earnings, firms with high local bias show pre announcement returns that are 10.4% more predictive of the upcoming earnings surprise compared to low local bias firms. | During the announcement window, firms with high local bias have earnings response coefficients (ERC) that are 34% to 43% lower than firms with low local bias, indicating a weaker immediate price reaction. | High local bias firms have abnormal bid ask spreads that are 10.9% to 11.9% higher during the announcement and 9.06% higher in the pre announcement period compared to low local bias firms. | Changes in a firm's local bias (increases vs. decreases) lead to significant shifts in these metrics, with the largest increases in local bias causing a 55% drop in announcement window ERCs and a 280% increase in pre announcement spreads.
for_the_app: The app should flag stocks with high 'local search bias' as candidates for a 'slow reaction' storyline: expect muted price moves on the news day and a higher probability of a drift (continued move) in the direction of the surprise over the following 4-6 weeks.

title: Price Discovery, Investor Distraction and Analyst Recommendations Under Continuous Disclosure Requirements in Australia
authors: Leonardo Fernandez
key_findings: Frequency of disclosure increases speed of price adjustment when above a threshold (more than one non periodic MSA per month). | High distraction days (many MSAs released same day) reduce magnitude and speed of short term market reaction to MSAs (initial underreaction). | Post MSA upgrades on days +1 and +2 outperform standalone upward revisions by 69 (47) and 84 (33) basis points respectively (mean/median). | Downgrades released the day after a MSA possess the highest abnormal return over standalone downward revisions (-1.57% mean, -0.77% median difference). | Same day downgrades outperform standalone downward revisions by 1.50% (mean) and 0.79% (median).
for_the_app: Flag analyst revisions occurring within 1-2 days of a market sensitive announcement as higher signal strength for storyline confirmation.

title: Distracted Institutional Investors
authors: Daniel M. Schmidt
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
key_findings: Managers with a large fraction of portfolio stocks announcing earnings are significantly less likely to trade in other stocks. | The distraction effect is more pronounced for nonpassive managers who engage in active stock selection. | Distracted managers trade less profitably. | Distracted managers incur slightly higher transaction costs. | Distracted managers are less likely to close losing positions.
for_the_app: The app should flag stocks that are currently 'distracted' by institutional portfolio churn (e.g., when a major holding of a known fund has earnings) and highlight potential underreaction in the target stock's price over the following days.

title: An Empirical Investigation On The Post-Earnings Announcement Drift And AlgorithmicTrading
authors: Joe Ruiwang Zhang
venue: The Sydney eScholarship Repository (The University of Sydney)
key_findings: After controlling for a large set of explanatory variables, the PEAD anomaly remains significant at approximately 2% over the 60 trading days following the earnings announcement (US, 1995-2011). | When conditioning on earnings surprise, the average 60-day PEAD effect is approximately 4% before full risk adjustment, but drops to just under 2% after jointly controlling for other factors. | The persistence of PEAD is associated with high arbitrage risk (idiosyncratic risk) and high transaction costs, which prevent sophisticated traders from fully correcting the mispricing. | Low investor sophistication is identified as a primary cause for the initial under reaction to earnings news. | The study finds an insignificant direct relation between the level of algorithmic trading (AT) and the attenuation of PEAD, though AT is linked to improved price discovery.
for_the_app: The app should flag earnings surprises as potential 'storyline' triggers but must filter out stocks with high idiosyncratic risk or low liquidity, as the drift is strongest where retail traders can trade but is hardest to capture due to costs.

title: Investor Underreaction to Earnings Surprises and Overreaction to Product News in the Drug Industry
authors: Dov Fischer
key_findings: Investors underreacted to earnings news, causing stock prices to drift in the direction of the surprise for 3 to 12 months. | Investors overreacted to product news, causing stock prices to reverse the initial reaction after the event. | Product news is more 'salient' (vivid and dramatic) than earnings news, which is a summary statistic lacking color or drama. | Overreaction to product news is followed by an 'overcorrection' where prices move back toward fair value. | Negative information releases in this context tend to garner a greater magnitude of overreaction and correction than positive ones (based on citing paper interpretation of Fischer, 2012).
for_the_app: The app should flag 'vivid' product news as a potential short term sell signal (expecting a reversal) and 'earnings surprises' as a potential long term buy/sell signal (expecting a drift), distinguishing between the two news types based on their emotional vividness.

title: On the Anomalous Stock Price Response to Management Earnings Forecasts
authors: Somnath Das, Kyonghee Kim, Sukesh Patro
key_findings: For bad news forecasts, a 15-day buy and hold strategy yields an alpha of 0.73% (t=2.05), but the mean bid ask spread of 1.66% eliminates these profits. | For bad news forecasts, extending the holding period to 30 days yields an alpha of 2.89% (t=3.14), resulting in an annualized alpha of approximately 10.25% net of the 1.66% transaction cost. | For good news forecasts, a 15-day strategy yields an alpha of 1.50% (t=4.20), which absorbs the lower mean bid ask spread of 1.03%, resulting in an annualized alpha of approximately 7.83%. | For good news forecasts, a 30-day strategy yields an alpha of 2.13% (t=2.66), resulting in an annualized alpha of approximately 9.20% net of the 1.03% transaction cost. | The market initially overreacts to bad news (price drops too much then drifts up) and underreacts to good news (price rises too little then drifts up), with the drift persisting until the actual earnings announcement.
for_the_app: The app should flag management earnings forecasts as 'storyline triggers' and automatically extend the holding period for bad news stories to 30 days to capture the reversal drift, while warning users that short term (under 15 days) trades on bad news may be wiped out by spreads.

title: Belief Overreaction and Stock Market Puzzles
authors: Pedro Bordalo, Nicola Gennaioli, Rafael La Porta et al.
key_findings: High long term earnings growth (LTG) expectations account for 25% of the variation in S&P 500 returns over the following five years (Table 2, Panel A). | A one standard deviation increase in the lagged LTG forecast is associated with a roughly 0.5 standard deviation lower future return, corresponding to losing between 19 and 25 months' worth of returns over a five year period (Section 3.2). | At the firm level, upward revisions in a firm's LTG forecast predict future disappointment in earnings growth (negative forecast errors) and lower future returns (Table 6). | The 'Pessimism minus Optimism' (PMO) portfolio, which buys the lowest LTG decile and sells the highest LTG decile, shows a strong positive return spread that widens after periods of aggregate optimism (Table 7, Column 3). | High LTG firms (Optimism) underperform low LTG firms (Pessimism) significantly over five year horizons, with the spread explained by belief overreaction rather than time varying risk premiums (Table 7 and Section 4.2).
for_the_app: The app should flag stocks with large upward revisions in long term earnings growth forecasts as 'Overheated/Overreacted' and suggest a 'Sell' or 'Avoid' signal with a 3-5 year warning horizon.

title: What Hundreds of Economic News Events Say About Belief Overreaction in the Stock Market
authors: Francesco Bianchi, Sydney C. Ludvigson, Sai Ma
key_findings: investors systematically overreact to perceptions about multiple fundamental shocks in a macro dynamic system | overreaction generates asymmetric compositional effects when real world events produce conflicting signals with counteracting market implications | such events can lead the market to underreact to news, even when investors overreact to all shocks
for_the_app: Add a logic check for 'conflicting signals' in news storylines; if a headline contains mixed positive and negative fundamental shocks, flag the event as a potential underreaction candidate rather than a confirmed trend.

title: Institutional Investment Constraints and Stock Prices
authors: Jie Cao, Bing Han, Qinghai Wang
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
key_findings: Momentum strategy on stocks with high institutional constraints (overweight winners, underweight losers) generates an average return of 0.91% per month (US, 1980-2013, 6-month holding). | Momentum strategy on unconstrained stocks (low overweight ratio) generates an average return of only 0.32% per month, which is 0.59% lower than the constrained strategy. | Stocks with positive earnings surprises that are already overweighted by institutions outperform those underweighted by 0.94% over the 60 trading days following the announcement. | Stocks with extreme negative earnings surprises that are underweighted by institutions underperform those overweighted by -0.86% over the 60 trading days following the announcement. | The predictive power of institutional constraints is U shaped: it is significant for recent winners and losers but not for stocks with no recent price trend.
for_the_app: The app should flag news events (earnings, analyst upgrades) where the stock's current institutional ownership is already at a constraint limit (overweight for good news, underweight for bad news), predicting a delayed price move rather than an immediate one.

title: How naive is the stock market's use of earnings information?
authors: Ray Ball, Eli Bartov
key_findings: Market underestimates the magnitude of serial correlation in earnings by approximately 50% on average | Market uses correct signs for serial correlation at lags 1-4 (pattern: +, +, +, -) | Replicates Bernard and Thomas (1990): Sum of coefficients on lagged SUEs in return regression is 2.44% (abnormal return) | Small firms incorporate the largest proportion of serial correlation into earnings expectations | Sample requires 15 consecutive quarters of earnings data, which may induce survivorship bias
for_the_app: Flag stocks where past earnings surprises contradict current price reaction based on serial correlation patterns to identify potential drift

title: Ownership Structure, Limits to Arbitrage, and Stock Returns: Evidence from Equity Lending Markets
authors: Melissa Porras Prado, Pedro A. C. Saffi, Jason D. Sturgess
key_findings: Stocks with concentrated ownership exhibit an additional negative abnormal return of -0.47% in the week following a positive shorting demand shock (Table 7). | An outward shorting demand shock decreases abnormal returns by approximately 0.2% per week generally, but by 0.452% per week (1.92% per month) in firms with high ownership concentration (Table 8). | Trading costs (estimated at 0.1% per week) and lending fees (0.035% per week) reduce the profitability of the concentrated ownership shorting strategy by about 30%, leaving a net return of -0.34% per week (Table 3.6.1). | Firms with concentrated ownership show smaller price reactions on the day of an earnings announcement (CAR1) but larger post earnings announcement drift (PEAD) over the following 10 days and quarter (Table 9). | The negative impact of shorting demand shocks on concentrated stocks is driven by short term investors; the effect diminishes if the top 5 holders have a long term investment horizon (Table 8, Column 3).
for_the_app: Add a 'Concentration Delay' metric: flag stocks with high ownership concentration that experience a sudden rise in shorting fees/volume, predicting a continued price decline over the next 5-10 days rather than an immediate correction.

title: Tax Expense Momentum
authors: Jacob K. Kandathil Thomas, Frank Zhang
key_findings: Hedge portfolio (Top 10% minus Bottom 10%) based on tax expense surprise generated an average return of 3.90% over a three month holding period (t statistic 11.26) from 1977 to 2006. | After controlling for earnings surprises, the residual tax expense surprise hedge portfolio still generated a 2.56% return over three months (t statistic 7.83), equivalent to about 10% annualized. | In the more recent sub period (1996–2006), the raw tax expense surprise hedge return dropped to 2.10% for the full sample, but rose to 3.29% when measuring returns starting just 3 days after the 10-Q/K filing date. | The anomaly is stronger for small firms (5.14% hedge return) than large firms (1.74% hedge return), suggesting the effect is driven by mispricing rather than risk. | Losses occurred in only 16 out of 120 quarters for the tax expense strategy, suggesting the returns are not compensation for a risky strategy.
for_the_app: The app should flag 'Tax Expense Surprise' as a key event in a company's storyline, explaining that a higher than expected tax bill often signals stronger core profitability and predicts a price rise over the next quarter.

title: Headline Salience, Managerial Opportunism, and Over- and Underreactions to Earnings
authors: Xuan Huang, Alexander Nekrasov, Siew Hong Teoh
key_findings: An increase in headline salience (from 0 to 1) increases the 3-day announcement return differential between top and bottom earnings surprise deciles by 1.4%. | An increase in headline salience (from 0 to 1) reduces the 60-day post announcement abnormal return by 2.2%, turning a neutral drift into a reversal. | For positive earnings surprises specifically, an increase in salience (from 0 to 1) leads to a 5.4% decrease in the 60-day post announcement abnormal return. | Managers are more likely to use high salience headlines when they plan to sell shares in the 30 days following the announcement. | The average sample does not show a standard Post Earnings Announcement Drift (PEAD); the drift is only negative (reversal) when headlines are salient.
for_the_app: Flag earnings announcements with headlines containing 3 or more quantitative figures as 'High Salience' and suggest a 'Sell' signal for positive surprises if the price has already rallied significantly on the announcement day, predicting a reversal over the next 4-6 weeks.

title: Limited attention and financial decision-making
authors: Alexander Nekrasov, Siew Hong Teoh, Shijia Wu
key_findings: When some investors are inattentive, the immediate market reaction to news is incomplete, leading to post announcement drift (prices continue to move in the direction of the news after the announcement). | Underreaction is stronger when investor attention is distracted by competing stimuli. | Underreaction is stronger when the information is less salient or harder to process. | Underreaction is stronger when investors are less sophisticated. | Firms exploit limited attention by choosing disclosure timing and format to highlight good news and obscure bad news.
for_the_app: The app should flag news events that are complex, buried in long reports, or released during high attention periods (like earnings season) as potential candidates for delayed price reactions.

title: Limited attention and stock price drift following earnings announcements and 10‐K filings
authors: Haifeng You, Xiaojun Zhang
key_findings: Among large firms, investors under react more to the information contained in 10-K filings than earnings announcements. | Underreaction to earnings announcements tends to be stronger for small firms than large firms. | There is a negative relationship between the degree of underreaction and the timeliness of information release (earlier reports lead to less underreaction). | The SEC ruling to accelerate 10-K filing dates had little impact on the degree of investors' underreaction to 10-K information. | The study concludes that investor failure to devote enough attention to an economic event leads to underreaction, and the degree of underreaction is negatively correlated with the amount of investor attention.
for_the_app: The app should flag small cap earnings announcements and 10-K filings as high potential 'underreaction' storylines, specifically tracking the time gap between the release and the market's full price adjustment.

title: Alliances and Return Predictability
authors: Jie Cao, Tarun Chordia, Chen Lin
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
key_findings: A long short portfolio sorted on lagged returns of strategic alliance partners provides a return of 89 basis points per month. | The return is robust to a number of specifications. | Investor inattention and limits to arbitrage are suggested as the source of the underreaction.
for_the_app: Feature: When a news event impacts a company, automatically flag its alliance partners and calculate the 'lagged partner return' metric to suggest a potential delayed reaction trade.

title: Time Variation in the News–Returns Relationship
authors: Paul Glasserman, Fulin Li, Harry Mamaysky
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
key_findings: Price reactions to news vary significantly over time. | Higher risk bearing capacity of financial intermediaries, lower passive ownership, and more informative news increase the immediate price response to news. | Surprisingly, these same factors also increase price responses to lagged news, indicating stronger underreaction in those conditions. | A simple model with limited attention and three investor types predicts the observed variation in news responses. | A long short trading strategy based on news sentiment earns high returns, which increase when conditioning on the interaction variables.
for_the_app: The app should calculate a 'reaction potential' score for each news event based on current passive ownership and intermediary risk levels to decide whether to expect an immediate move or a delayed drift.

title: Post loss/profit announcement drift
authors: Karthik Balakrishnan, Eli Bartov, Lucile Faurel
key_findings: Over 120 trading days, the extreme profit portfolio drifted up by 4.42%, while the extreme loss portfolio drifted down by 5.79%. | The hedge portfolio (Long Extreme Profit / Short Extreme Loss) generated a 10.21% abnormal return over 120 days, which is approximately 21% annualized. | The strategy remained profitable in 27 out of 30 calendar years (1976-2005) and worked in both up and down markets. | The effect is robust to transaction costs up to 100 basis points per round trip trade, even after excluding small firms and hard to borrow stocks. | The mispricing is strongest for firms with no analyst following (14.03% hedge return) and weakest for those with high analyst following (3.14% hedge return).
for_the_app: The app should flag 'extreme loss' and 'extreme profit' announcements as high probability storylines for a 4-month drift, but must warn the user that shorting the losers is the primary source of alpha and requires careful risk management.

title: Overconfident Institutions and Their Self-Attribution Bias: Evidence from Earnings Announcements
authors: Hsin-I Chou, Mingyi Li, Xiangkang Yin et al.
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
key_findings: Pre announcement CAID is negatively related to subsequent CAR | 61.02% of institutions continue pre announcement direction over [2,20] with confirming news | 10.11% of institutions continue pre announcement direction over [2,20] with disconfirming news | SUE positively related to CAR[2,60] for disconfirming news | SUE negatively related to CAR[61,120] for confirming news
for_the_app: Flag earnings where institutional flow contradicts the news surprise to predict drift, or flow confirms news to warn of delayed reversal.

title: Costly short -selling and stock price adjustment to earnings announcements
authors: Adam V. Reed
key_findings: Announcement day absolute returns larger when short selling costly (0.076 vs 0.058). | Announcement day returns more left skewed when short selling costly (0.228 vs 4.222 skewness). | Constrained stocks with bad news drift down -9.45% over 120 days; non constrained drift up 1.36%. | Constrained stocks realize 32% less of total drift on announcement day (35-36% vs 67%). | Short sale constraints decrease informativeness of trades by 30%.
for_the_app: Flag 'hard to borrow' status with earnings news to adjust expected reaction speed and drift duration.

title: Price revelation from insider trading: Evidence from hacked earnings news
authors: Pat Akey, Vincent Grégoire, Charles Martineau
key_findings: Hackers traded on both hard (quantitative) and soft (qualitative) information, causing 15% more of the total earnings news to be incorporated into prices before the public release. | Liquidity providers responded to the illegal trading by widening effective spreads by 3% of a standard deviation, primarily due to increased realized spreads rather than price impact per trade. | The sensitivity of prices to soft information was reduced more robustly in the hacked window than the sensitivity to hard information, suggesting soft info is harder to price in quickly without the leak. | Volume and turnover increased significantly (4.9% and 3.5% of a standard deviation, respectively) during the pre release hacking window, while option volume rose by 7.2%. | There was no increase in absolute order imbalance, suggesting informed traders used a mix of market and limit orders or that liquidity providers managed inventory dynamically.
for_the_app: The app should flag earnings announcements from companies with high institutional ownership or low liquidity as 'high risk of pre pricing' and warn users that the initial price jump on the news might be smaller than expected because informed traders likely acted earlier.

title: IMPACT OF THE GALLEON CASE ON INFORMED TRADING BEFORE MERGER ANNOUNCEMENTS
authors: Inga Chira, Jeff Madura
key_findings: Mean abnormal stock price runup of targets declined from 5.12% (2002-2009) to 2.84% (2009-2011) over 42 days before announcement | Proportional runup (of takeover premium) declined from 14.80% to 7.90% over 42 days | Total abnormal return (runup + announcement day) remained stable at 34.49% (pre) and 35.98% (post) | Decline is statistically significant using parametric and nonparametric tests | Reduction attributed to decreased illegal insider trading, not adept public information traders
for_the_app: Flag merger targets with unusual pre announcement volume but warn that returns have dropped since 2009 enforcement

title: High-Frequency Measures of Informed Trading and Corporate Announcements
authors: Michael John Brennan, Sahn-Wook Huh, Avanidhar Subrahmanyam
key_findings: There is evidence of informed trading before announcements. | A significant part of the news in announcements is impounded in stock prices before the announcements by pre event informed trading. | There is evidence of informed trading after the announcements. | The probability of informed trading after merger bids predicts the probability of the bid being withdrawn or met with a competing bid. | For other announcements, post announcement informed trading probabilities predict subsequent returns.
for_the_app: Feature: Add a 'Pre Event Drift' warning to show if a stock has moved significantly before a scheduled announcement; Feature: Add a 'Post Event Signal' metric that flags unusual informed buying/selling volume after news to predict if a merger will fail or if a trend will continue.

themes: Already priced in or not; Does it still work
title: The Earnings Announcement Premium and Trading Volume
authors: Owen A Lamont, Andrea Frazzini
key_findings: Expected announcers earn a monthly excess return of 0.613% (approx. 7.4% per year) over non announcers from 1973–2004, with a t statistic of 5.30. | The premium is distributed over time: 25 basis points in the 10 days before the announcement, 21 basis points during the 3-day announcement window, and 30 basis points in the 10 days after. | Stocks with high past volume concentration around announcement dates earn the highest premium; the long/short spread for the top quintile of volume concentration is 1.369% per month (approx. 16.4% per year). | The premium is robust across sub periods, delivering between 40 and 92 basis points a month in every decade from 1973 to 2004. | Small investors (trades under $5,000) show significant net buying pressure around announcement dates, particularly in stocks with high volume concentration, suggesting the premium is driven by attention driven buying rather than informed trading.
for_the_app: The app should flag stocks with high historical volume concentration around earnings as 'high attention' candidates, and alert users that price momentum often continues for 10 days after the announcement, countering the belief that news is fully priced in immediately.

title: Informed Trading through the Accounts of Children
authors: Henk Berkman, Paul D. Koch, Peter Joakim Westerholm
key_findings: Underaged accounts outperform older investors by 9 basis points (bp) on the day after a trade, 7 bp after 2 days, and 5 bp after 3 days. | Before major earnings announcements, underaged accounts trade correctly 57% of the time and outperform by a cumulative abnormal return (CAR) of 1.1% over days 0 and +1. | Before large price changes, underaged accounts trade correctly 58% of the time with a CAR of 2.1% over days 0 and +1. | A monthly rebalanced hedge portfolio (high BABYPIN minus low BABYPIN) generated a raw return of 1.1% per month, with Fama French alphas of approximately 1.1% per month. | The average difference in returns between the top and bottom deciles of BABYPIN is 2.0% per month.
for_the_app: nothing

title: Anomalies and News
authors: JOSEPH ENGELBERG, R. David McLean, Jeffrey Pontiff
key_findings: Anomaly returns are 50% higher on corporate news days (3.84 basis points on non news days vs 5.62 basis points on news days for Net=10) | Anomaly returns are six times higher on earnings announcement days (3.84 basis points on non earnings days vs 21.64 basis points on earnings days for Net=10) | Most information is reflected in prices the day it is released (3-day window coefficients are smaller than 1-day window coefficients) | Anomaly shorts have lower abnormal returns during the three day announcement window, while anomaly longs have higher abnormal returns (no reversal of effect) | Effects are stronger in small stocks (Net x Earnings interaction is 3.067 for small stocks vs 0.715 for large stocks)
for_the_app: Flag stocks with high anomaly scores for earnings or news days to expect larger immediate moves, but warn users that the opportunity closes quickly (same day)

title: March Market Madness: The Impact of Value‐Irrelevant Events on the Market Pricing of Earnings News
authors: Michael S. Drake, Kurt H. Gee, Jacob R. Thornock
key_findings: Price reaction to earnings news released during March Madness is muted (Abstract) | It takes the market 30 to 60 days to correct for the distraction effect (Abstract) | Result is more muted for low institutional ownership firms (Abstract) | Association between announcement period returns and post announcement returns is significantly more positive for TourneyGame and Within TourneyDay samples in [ +2, +20] and [ +2, +30] windows (Table 9) | For the [ +2, +60] window, no significant difference found, suggesting full adjustment by a quarter (Table 9)
for_the_app: Flag earnings announcements during high distraction periods as potential underreaction candidates for storyline tracking.

themes: Does it still work; Skill or luck
title: Zeroing In on the Expected Returns of Anomalies
authors: Andrew Y. Chen, Mihail Velikov
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
key_findings: Average anomaly expected return is 8 bps per month net of costs and post publication effects | Academic implementations (equal weighted) show -3 bps per month net return in post publication and post-2005 data | Cost optimized implementations (value weighted + buy/hold spreads) show 13 bps per month net return in post publication and post-2005 data | Even the strongest anomalies (90th percentile) return only 20 bps per month after data mining adjustments | Size, Book to Market, and Momentum show mixed performance in post-2005 data (Size -26 bps, B/M 33 bps, Momentum 16 bps)
for_the_app: Warn users that anomaly signals often fail after costs; prioritize low turnover signals

title: Anomaly Time
authors: Boone Bowles, Adam V. Reed, Matthew C. Ringgenberg et al.
key_findings: Anomaly returns are concentrated in the first month after information release, with 52% of the four month return earned in that first month (1990-2019 sample). | In recent years (2005-2019), the concentration increased: 86% of the four month return was earned in the first month, and 50% in the first two weeks. | The Information rebalancing strategy generated an annualized mean daily abnormal return of 6.40% during the high activity period (February April), compared to 3.74% for the FF92 strategy, a difference of 2.56%. | In the recent period (2005-2019), the FF92 strategy produced insignificant returns (0.94% annualized) outside the earnings season, while the Information strategy still generated 4.03% in the February April window. | Transaction costs are higher for the Information strategy due to higher turnover, but net returns remain high in the immediate post release window, especially in recent years when trading costs have fallen.
for_the_app: The app must prioritize 'event time' logic: when a news event or filing is detected, the app should trigger a signal immediately and suggest a short holding period (1-4 weeks) rather than waiting for a monthly or quarterly rebalance, and it should warn users that the 'window of opportunity' closes rapidly (within 2 weeks in recent years).

title: Enhancing stock market anomalies with machine learning
authors: Vitor Azevedo, Christopher Hoegner
venue: Review of Quantitative Finance and Accounting
key_findings: Individual anomalies drop from an average monthly return of 0.53% (original settings) to 0.31% (standardized 1979-2019), with significance falling from 70% to 33% of anomalies passing the t statistic hurdle of 1.96. | The linear baseline factor (average of 299 anomalies) yields a monthly return of 0.92% (value weighted) from 2003 onwards, with a t statistic of 3.87. | Top machine learning models (e.g., DRF, GBM) achieve monthly returns between 1.76% and 2.33% (value weighted) with t statistics above 4.0, significantly outperforming the baseline. | The best models remain profitable with estimated round trip transaction costs of up to 2.4% (e.g., DRF.RETURN.ELASTICNET.STATIC allows 2.4% costs while yielding 2.33% monthly return). | Including only anomalies published after their respective dates (post publication test) still yields significant positive alphas, suggesting the patterns are not solely due to data mining or publication bias.
for_the_app: The app should prioritize aggregating multiple news derived signals into a composite score rather than trading single events, and must include a 'turnover cost' warning when suggesting trades that require frequent rebalancing of many positions.

title: Replicating Anomalies
authors: Kewei Hou, Xue Chen, Lu Zhang
key_findings: 286 out of 447 anomalies (64%) are statistically insignificant when using NYSE breakpoints to filter out tiny microcaps. | 95 out of 102 liquidity variables (93%) become insignificant under the same improved testing conditions. | Imposing a stricter cutoff (t value of 3) makes 380 anomalies (85%) insignificant. | For the 161 anomalies that still appear significant, their actual return sizes are often much lower than originally reported. | When tested against the authors' 'q factor model' (a benchmark for expected returns), 115 of the 161 significant anomalies (71%) become insignificant.
for_the_app: The app should include a 'survival probability' metric for any storyline it generates, warning users that most historical patterns fail strict statistical tests, and prioritize only those events with very strong, recent evidence.

title: Exploit Lifecycle: anomaly inversion after publication
authors: Tom Visser
key_findings: The paper is a pre registered test design; no results or return numbers are reported in the abstract. | The test aims to see if returns go below zero (invert) rather than just halving. | The study focuses on an 'embedded' subset of predictors from top finance journals (JF, JFE, RFS).
for_the_app: nothing

title: Do Anomalies Die When They Are Published?
authors: Christopher Dadoo, Lei Gao
key_findings: Average anomaly return is 0.61% per month in sample, falling to 0.42% out of sample, and 0.30% after publication. | The return decline after publication is -51% relative to the in sample period (paired t=-7.6). | In a pooled analysis, the post publication return is 0.27 percentage points lower per month than the pre publication period (t=-7.9). | Anomalies with above median in sample returns lose an extra 0.28 percentage points per month after publication (t=-4.3). | The drop in returns appears to be a gradual out of sample trend rather than a sudden drop exactly on the publication date (randomization inference p=0.31 for the level decay).
for_the_app: The app must include a 'decay factor' that automatically reduces the expected return of any identified news pattern based on how long ago the pattern was first published and how strong it was originally.

themes: Does it still work; Skill or luck
title: Publication Bias and the Cross-Section of Stock Returns
authors: Andrew Y. Chen, Tom Zimmermann
key_findings: typical equal weighted quintile long short return is about 8% per year (Page 1) | bias adjusted return is (1− 0.12)8% ≈ 7% (Page 1) | average post publication return is 25 basis points per month lower than the average bias adjusted return (Page 40) | Non statistical deterioration accounts for a significant 34% of the average in sample return (Page 40) | The returns in the original samples are around 0.70% per month on average (Page 18)
for_the_app: Account for 25 basis points per month return drop after publication

themes: Does it still work; Skill or luck
title: The History of the Cross-Section of Stock Returns
authors: Juhani T. Linnainmaa, Michael R. Roberts
key_findings: Average anomaly earns 28 basis points per month in sample, but only 8 basis points pre discovery and 10 basis points post discovery | Profitability factor earns 30 basis points per month (1963-2014) but only 2 basis points pre-1963 | Investment factor earns 25 basis points per month (1963-2014) but only 9 basis points pre-1963 | Distress risk earns 55 basis points per month alpha post discovery | Piotroski F score earns 60 basis points per month alpha in sample
for_the_app: Use distress signals; validate with out of sample history before relying on profitability factors

themes: Does it still work; Text and attention signals
title: The Short of It: Investor Sentiment and Anomalies
authors: Robert F. Stambaugh, Jianfeng Yu, Yu Yuan
key_findings: The combined long short strategy earns 93 basis points (0.93%) more per month following high sentiment than low sentiment (t statistic: 4.25). | The short leg of the combined strategy earns -68 basis points per month following high sentiment, compared to +65 basis points following low sentiment. | Following high sentiment, the short leg of the combined strategy earns 132 basis points less per month than it does following low sentiment (t statistic: -2.41). | Sentiment has no significant effect on the long leg of the strategies; the benchmark adjusted return difference between high and low sentiment periods is only 4 basis points. | In high sentiment months, the short leg of the combined strategy accounts for 78% of the total profits earned by that strategy across all months.
for_the_app: Add a 'Sentiment Filter' feature: when the app detects a high sentiment environment (based on broad market news tone), it should flag or suppress any 'sell' signals derived from fundamental anomalies, as shorting is likely to fail.

themes: Does it still work; Skill or luck
title: Does Academic Research Destroy Stock Return Predictability?
authors: R. David McLean, Jeffrey Pontiff
key_findings: Portfolio returns are 26% lower out of sample (after the original study period) compared to the original sample. | Portfolio returns are 58% lower post publication compared to the original sample. | The average in sample mean return for a predictor is 58.2 basis points per month. | Post publication, trading volume increases by 18.7% and dollar volume by 9.7% in predictor portfolios. | Post publication, the difference in short interest between the short and long sides of portfolios increases by 0.315% (a three fold increase relative to in sample levels).
for_the_app: The app should flag any news or event that matches a known academic predictor as 'high decay risk' if the paper was published recently, and prioritize storylines involving illiquid stocks where arbitrage is harder.

title: Anomalies and Their Short-Sale Costs
authors: Dmitriy Muravyev, Neil D. Pearson, Joshua Matthew Pollet
key_findings: average long short portfolio return is a significant 0.14% per month before short sale costs | average is −0.01% once returns are adjusted for borrow fees | anomalies are not profitable even before fees if the high fee observations, representing 12% of stock dates, are excluded | microcap stocks... average return of 0.36% per month... before consideration of the borrow fee | net of fee returns on anomaly portfolios are near zero
for_the_app: Add a borrow fee filter to block short signals on high cost stocks; warn users that event based short strategies may fail due to costs

themes: Does it still work; From signal to trade
title: A Taxonomy of Anomalies and their Trading Costs
authors: Robert Novy‐Marx, Mihail Velikov
key_findings: Round trip transaction costs for typical value weighted strategies average over 50 basis points (0.50%) per trade, reducing realized spreads by more than 1% for every 1% of monthly turnover. | Most anomalies with one sided monthly turnover lower than 50% continue to generate statistically significant net spreads after costs, provided they use cost mitigation strategies like the buy/hold spread. | Strategies with higher turnover (above 50% monthly) generally fail to generate significant net returns after costs, even with mitigation. | Equal weighted portfolios (giving small stocks the same weight as large ones) are often misleading because their high trading costs (2-3x higher than value weighted) erase their apparent gross profits. | The 'buy/hold spread' (trading hysteresis) is the single most effective simple strategy to reduce costs, often preserving more profit than simply trading less frequently or restricting to low cost stocks.
for_the_app: The app should implement a 'holding filter' that prevents selling a stock in a storyline unless the new event strongly contradicts the original thesis, effectively mimicking the 'buy/hold spread' to reduce turnover and costs.

title: Replicating Anomalies
authors: Kewei Hou, Xue Chen, Lu Zhang
key_findings: 65% of the 452 anomalies fail to clear the single test hurdle of |t| ≥ 1.96 when using NYSE breakpoints and value weighted returns. | Imposing the multiple test hurdle of |t| ≥ 2.78 raises the failure rate to 82%. | The high minus low customer momentum (Cm) decile earns 0.78% per month (t=3.85) at a 1-month horizon, substantially lower than the original 1.58% reported. | The high minus low 5-year sales growth (Sr) decile earns -0.19% per month (t=-1.08) with NYSE value weighting, failing to replicate the original negative growth premium. | The high minus low book to market (Bm) decile earns 0.54% per month (t=2.61) with NYSE value weighting, which is smaller than the 1.41% reported in the original 1973-1984 sample.
for_the_app: The app should flag any 'storyline' based on a known anomaly with a warning that the effect is likely weak, statistically insignificant, or driven by microcaps, and should prioritize strategies that survive the 2.78 t value hurdle.

title: On Persistence in Mutual Fund Performance
authors: Mark M. Carhart
key_findings: Buying last year's top decile mutual funds and selling last year's bottom decile funds yields a return spread of approximately 8 percent per year (US, 1963 to 1993). | Common factors (market, size, book to market, and momentum) explain 4.6 percent of the 8 percent spread, while expense ratios explain 0.7 percent and transaction costs explain 1 percent. | The only significant unexplained persistence is concentrated in the strong underperformance of the worst performing funds (bottom decile), which underperform T bills by 25 basis points per month in the year after ranking. | For every 100-basis point increase in expense ratios, annual abnormal return drops by about 154 basis points; for every 100-basis point increase in turnover, annual abnormal return drops by about 95 basis points. | Load funds underperform no load funds by approximately 80 basis points per year after controlling for expenses, likely due to higher transaction costs.
for_the_app: Feature: Flag funds with high turnover and expense ratios as 'cost traps' that likely underperform; Warning: Do not rely on 'hot hands' (past winners) for long term alpha, as the effect fades after one year.

title: Trading Costs of Asset Pricing Anomalies
authors: Andrea Frazzini, Ronen Israel, Tobias J. Moskowitz
key_findings: Actual trading costs are an order of magnitude smaller than previous studies suggest. | SMB net return 1.48% per year (historical mean) at $18.2 billion fund size, cost 1.47% per year. | HML net return 3.61% per year (historical mean) at $9.42 billion fund size, cost 1.35% per year. | UMD net return 5.17% per year at $6.2 billion fund size, cost 3.03% per year. | Combo net return 3.93% per year at $17 billion fund size, cost 1.46% per year.
for_the_app: nothing

title: What You See Is Not What You Get: The Costs of Trading Market Anomalies
authors: Andrew J. Patton, Brian Weller
key_findings: Momentum implementation costs are 2.2%-8.3% per year, eliminating most profits (1970-2016). | Value implementation costs are 2.4%-5.3% per year, sharply reducing returns. | Market and Size factors are implemented relatively well compared to academic benchmarks. | Excluding microcaps reduces the implementation gap by at most 27% for value and 18% for momentum. | Implementation costs are stationary over time despite declines in bid ask spreads.
for_the_app: Add a 'cost feasibility' warning for strategies relying on momentum or value factors, noting that reported returns often exclude trading friction.

title: Trading costs, short sale constraints, and the performance of stock market anomalies in Emerging Europe
authors: Adam Zaremba, Jerzy Nikorowski
key_findings: Over 30 strategies (mostly value, momentum, technical analysis, profitability, and issuance effects) delivered significant abnormal returns before costs. | Once trading costs, short sale constraints, and other filters were applied, only a 'handful' of anomalies remained significantly profitable. | The impact of costs and constraints was described as 'truly lethal' to most strategies. | The study covered 70 anomalies across 5 countries and 1,800 stocks. | The majority of anomalies ceased to be profitable once transaction costs were taken into account, regardless of rebalancing frequency.
for_the_app: The app should include a 'cost sensitivity' filter that automatically discounts any news based strategy if the expected return is lower than the estimated bid ask spread and commission for that specific stock's liquidity.

title: Have capital market anomalies attenuated in the recent era of high liquidity and trading activity?
authors: Tarun Chordia, Avanidhar Subrahmanyam, Qing Tong
key_findings: Average returns from a portfolio strategy based on prominent anomalies have approximately halved after decimalization | EW hedge portfolio return decreases from an average of 0.85% per month in the first half of the sample to 0.46% per month in the second half | Momentum strategy has a monthly return of 1.44% (t statistic=4.61) in the full sample | Size (value) anomaly provides a monthly return of about 0.56% (1.0%) | Momentum and PEAD are statistically insignificant in the second sub period (1994-2011)
for_the_app: Warning: Historical factor returns may not persist; focus on unique news linkages
