title: Price Impact in Closing Auctions, Opening Auctions, and Continuous Markets: A Benchmark for Cost of Trading on Anomalies
authors: Amit Goyal, Narasimhan Jegadeesh, Yanbin Wu
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
key_findings: Closing auctions account for about 10% of daily trading volume. | Price impact is lower in closing auctions than in the continuous market for all stocks except Nasdaq microcaps. | Opening auctions are illiquid. | Annualized trading costs for long/short portfolios based on profitability and investment ratios range from 17 to 41 basis points (bps) when using optimal mechanisms. | Excluding microcaps, annualized trading costs fall to 9–21 bps in closing auctions.
for_the_app: The app should include a feature that suggests routing trades for event driven strategies to the closing auction (last few minutes of the day) to minimize slippage, while flagging Nasdaq microcaps as high cost exceptions.

title: The Accruals Anomaly: Can Implementable Portfolio Strategies Be Developed That Are Pofitable Net of Transactions Costs in the UK?
authors: Nuno F. Soares, Andrew W. Stark
key_findings: Average annual abnormal returns generally decline as prior period accruals move from low to high, consistent with the accruals anomaly. | The hedge portfolio (long low accruals, short high accruals) generates losses when using an equally weighted approach after accounting for conservative transaction costs. | The hedge portfolio generates positive, but not statistically significant, abnormal returns when using a value weighted approach after accounting for conservative transaction costs. | Profitable exploitation of the anomaly generally requires taking short positions in portfolios featuring relatively small capitalisation firms. | The accruals anomaly is not egregious enough in the UK to challenge the semi strong version of the efficient markets hypothesis once costs are considered.
for_the_app: The app should flag 'Accruals' as a high risk signal for retail traders due to low liquidity and high transaction costs, and perhaps filter out small cap stocks when evaluating this specific event type.

title: The Persistence of the Accruals Anomaly*
authors: Baruch Itamar Lev, Doron Nissim
key_findings: The accruals anomaly generated mean annual abnormal returns between 7.5% and 8.9% over the sample period (1965-2002). | The magnitude of the anomaly did not decline over time; the trend coefficient was statistically insignificant. | Over 70% of the total strategy return came from shorting high accruals firms (average 5.4% annual gain), while long positions in low accruals firms yielded only 2.1% (barely significant). | To achieve statistically significant returns (t statistic ≥ 2.0), a portfolio required approximately 40 securities in each decile. | Even with 40 securities, the strategy produced positive abnormal returns in only two thirds of the years before transaction costs.
for_the_app: The app should flag 'High Accruals' as a negative signal but warn users that acting on it requires a diversified portfolio (40+ stocks) and that shorting these specific stocks is costly and risky for retail investors.

title: The Going‐Concern Market Anomaly
authors: Asad Kausar, Richard Taffler, Christine E.L. Tan
key_findings: The market underreacts to GC announcements, resulting in a downward drift of -14% over the 12-month period following the announcement (control firm matched method). | The 6-month abnormal return is -9% (control firm matched method) and -5% (five factor model). | After adjusting for transaction costs (bid ask, commissions, and shorting fees), the arbitrage strategy is no longer profitable; net returns become statistically insignificant or negative. | The anomaly is driven by small, low priced firms: the 12-month abnormal return for firms below the median price ($1.16) is -15%, while it is only -8% for firms above the median price. | The market processes 'good news' (withdrawal of a GC opinion) efficiently, showing no significant drift, unlike the bad news (GC opinion) which shows a delayed reaction.
for_the_app: Add a 'Distress Warning' feature that flags stocks receiving first time GC opinions as high risk for continued decline, but explicitly warn users that 'shorting' these stocks is likely unprofitable due to high friction costs; instead, use the signal to avoid holding these stocks.

title: Betting against beta
authors: Andrea Frazzini, Lasse Heje Pedersen
key_findings: US equities (1926–2012): The BAB factor produced a CAPM alpha of 0.73% per month (t stat 7.44) and a Sharpe ratio of 0.78. | International equities (1984–2012): The BAB factor produced a CAPM alpha of 0.64% per month (t stat 4.68) and a Sharpe ratio of 0.95. | US Treasury bonds (1952–2012): The BAB factor produced a CAPM alpha of 0.17% per month (t stat 4.44) and a Sharpe ratio of 1.02. | US corporate bonds (1973–2012): The BAB factor produced a CAPM alpha of 0.57% per month (t stat 3.72) and a Sharpe ratio of 1.02. | The strategy works because constrained investors (who cannot borrow easily) bid up the prices of high beta assets, making them offer lower risk adjusted returns, while unconstrained investors buy low beta assets and leverage them up.
for_the_app: The app should flag 'high beta' stocks (those that swing more than the market) as potentially overvalued in the storyline context, and suggest 'low beta' stocks as stable anchors for a portfolio, while warning users that shorting the high beta side is likely not feasible for them.

title: The Shorting Premium and Asset Pricing Anomalies
authors: Itamar Drechsler, Qingyi Song Drechsler
key_findings: CME portfolio (long cheap to short, short expensive to short) has monthly gross return of 1.43%, net return of 0.91%, and 1.53% four factor alpha (Abstract) | Anomaly returns (8 types) are small and insignificant among low fee stocks (80% of stocks) but amplified among high fee stocks (Conclusion) | Top 5% high fee stocks (1-minus-10b portfolio) have gross return of 2.13% per month, net return of 1.27% per month, and 2.27% four factor alpha (Conclusion) | SIR IO based 1-minus-10b portfolio has raw return of 1.88% per month and FF4 alpha of 1.96% per month (Section 5.1) | Adding a shorting risk factor (CME) to Fama French model reduces anomaly alphas to near zero (Conclusion)
for_the_app: Filter anomaly signals by shorting fee levels; warn users that news driven anomalies may fail if short fees are low

title: Navigating the factor zoo around the world: an institutional investor perspective
authors: Söhnke M. Bartram, Harald Lohre, Peter F. Pope et al.
key_findings: Momentum had the highest return (11.10% p.a. globally) and outperformed the market by 4.26% p.a. | Value underperformed the market with an annualized active return of -1.41% p.a. globally | Quality and Low Volatility displayed positive active returns (2.47% and 1.94% p.a. respectively) | Low Volatility had the lowest volatility (10.54% p.a.) and highest Sharpe ratio (0.67) | Except for equity value, all style factors (including fixed income and commodities) displayed positive excess returns throughout the sample period
for_the_app: Prioritize Quality and Momentum storylines over Value; ensure the app filters for liquid large/mid cap stocks to match investable universes.

title: Breaking the Selection Link: A Pre-Registered Validation Audit of the Factor Zoo
authors: Oussama Souihli
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
key_findings: On 210 tested factors from the Chen Zimmermann list, only 64 were certified as still working after publication. | On 142 JKP USA factors, only 3 were certified as still working. | The actual number of working factors was far lower than the optimistic prediction that 88% would retain significance. | The actual number of working factors was higher than the pessimistic prediction that 80% would be false, suggesting about 39% of the Chen Zimmermann factors are likely real. | The study found very few 'sign inversions' (factors that flipped from positive to negative returns), contradicting the idea that most published results are just random noise.
for_the_app: The app should include a 'validity decay' warning for any news driven strategy, indicating that the statistical edge of a pattern likely decreases significantly a few years after it is published.

title: The Causal Effect of Limits to Arbitrage on Asset Pricing Anomalies
authors: Yongqiang Chu, David A. Hirshleifer, Liang Ma
key_findings: Pilot program reduced combined anomaly long short returns by 72 basis points per month (Abstract) | Effect comes only from short legs (Abstract) | Anomalies survive risk adjustment (Table A.2, FF adjusted alphas positive for 11 anomalies) | Effect more pronounced on small stocks (95 bps reduction vs 47 bps for large, Section 5.1) | Effect more pronounced on more restricted stocks (109 bps reduction vs 33 bps, Section 5.1)
for_the_app: warn that short side signals are sensitive to liquidity constraints

title: Short Arbitrage, Return Asymmetry, and the Accrual Anomaly
authors: David A. Hirshleifer, Siew Hong Teoh, Jeff Jiewei Yu
key_findings: The monthly return spread between the lowest and highest accrual deciles is 105 basis points (t = 5.57) for the full sample (1988-2002). | On NASDAQ, the highest accrual decile loses 80 basis points per month (t = -7.62), while the lowest accrual decile gains only 19 basis points per month, creating significant asymmetry. | On NYSE, the highest accrual decile loses 25 basis points per month (t = -2.37), and the strategy is more symmetric between long and short sides. | When institutional ownership drops below 5%, abnormal return asymmetry increases by 2.2% per month (26.4% annualized). | The asymmetry is significantly stronger among firms with low liquidity (small size, low turnover) and high residual volatility.
for_the_app: The app should flag high accrual stocks as potential short candidates but must cross reference with institutional ownership and liquidity metrics; if a stock has low institutional holdings or low turnover, the app should warn that the expected price drop may be delayed or muted due to short sale constraints.

title: Volatility‐Managed Portfolios
authors: Alan Moreira, Tyler Muir
key_findings: The volatility managed Market Portfolio produced an annualized alpha of 4.86% (Table 1, Panel A) and increased the buy and hold Sharpe ratio by 25% (Introduction). | The volatility managed Momentum (Mom) Portfolio produced the highest annualized alpha of 12.51% (Table 1, Panel A). | The strategy survives realistic transaction costs: even with a 10 basis point cost per trade and an additional 4 basis points during high volatility (VIX 20% to 40%), the Market Portfolio alpha remains positive (Section 3.2). | In 80% of 20 OECD countries, the volatility managed stock market index had a higher Sharpe ratio than the passive buy and hold strategy (Appendix A.2). | The strategy reduces risk exposure during recessions (beta drops by roughly 0.4 to 0.5 in recessions) while still earning high average returns, contradicting standard risk based explanations (Table 3 and Introduction).
for_the_app: Implement a 'Volatility Sizing' feature that automatically adjusts the recommended position size for any stock or portfolio based on the previous month's realized volatility of the broader market or the specific sector, reducing exposure when volatility spikes.

themes: From signal to trade; Skill or luck
title: Do Investors Trade Too Much?
authors: Terrance Odean B
key_findings: Securities bought underperform securities sold by 1.36% over 84 trading days (Panel A) | Securities bought underperform securities sold by 3.31% over 252 trading days (Panel A) | Average total cost of a round trip trade is about 5.9 percent (commission plus spread) | Calendar time portfolios show monthly excess returns of -0.293% for 4-month formation periods (Table 2) | Even when controlling for size and book to market, purchases underperform sales (Table 3)
for_the_app: Flag when a user's trade mirrors the average retail investor behavior (buying recent winners) and warn about expected underperformance

title: Just How Much Do Individual Investors Lose By Trading?
authors: Brad M. Barber, Yi‐Tsung Lee, Yu‐Jane Liu et al.
key_findings: Individual investor portfolios suffered an annual performance penalty of 3.8 percentage points (Taiwan, 1995–1999). | Institutional investors enjoyed an annual performance boost of 1.5 percentage points after commissions and taxes (Taiwan, 1995–1999). | Virtually all individual trading losses are traced to their aggressive orders, while both aggressive and passive institutional trades are profitable. | Total losses for individual investors from 1995 to 1999 were $NT 935 billion, equivalent to 2.2% of Taiwan's GDP or 2.8% of total personal income. | Most losses and gains accrue within a few weeks of the trade and reach an asymptote at a horizon of six months.
for_the_app: The app should include a 'Cost of Trading' calculator that estimates the drag on returns based on a user's current turnover rate and order aggressiveness, warning them if their projected costs exceed the 3.8% annual penalty observed in the study.

title: Do Individual Investors Ignore Transaction Costs?
authors: Deniz Anginer, Snow Xue Han, Çelim Yıldızhan
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
key_findings: Individual investors with longer holding periods tend to hold less liquid stocks (US and Finland data). | The link between holding periods and transaction costs is stronger for financially sophisticated households. | Findings are confirmed by analyzing changes around exogenous shocks to stock liquidity. | Individual investors do not ignore non salient costs like transaction fees; they are aware of trading costs.
for_the_app: Add a warning metric that flags when a user's portfolio holds illiquid stocks for long periods, suggesting they may be paying hidden costs that erode returns.

title: Investor Overconfidence and Trading Volume
authors: Meir Statman, Steven R. Thorley, Keith Vorkink
key_findings: Market wide turnover is positively related to lagged market returns for many months; a 7% market return versus -5% leads to an 'extra month' of volume spread over the next six months. | Individual security turnover is positively related to both lagged security returns (disposition effect) and lagged market returns (overconfidence), with market shocks having a larger impact than security specific shocks. | The relationship between past returns and trading volume is more pronounced in small cap stocks and in earlier periods (1963–1982) where individual investors held a greater proportion of shares. | In the most recent subperiod (1993–2002), the evidence for the disposition effect (selling winners, holding losers) largely disappears, and the sensitivity of volume to market returns is weaker compared to earlier decades. | The lead lag relationship between returns and volume is statistically significant at the 0.01 level for the first six months following a market return shock in the full sample.
for_the_app: Add a 'Sentiment/Overconfidence' metric that flags when a user's portfolio or the broader market has had strong recent gains, warning that trading volume may be driven by emotion rather than new information.

title: Tax-Motivated Trading by Individual Investors
authors: Zoran Ivkovich, James M. Poterba, Scott J. Weisbenner
key_findings: Hazard rate for stock sale drops from fifteen percent in the first month to less than five percent per month after six months | By one year after purchase, probability stock has been sold is more than 50 percent if gain, 44 percent if loss | Expected holding period for stock in taxable account at time of purchase is just over six years | Expected holding period rises to just under 14 years after a stock has been held for a year | Chance stock will be repurchased within 30 days if sold at loss in December is substantially lower than other months
for_the_app: Feature: flag stocks with losses in December for potential selling pressure; warning: lock in may reduce selling pressure on winners over time

title: Portfolio Concentration and the Performance of Individual Investors
authors: Zoran Ivković, Clemens Sialm, Scott J. Weisbenner
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
key_findings: Stocks purchased by all households have an average excess return of –1.6 percent during the year following the purchase, while stocks sold have 0.2 percent | Trades of concentrated investors outperform those made by diversified investors by 0.8 percentage points on an annual basis (all households) | For households with portfolios of at least $100,000, concentrated trades outperform diversified trades by 3.3 percentage points per year (excess return) | Intersection of non S&P 500 and local stocks yields 59 basis points per month (7.3 percentage points annualized) for all households | Holdings of concentrated investors outperform diversified holdings by 16 basis points per month (1.9 percentage points annualized)
for_the_app: Flag when a tracked investor concentrates on a stock with a developing news storyline as a potential skill signal

title: Talk and Action: What Individual Investors Say and What They Do
authors: Daniel Dorn, Gur Huberman
key_findings: Self reported risk aversion is the single most important determinant of both portfolio diversification and trading turnover. | Investors who report being more risk tolerant hold less diversified portfolios and trade more aggressively. | Less experienced investors tend to churn poorly diversified portfolios; a one standard deviation increase in experience is associated with a decrease in monthly turnover from 9.5% to 8%. | Investors who think they are more knowledgeable than the average investor churn their portfolios more, even if they hold better diversified portfolios. | The most aggressive traders earn significantly lower portfolio returns than the least aggressive traders, but their performance is similar before transaction costs, indicating trading costs are the primary cause of underperformance.
for_the_app: The app should include a 'behavioral check' feature that asks users to rate their risk tolerance and confidence before executing a trade, warning them if their stated profile suggests they are overtrading or under diversifying based on the patterns found in this study.

themes: From signal to trade; Skill or luck
title: Are Investors Reluctant to Realize Their Losses?
authors: Terrance Odean B
key_findings: Investors realized 20.1% of gains but only 12.6% of losses in the 1987–1990 period (t statistic -23.0), showing a strong preference for selling winners. | In December, the pattern reverses slightly due to tax motives: 12.9% of gains were realized versus 14.3% of losses (t statistic 1.9), but the effect is weaker than the annual average. | Over the next 252 trading days (one year), stocks sold for a profit outperformed the market by 2.35%, while stocks held at a loss underperformed the market by 1.06%. | The difference in excess returns between sold winners and held losers is 3.41% over one year, with a p value of 0.001, indicating the mistake is statistically significant. | A hypothetical investor who sold a winner instead of a loser would lose an estimated 4.4% in value over the next year due to missed gains and lost tax benefits.
for_the_app: The app should flag positions that are currently at a loss and have been held for a long time, warning the user that historical evidence suggests these stocks are likely to underperform the market if held further.

title: The Long‐Run Performance of initial Public Offerings
authors: Jay R. Ritter
key_findings: IPOs had an average 3-year holding period return of 34.47% (exclusive of the initial first day gain), while matching firms returned 61.86% over the same period. | By the end of 36 months, the cumulative average matching firm adjusted return for IPOs was -29.13% (t statistic -5.89). | The median 3-year return for IPOs was -16.67%, compared to +38.54% for matching firms. | IPOs issued in high volume years (like 1983) performed the worst, with the underperformance concentrated in young growth companies. | Even though IPOs had higher average betas (1.39 in the first year) than matching firms (1.14), the underperformance remained significant, suggesting risk adjustment alone does not explain the result.
for_the_app: Add a 'Long Run IPO Warning' feature: if a stock is in its first 3 years post IPO, flag it as historically likely to underperform its sector peers, and suggest reducing position size or avoiding new entries after the initial hype.

title: Bayesian Kelly criterion as an allocation strategy in Finnish stock markets
authors: Risto K. Heikkinen
venue: Jyväskylä University Digital Archive (University of Jyväskylä)
key_findings: Bayes Kelly strategies produced better risk adjusted returns than all comparison methods based on the Sharpe ratio (Finnish market, 2010-2019). | Solidium's capital development nearly matched the Bayes Kelly strategy with a 20% acceptable annual loss limit, but Solidium lost the Sharpe ratio comparison due to higher return volatility. | Adding the most promising single stock to the portfolio based on analyst target prices did not significantly affect final wealth. | Adding the single stock reduced return volatility and slightly improved the Sharpe ratio. | The study found no clear consensus on the fixed constant for risk allocation in previous literature, which this paper addresses by combining multiple extensions.
for_the_app: Implement a dynamic position sizing feature that adjusts exposure based on a user defined maximum acceptable loss (e.g., 20%) rather than fixed weights, and warn users that adding single stocks based on analyst targets may only reduce volatility without increasing returns.

title: Practical Implementation of the Kelly Criterion: Optimal Growth Rate, Number of Trades, and Rebalancing Frequency for Equity Portfolios
authors: Andrea Carta, Claudio Conversano
venue: Frontiers in Applied Mathematics and Statistics
key_findings: Full Kelly maximizes expected growth rate and median terminal wealth in simulations | Triple Kelly leads to ruin (losing wealth almost 80% of times in 10,000 trades simulation) | Rolling Kelly (2-year window, monthly rebalancing) CAGR 15.01% vs Tangent 10.55% (EuroStoxx50 2007-2018) | Kelly portfolio is less diversified (3 assets vs 8 in Tangent) and has higher volatility | Short window (2 years) for Kelly optimization outperforms longer windows
for_the_app: Feature to calculate position sizing based on estimated edge, but warn about estimation risk and recommend Half Kelly

title: How Does the Fortune’s Formula Kelly CapitalGrowth Model Perform?
authors: Leonard C. MacLean, Edward O. Thorp, Yonggan Zhao et al.
key_findings: Full Kelly and close to full Kelly strategies show great superiority over longer horizons, earning very large gains a large fraction of the time. | Kelly and high fractional Kelly strategies exhibit very risky short term performance. | There is a consistent trade off of growth versus security as a function of the bet size determined by the various strategies. | No matter how favorable the opportunities are, a sequence of bad scenarios can lead to very poor final wealth outcomes with a loss of most of the investor's initial capital. | In the two asset case (U.S. equity and T bills with annual re balancing), there is a confirmed trade off between terminal wealth and risk: the more aggressive the strategy, the higher the risk.
for_the_app: The app should include a 'risk of ruin' warning when suggesting position sizes based on Kelly criteria, and default to fractional Kelly (e.g., half Kelly) to prevent the 'devastating collapse' described in the findings.

title: Dynamic stop-loss rules as universal performance enhancers
authors: Dimitrios D. Thomakos, Rafael Yahlomi
key_findings: Daily stop loss rules significantly outperform buy and hold equity and bond benchmarks, equally weighted portfolios, and simple moving average trend following strategies. | Longer term stop loss rules help avoid market crashes by exiting the market but cause investors to miss up market days. | Shorter term stop loss rules allow investors to stay in the market longer during good days but come at the expense of increased risk and higher drawdowns. | Performance enhancements are robust to various variations on the initial theme. | Performance improvements can come from sources related to static stop loss rules.
for_the_app: Implement a configurable stop loss feature that allows users to choose between 'longer term' (crash protection) and 'shorter term' (capture more upside) modes, with a warning about the trade off between missed gains and reduced drawdowns.

title: PERFORMANCE OF STOP-LOSS RULES VS. BUY-AND-HOLD STRATEGY
authors: Garib Yusupov, Bergsveinn Snorrason
venue: Lund University Publications Student Papers (Lund University)
key_findings: Trailing Stop Loss (TSL) at a 15% loss limit achieved the highest cumulative return of 74% over the period, compared to Buy and Hold (BH) which had a cumulative excess return that was substantially negative. | Traditional Stop Loss (SL) at a 10% loss limit achieved the highest cumulative return of 57%, with the 15% limit close behind at 53%. | The TSL strategy at a 20% loss limit produced the highest average quarterly return of 1.7%, while the SL strategy at 15% produced 1.5%. | Stop loss strategies significantly reduced portfolio variance (risk); the 5% TSL limit had a variance of 0.15%, which was ten times lower than the BH strategy's variance of 1.5%. | The 5% TSL limit resulted in negative returns (average -0.1%, cumulative -8.1%), indicating that too tight a stop loss can hurt performance in this dataset.
for_the_app: Implement a 'Risk Adjusted Exit' feature that suggests stop loss levels (e.g., 10-15%) based on the asset's volatility, and warn users that very tight stops (under 10%) may increase the chance of being stopped out by noise rather than a true trend change.

title: On the efficacy of stop-loss rules in the presence of overnight gaps
authors: Argimiro Arratia, Albert Dorador
key_findings: Fixed percentage rule: Sharpe Ratio multiplied by ~3, Sortino by ~8 in Regime Switching model with gap (Table 3) | In rising markets, stop loss improves risk adjusted return but absolute return is slightly lower (usually less than 100 bps drop) | In falling markets, stop loss improves absolute expected return (e.g., Ford: 11.3 percentage points higher than Buy and Hold in 2.5 months) | Flash crashes trigger Fixed % and ATR rules reducing returns, but RSI and MA crossover rules are robust to flash crashes | Overnight gaps make stop loss performance appear better than models without gaps suggest (gaps bypass stops, but modeling them shows the risk)
for_the_app: Add a Stop Loss Calculator feature that warns users about overnight gap risk and suggests volatility based (ATR) or trend based (MA) exits over fixed % for robustness

title: Do initial stop-losses stop losses?
authors: Bruce James Vanstone
key_findings: The benchmark system (no stops) achieved a Daily Mean Return of $1.76 per trade with an average holding period of 15.85 days. | Adding fixed percentage stops (1% to 10%) reduced the Daily Mean Return in every case, with the 1% stop yielding only $0.34 per trade. | Adding ATR based stops (1x to 5x ATR) resulted in negative Daily Mean Returns for all tested levels, ranging from -$18.28 (1x ATR) to -$0.54 (5x ATR). | The Sharpe ratio for the no stop portfolio was 0.50, while all stop loss variations resulted in lower ratios (e.g., 0.25 for 1% stop, -3.27 for 1x ATR stop). | Statistical tests (ANOVA) found no significant difference where stops improved performance; the 1x ATR stop was statistically worse than the no stop strategy.
for_the_app: The app should warn users that adding fixed initial stop losses to a positive expectation strategy may reduce overall returns, and suggest that stop loss logic should be validated against the specific strategy's historical data before implementation.

title: A Framework for Stop-Loss Analysis on Trading Strategies
authors: Oliver Chan, Alfred Ka Chun Ma
key_findings: No numerical findings are reported in the provided text. | The text only introduces a framework for analysis rather than presenting empirical results.
for_the_app: Implement a 'risk return trade off' calculator that visualizes the Maximum Unrealized Loss (MUL) for different stop loss settings before a trade is executed.

title: Trading to Stops
authors: Nora Imkeller, L. C. G. Rogers
key_findings: Uncertainty about drift justifies using stops (if drift known positive, no lower stop needed). | Story (C) (switch funds only on loss) performed best (Objective 20.216 in Table 7). | Fixed stops often perform close to optimal stopping rules (e.g., 1.6305 vs 1.6770 in Table 14). | Time dependent slopes improve objectives slightly (e.g., Story C improvement 1.7%). | Mean trade times vary (e.g., 0.0998 to 0.0125 in Tables 2-7).
for_the_app: Feature to calculate optimal stop levels based on news uncertainty; warn against frequent switching.

title: Equity Portfolio Diversification: How Many Stocks are Enough? Evidence from Five Developed Markets
authors: Vitali Alexeev, Francis Tapon
key_findings: Using Standard Deviation, an average US investor needed 24 stocks (2004-2005) to reduce diversifiable risk by 90%, but needed 56-73 stocks during the 2008-2011 Global Financial Crisis. | To achieve a 90% reduction in diversifiable risk 90% of the time in the US using Expected Shortfall (ES1%), a portfolio of 33 to 55 stocks was required for most years, spiking to 63-72 stocks during 2008-2011. | Using Terminal Wealth Standard Deviation (TWSD), the US required a relatively constant portfolio of 83-99 stocks to achieve 90% risk reduction. | In Japan, the average correlation among stocks was highest (0.16), while in Australia it was lowest (0.07); higher correlations generally meant fewer stocks were needed to diversify. | During periods of high market volatility and high correlations (crises), the number of stocks required to assure risk reduction 90% of the time increased significantly compared to calm periods.
for_the_app: Add a 'Diversification Health' metric that compares the user's current portfolio size against the dynamic, crisis adjusted thresholds (e.g., 'You hold 15 stocks; during the 2008 crisis, 63 were needed for 90% risk reduction confidence') to warn users of concentration risk.

title: Transaction Costs of Factor-Investing Strategies
authors: Feifei Li, Tzee-man Chow, Alex Pickard et al.
key_findings: Implicit market impact costs may substantially erode a strategy's expected excess returns (Abstract). | Costs are related to liquidity characteristics such as turnover rate and turnover concentration (Citing paper: Is Factor Investing Sustainable after Price Impact Costs? The Capacity of Factor Investing in Korea, 2019). | Index construction methods, when thoughtfully designed, can reduce market impact costs (Abstract). | Estimates for actual transaction costs vary widely and depend on a variety of factors (Citing paper: Pairs trading in the German stock market: is there still life in the old dog?, 2025). | For relatively simple factor strategies, it is difficult to provide accurate estimates of these costs (Citing paper: On the performance of factor investing: an analysis based on constant mix and buy and hold strategies, 2025).
for_the_app: The app should include a 'cost estimator' feature that flags news driven storylines involving high turnover stocks or sectors, warning users that frequent rebalancing might erase the expected gains from the event.

title: Chinese securities investment funds: the role of luck in performance
authors: Jun Gao, Niall O’Sullivan, Meadhbh Sherman
key_findings: The evidence does not support the existence of 'genuine' skilled fund managers. | Top ranked funds with positive abnormal performance are attributed to 'good luck' rather than 'good skill'. | Poor performance in bottom funds is mainly due to 'bad skill' (bad stock picking). | Survivorship bias (dropping failed funds from data) was a concern addressed in the study design. | Findings are robust across different sub periods and market conditions.
for_the_app: Add a warning feature that flags 'hot' funds (top performers) as likely luck driven and suggests avoiding them, while highlighting 'cold' funds (bottom performers) as likely skill driven and recommending avoidance.

title: Mutual Fund Performance: Skill Or Luck?
authors: Dirk Nitzsche, Keith Cuthbertson, Niall O’Sullivan
key_findings: The best performing fund achieved an abnormal return of 0.745% per month (8.94% per year) with a t statistic of 4.023, but the bootstrap p value was 0.056, meaning it marginally fails to reject the hypothesis that this result was due to luck alone. | At the negative end of the performance scale, the analysis strongly rejects the hypothesis that poor funds are merely unlucky; these funds demonstrate 'bad skill'. | Genuine stock picking ability was found in a small number of top performing 'equity income' and 'equity growth' funds, but not in 'small stock' or 'general equity' funds. | Positive performance in 'onshore' funds was attributed to genuine skill, whereas positive performance in 'offshore' funds was attributed to luck. | The average risk adjusted abnormal performance across the entire industry was negative or zero, consistent with the view that most active managers underperform after costs.
for_the_app: The app should implement a 'skill vs. luck' filter that uses bootstrapping or similar statistical tests on a fund's or stock's track record to warn users when a recent winning streak is statistically indistinguishable from random noise.

title: An Empirical Investigation of the Performance of Japanese Mutual Funds: Skill or Luck?
authors: Keith Pılbeam, Hamish Preston
key_findings: Japanese Mutual Funds fail to outperform the benchmark four factor capital asset pricing model based on equal weight portfolio and Jensen's alpha measures. | 33 funds showed significant positive market timing ability, while 31 funds showed significant negative timing ability, largely offsetting each other. | A large proportion of funds fail to outperform a hypothetical world with no skill, even after correcting for non normality using Fama and French's cross sectional bootstrap. | There is stronger persistence for poor performing funds than for strong performing funds. | About 9.30% of the funds were identified as having market timing ability (as noted in citing papers summarizing the T M model results).
for_the_app: nothing

title: U.S. Mutual Fund Performance: Skill or Luck?
authors: Kenneth Nordlund Hoem, Erik Rosmer Aasland
key_findings: Regression results for an equal weighted portfolio suggest that fund managers in aggregate do not possess sufficient skill to cover their costs. | Bootstrap results show that a sizeable minority of fund managers do have sufficient skill to cover their costs. | The evidence of skill is stronger when examining performance gross of management fees. | Under the assumption that true alpha follows a normal distribution, the standard deviation (sigma) for the left tail (unskilled) is about 0.75% a year. | Under the same assumption, the standard deviation (sigma) for the right tail (skilled) is about 1.25% a year.
for_the_app: nothing

title: Reassessing False Discoveries in Mutual Fund Performance: Skill, Luck, or Lack of Power?
authors: Angie Andrikogiannopoulou, Filippos Papakonstantinou
key_findings: The FDR method misclassifies 65% of funds with economically large alphas of ±2% per year as having zero alpha (no skill). | In simulations where the true proportion of zero alpha funds was 1%, the FDR method estimated it to be 70%. | The accuracy of the FDR method does not improve by adding more funds to the sample (large N); it only improves by adding more years of data per fund (large T), and even then, convergence is very slow. | The method assumes that p values above a certain threshold come only from zero skill funds, but in reality, low skill funds also produce p values in this range, causing the method to overestimate the number of zero skill funds. | Realistic levels of correlation between funds increase the variability of the FDR estimates by 2.5 to 2.8 times compared to assuming funds are independent.
for_the_app: nothing

title: False Discoveries in Mutual Fund Performance: Measuring Luck in Estimated Alphas
authors: Laurent Barras, Olivier Scaillet B, Russ R. Wermers
key_findings: About one fifth (20%) of the funds in the population truly yield negative alphas, dispersed in the left tail of the distribution. | A small proportion of funds have truly positive performance, concentrated in the extreme right tail of the distribution. | For 'All' funds, standard tests at a 20% significance level (gamma=0.20) suggest 17.9% have negative alphas, but the FDR method corrects this to 9.9%. | In 'Growth and Income' (GI) funds, the FDR for the best funds is 100%, meaning all funds identified as 'best' by standard tests were actually lucky (zero true alpha). | Aggressive Growth (AG) funds showed a low FDR among the best funds (23.3% at gamma=0.05), implying a genuine proportion of skilled managers in this specific category.
for_the_app: The app should include a 'Luck Adjustment' metric that calculates the False Discovery Rate for any news driven strategy or stock it recommends, warning the user if the signal is likely a statistical fluke rather than a genuine edge.

title: Distinguishing between skill and luck in the returns of Norwegian mutual funds
authors: Mathias Tidemann Krafft, Petter Bringedal
key_findings: After adjusting for luck, the top 5% of funds exhibit skills to earn 3.3% or more in annual alpha above the fees they charge. | The bottom 5% of funds destroy at least 3.7% per year in value (negative alpha after fees). | The average active fund as a whole does not possess sufficient skill to cover costs; the average alpha is not significantly different from zero or negative depending on the model. | There is no evidence of performance persistence; past success does not reliably predict future success, making it difficult to choose winners before the fact. | Survivorship bias is significant: defunct funds underperformed active funds by an average of 2.79% per year, meaning studies ignoring dead funds overstate the industry's performance.
for_the_app: The app should implement a 'luck adjusted' scoring system that compares a stock's or fund's recent performance against a simulated distribution of random outcomes to flag whether a recent streak is likely skill or noise.

title: Passive versus Active Fund Performance: Do Index Funds Have Skill?
authors: Alan D. Crane, Kevin Crotty
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
key_findings: Tests imply index fund skill exists, is persistent, and is in similar proportion as in active funds. | Outperformance by top active funds is lower when benchmarked to the index fund distribution. | Active fund outperformance disappears when accounting for residual risk. | Stochastic dominance tests suggest no risk averse investor should choose a random active fund over a random index fund.
for_the_app: nothing

title: Mutual Fund Managers’ Prior Work Experience and Their Investment Skill
authors: Rui Chen, Zhennan Gao, Xueyong Zhang et al.
key_findings: Managers with prior industry analyst experience exhibit superior stock picking skills | Managers with prior macroanalyst experience time the market better | Bootstrap analyses suggest the performance difference between the two manager types cannot be attributed purely to luck | Chinese mutual funds are largely managed by solo fund managers rather than teams (70% single managed in 2016) | Chinese market is quite volatile with monthly stock market volatility reaching 9.65% compared to 4.45% on the S&P 500 between 1996 and 2015
for_the_app: Add a feature to scan and display a fund manager's prior work experience (industry analyst vs. macroanalyst) as a context clue for their likely strength (stock picking vs. market timing) when linking news events to portfolio decisions

title: Returns to individual traders in agricultural futures markets: skill or luck?
authors: Nicole M. Aulerich, Scott H. Irwin, Philip Garcia
key_findings: Traders in the top half of the profit distribution in one period tended to stay in the top half in the next period. | Differences in profitability magnitude between the top and bottom deciles support the existence of persistent skill among the top 10% of traders. | Annual rankings showed persistence in profits for a smaller subset of traders who were most continuously active in the markets. | The study found an indication of persistence even in the face of losses for some traders. | Results were observed across monthly, quarterly, and annual time horizons.
for_the_app: nothing

title: Does Herding Behavior Reveal Skill? An Analysis of Mutual Fund Performance
authors: Hao Jiang, Michela Verardo
key_findings: Top decile herding funds underperform bottom decile antiherding funds by 19 basis points per month, which equals 2.28% per year (US, 1990-2009). | After adjusting for risk factors (CAPM, Fama French, Carhart), the performance gap (alpha) ranges from 1.68% to 2.52% per year. | The performance gap is persistent over holding periods of 6 to 24 months, with the gap widening as the horizon extends. | Funds with a herding tendency 1.65 standard deviations above average underperform those 1.65 standard deviations below average by 11 basis points per month (1.32% per year). | The negative relation between herding and performance holds even when controlling for fund size, age, turnover, expense ratios, and past performance.
for_the_app: Add a 'Herding Score' metric to fund profiles; flag funds with high positive scores as 'Low Skill/High Imitation' and suggest avoiding them or shorting them if possible.

title: False Discoveries in UK Mutual Fund Performance
authors: Keith Cuthbertson, Dirk Nitzsche, Niall O’Sullivan
key_findings: At a 10% significance level, the False Discovery Rate (FDR) for the best performing funds is 67%, meaning only about 2% of all funds truly outperform their benchmarks. | For the worst performing funds, the FDR is relatively low at 15.9%, resulting in 20% of all funds truly underperforming their benchmarks. | When controlling the overall FDR at a 10% threshold, a portfolio of the 'best' funds (approx. 10-20 funds) generates an expected alpha between 4.57% and 10.1% per annum. | A portfolio of the 'worst' funds (approx. 40-85 funds) selected under the same 10% FDR threshold generates an expected alpha of approximately -3.6% per annum. | The pattern of very few genuine winners and a larger number of genuine losers holds across different investment styles (all companies, small companies, and equity income), though equity income funds show fewer genuine losers.
for_the_app: The app should implement a 'False Discovery' filter: when the app identifies a potential 'winner' story, it should flag that the probability of this being a false positive is high (e.g., >60%) unless the signal is extremely strong, and prioritize 'loser' stories as they are more likely to be genuine.

title: Mutual fund performance evaluation methodology and local false discovery rate approach
authors: Nik Tuzov
key_findings: The previous method by Barras et al. (2008) has both statistically and practically significant bias, making it too optimistic about mutual fund performance. | The new method shows that Barras et al. overestimated the number of skilled funds. | A typical study using monthly data and standard models has very low statistical power, meaning it struggles to find skilled managers even if they exist. | It usually requires many years of data to confidently identify outperforming funds due to low statistical power. | The new method offers a way to account for errors in the performance evaluation model itself, which previous methods often ignored.
for_the_app: The app should warn users that a short history of good news linked trades does not prove skill; it should require a minimum track record length (e.g., 3-5 years) before labeling a strategy as 'confirmed' to avoid false positives.

title: Bond mutual fund performance: Evidence from the skill ratio and false discovery rate
authors: Lifa Huang, Wayne Y Lee, Craig G. Rennie
key_findings: 28.7% of actively managed bond fund managers are highly skilled, including 36.3% of corporate bond funds and 17.3% of government bond funds (US, 1999-2016). | Only 2.4% of all bond fund managers add net value to investors after fees, including 5.0% of corporate funds and 0.0% of government funds. | In large corporate bond funds, 55.5% of managers are skilled, compared to 29.9% in small corporate funds. | 14.2% of midsize corporate bond funds produce positive net value added for investors, compared to 4.7% for large and 8.1% for small funds. | 47.4% of small corporate bond funds generate negative net value added for investors, compared to 19.5% for midsize and 19.9% for large funds.
for_the_app: nothing

title: False Discoveries in the Performance of Canadian Equity Mutual Funds
authors: Nhan Viet Tran
key_findings: Approximately 85% of the sampled Canadian equity mutual funds are genuinely zero alpha (no skill). | False positive rates (lucky funds mistaken for skilled) are approximately 20% for gross returns and 55% for net returns. | False negative rates (unlucky zero alpha funds mistaken for unskilled) are 6% for gross returns and 22% for net returns. | True skilled managers are concentrated in the extreme right tail of the performance distribution, representing less than 2% of the industry. | Stock picking skill has been on a downward trend and correlates negatively with the total number of funds, making it a rare resource.
for_the_app: The app should include a 'luck vs. skill' warning metric for any news driven strategy or fund it analyzes, calculating the probability that recent outperformance is statistically significant versus a false discovery.

title: Skilled Mutual Fund Selection: False Discovery Control Under Dependence
authors: Lijia Wang, Xu Han, Xin Tong
venue: Journal of Business and Economic Statistics
key_findings: d group cumulative returns median >150% during 2010-2019, p group (p value selection) had negative median returns | Skilled funds generated positive median annual alphas for most scenarios, some above 2.5% | Unskilled group median annual alphas were all negative | Selected skilled funds strongly outperformed S&P 500 index during same period | Predictive power deteriorates over long horizon (distinction among groups narrows over time)
for_the_app: Add a 'skill vs luck' metric that calculates probability of true skill across similar funds, warn users when predictive signals fade after 5+ years, track turnover ratios as a risk indicator

title: Split-Sample Strategies for Avoiding False Discoveries
authors: Michael Anderson, Jeremy Magruder
key_findings: An optimized split sample approach achieves 90% of the statistical power of an optimal Preanalysis Plan (PAP) without requiring preregistration. | In a specific simulation with one true effect and 19 null hypotheses, setting a low pass threshold (t statistic of 1) and using a small exploratory sample (26% of data) increased power by 39% compared to a standard 50/50 split with a higher threshold. | Re analyzing the GoBiFo data with a hybrid approach would have identified that the program increased local governance participation (a 'software' outcome) with a full sample t statistic of 4.4, which was missed by the original PAP. | The hybrid approach revealed meaningful heterogeneity: the program was more effective in smaller villages and in villages with an 'extractive chief,' findings that were not robust under the original PAP. | Under a hybrid approach with False Discovery Rate (FDR) control, there was a 51-58% chance of identifying that larger villages were less effective at improving infrastructure, a finding missed by pure PAPs.
for_the_app: Implement a 'Holdout Validator' feature: when the app identifies a potential storyline, it must withhold the most recent data (e.g., the last 20% of the timeline) to confirm the pattern holds before recommending a trade, preventing the app from overfitting to noise.

title: The Deflated Sharpe Ratio: Correcting for Selection Bias, Backtest Overfitting, and Non-Normality
authors: David H. Bailey, Marcos López de Prado
key_findings: As the number of independent trials (N) increases, the expected maximum Sharpe ratio of the 'best' strategy increases purely by chance, even if the true skill is zero. | In a numerical example, a strategy with an annualized Sharpe ratio of 2.5 over 5 years (1,250 days) was deemed statistically insignificant (only 90% confidence) because it resulted from 88 independent trials. | If the same strategy had been the result of only 46 independent trials, it would have been considered significant (above 95% confidence). | Non normal returns (skewness and kurtosis) further inflate performance estimates, making it harder to distinguish skill from luck. | The optimal number of trials to test before selecting a strategy is approximately 37% (1/e) of the total set of theoretically justifiable configurations, following the 'secretary problem' logic.
for_the_app: The app should include a 'Backtest Overfitting Risk' metric that calculates the Deflated Sharpe Ratio for any storyline it generates, requiring the user to input or estimate the number of alternative storylines considered to adjust the confidence level.

title: The Deflated Sharpe Ratio: A Unified Framework for Search-Adjusted Performance Inference
authors: Marcos López de Prado, Emilio Porcu
key_findings: The Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) addresses the problem that a strategy selected after searching many options cannot be evaluated as if it were pre specified. | DSR L provides a parsimonious location benchmark for determining if a result is significant after accounting for the search process. | DSR LS adds the dispersion of the selected maximum to support power analysis and minimum track record calculations. | DSR EO uses the complete search distribution when exact tail inference is available. | The shape of the return distribution (Gaussian vs. Student t) can alter both the magnitude and direction of approximation errors in performance evaluation.
for_the_app: Implement a 'Search Penalty' metric that reduces the reported confidence score of any strategy based on the number of variations (parameters, news triggers, or holding periods) the user or the system tested to find it.

title: Practical Applications of The Deflated Sharpe Ratio: Correcting for Selection Bias, Backtest Overfitting, and Non-Normality
authors: David H. Bailey, Marcos López de Prado
key_findings: The Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) adjusts the observed Sharpe ratio based on the number of trials (N), the variance of the trials' Sharpe ratios, and the non normality (skewness and kurtosis) of the return series. | A strategy selected as the best among many specifications has an upward biased performance estimate, where the bias grows with the number of specifications tried and shrinks with the length of the evaluation window. | High simulated performance is easily achievable after backtesting relatively few strategy configurations due to memory effects in financial series, leading to systematic under performance in live trading. | The paper introduces the concept of 'Minimum Backtest Length' (MinBTL) to determine the sample size required to avoid selecting a strategy that looks good in sample but fails out of sample. | Citing papers note that without DSR adjustment, a Sharpe ratio computed on a sample without accounting for the number of trials that produced the winning trades will overstate the strategy's true skill.
for_the_app: The app should include a 'search pressure' metric that counts how many news event combinations or storylines were tested before selecting the final signal, and automatically adjust the confidence score of the recommendation downward if the search space was large.

title: purgedcv: scikit-learn-compatible purged and combinatorial cross-validation for time-series and financial machine learning
authors: Евгений Лазарев
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
key_findings: The text is an abstract for a software library and does not report empirical market returns, specific holding periods, or trading results. | The library implements the 'Deflated Sharpe Ratio' and 'Minimum Track Record Length' to help distinguish skill from luck when testing many ideas. | The library uses 'Purged and Embargoing' techniques to handle overlapping labels in time series data, preventing look ahead bias. | The algorithms are based on prior work by Marcos Lopez de Prado (2018) and Bailey and Lopez de Prado (2012, 2014), not new empirical findings in this specific text. | No specific stock universe, market years, or cost assumptions are tested or reported in this abstract.
for_the_app: Integrate a 'Deflated Sharpe Ratio' calculator and 'Minimum Track Record Length' estimator into the app's backtesting engine to warn users when a strategy's success is likely due to luck or overfitting.

title: In-Sample and Out-of-Sample Sharpe Ratios for Linear Predictive Models
authors: Antoine Jacquier, Johannes Muhle‐Karbe, Mulligan, Joseph
key_findings: Replication ratio diminishes for complex strategies with many assets and many weak signals. | Replication ratio increases when more training data is used. | Panel regression (simpler model) had 68% replication ratio vs 9% for full model on real data. | Panel out of sample Sharpe ratio was 0.5 vs 0.3 for full model (full model in sample was 3.6). | Low true Sharpe ratio signals are particularly vulnerable to overfitting.
for_the_app: Add a 'replication ratio' warning metric to alert users when a storyline relies on too many weak signals or short data history.

title: Twelve Rejections: Pre-Registered Kill Criteria and the Non-Monotone Cost of Clean Data in Retail-Scale Systematic Trading
authors: Brian Kilgore
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
key_findings: Split adjustment caused Post Earnings Announcement Drift to flip from a positive t statistic of 0.495 to a negative t statistic of -0.258. | Split adjustment caused Market Residual Momentum to improve from a t statistic of 1.868 to 2.017, crossing the pre registered kill threshold of 2.0. | Correcting a 2x undercharge in transaction costs for the Market Residual Momentum strategy returned its t statistic to 1.909, causing it to fail the significance gate again. | Even when a factor cleared the primary significance gate after corrections, it was rejected by a second pre registered gate (deflated Sharpe ratio) accounting for multiple testing, resulting in a 'DEAD_DSR' verdict. | A single gate pre registration would have produced a false positive that survived until a cost bug was found, as the candidate was flattered by two defects: a survivorship affected universe and an undercharged cost model.
for_the_app: Implement a 'pre registration' logic module for the app that requires a strategy to pass multiple independent statistical gates (e.g., t stat AND deflated Sharpe) before flagging a storyline as valid, and explicitly model the impact of data corrections (like splits) on signal direction.

title: Equity Strategy Backtesting: Luck or Edge? The MinervaScore as a Statistical Robustness Grade
authors: Maria Laura Santoni, Vincent Jouanne, Matthew L. Scullin
key_findings: In synthetic markets with known ground truth, the MinervaScore separates true signals from lucky backtests with an AUROC of 0.989. | In a pre registered test on unseen real market data, the score showed no significant forward relationship with future performance (Spearman ρ = 0.013, p = 0.40) in a population with limited surviving edge. | On the production population of 359,062 records, only 3,848 (1.07%) cleared all five validation gates to receive the Robustness Seal. | The score successfully avoids 'saturation' where too many strategies get high scores; only 0.002% of raw scores were ≥ 0.99. | One specific model family (Bollinger) showed a nominally positive correlation (ρ = 0.134) in a sub analysis, but this was not statistically significant after correcting for multiple comparisons and does not prove general predictive power.
for_the_app: Integrate a 'Robustness Check' feature that calculates the Deflated Sharpe Ratio and Probability of Backtest Overfitting for any user defined storyline or strategy, warning the user if the score is low due to excessive parameter searching.

title: Learning by Trading
authors: Amit Seru, Tyler Shumway, Noah Stoffman
key_findings: Average individual investors underperformed the market by 48 basis points (0.48%) over a 30-day horizon and 50 basis points over a 60-day horizon. | Performance is persistent: investors in the top quartile of returns in one year tend to outperform those in the bottom quartile in subsequent years (Spearman rank correlation of 0.164). | Two types of learning exist: some investors genuinely improve their trading ability with experience, while others stop trading after realizing they are unskilled. | Failure to account for investors leaving the market (attrition) significantly overestimates how quickly the average investor learns to trade successfully. | Investors who trade options (a proxy for sophistication) are more likely to trade frequently and show different learning patterns than the average investor.
for_the_app: The app should include a 'survival' metric that flags users who consistently underperform and suggests they stop trading or reduce position sizes, rather than assuming they will improve with more trades.

title: Do individual investors learn from their trading experience?
authors: Gina Nicolosi, Liang Peng, Ning Zhu
key_findings: Ability to forecast excess returns over 20 trading days significantly increases stock purchases (coefficients for sign and magnitude forecasts are positive and significant at 1% level). | Ability to forecast excess returns over 5 trading days does not significantly affect purchase decisions (sign forecast coefficient is negative, magnitude forecast is insignificant). | Trading experience (measured by number of purchases, number of unique stocks, and variance of purchase amounts) significantly improves future risk adjusted portfolio returns. | Learning behavior is heterogeneous: inactive traders benefit more from experience than active traders, and 'losers' (bottom third performers) adjust trading activity more dramatically based on inferred ability than 'winners'. | Individual investors adjust trading based on inferred ability over a one month horizon, suggesting they learn from mistakes over this timeframe rather than the very short term.
for_the_app: Implement a 'Personal Learning Tracker' feature that calculates a user's rolling 20-day stock selection ability score and suggests increasing trade size if the score is positive, while warning against reacting to 5-day noise.

title: The Behavior of Individual Investors
authors: Brad M. Barber, Terrance Odean B
venue: Handbook of the economics of finance
key_findings: The average individual investor underperforms a market index by 1.5% per year; the most active traders underperform by 6.5% annually (US, 1991-1996). | Stocks bought by individual investors underperform stocks sold by 23 basis points per month over the 12 months following the trade (US, 1987-1993). | Stocks heavily bought by individuals over short horizons (1 day to 1 week) earn strong returns in the subsequent week, while heavily sold stocks earn poor returns (US, 2000-2003). | Individual investors earn strong returns on local stocks (headquartered within 240 miles), but this finding is not robust to reasonable variations in methodology (US, 1991-1996). | High IQ investors are more likely to hold mutual funds and larger numbers of stocks, suggesting better diversification, but the paper does not explicitly state they outperform after costs in this specific context (Finland, 1995-2002).
for_the_app: The app should flag 'local bias' and 'familiarity' as negative signals, warn users when they are selling winners too early (disposition effect), and highlight that short term momentum in retail buying is a valid but fleeting signal that requires quick exits.

title: Investor Attention and Insider Trading
authors: Sattar Mansi, Lin Peng, Jianping Qi et al.
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
key_findings: Insider sales during high attention months are followed by a significantly lower return of 73.7 basis points compared to sales during normal months (coefficient -0.682, t stat -2.93). | Insider purchases during low attention months yield higher abnormal returns (111.6 basis points) compared to purchases during high attention months (91.1 basis points), a difference of -20.5 basis points. | A conditional long short strategy (buying on insider buys when attention is low, selling on insider sells when attention is high) generates a 5-factor alpha of 136.7 basis points per month for value weighted portfolios, compared to 89.7 basis points for the unconditional strategy. | The conditional strategy's excess return is driven by the 'Attention' subsample, where insider sales are followed by significantly larger negative returns than in the non attention subsample. | The effect is stronger for 'lottery type' stocks (low price, high volatility/skewness) and firms with low institutional ownership (high retail ownership).
for_the_app: The app should integrate a 'Retail Attention' metric (e.g., Google Trends or similar) and flag insider trades: warn users against buying if an insider bought during a spike in attention, and highlight insider buys as strong signals if attention is currently low.

title: Analysis of herding behavior in individual investor portfolios using machine learning algorithms
authors: Taylan Mavruk
venue: Research in International Business and Finance
key_findings: Individual investors who herd do not outperform either the market or non herd portfolios. | The disposition effect (selling winners too early, holding losers too long) and attention effect explain herding at the stock level. | At the individual level, a higher cumulative number of buys and larger portfolio values reduce the likelihood of herding. | High portfolio returns lead to a small increase in herding behavior. | Market risk premium is the most predictive factor in performance tests; equally weighted factors provide more consistent results than value weighted factors.
for_the_app: Add a 'herding risk' metric to the app that flags stocks where retail trading volume or search volume spikes unusually, warning users that such moves often lead to temporary price inflation followed by a reversal.

title: Overconfidence Among Professional Investors: Evidence from Mutual Fund Managers
authors: Alexander Puetz, Stefan Ruenzi
key_findings: Top performing funds with high subsequent turnover underperform top performing funds with low subsequent turnover by 1.6% to 1.9% per year (US, 1999 to 2008). | The performance gap is statistically significant at the 5% level when selecting the top 10% of funds, but weaker and only significant with four factor alphas when selecting the top 20%. | High turnover after good performance is driven by the fund's individual past performance, not the general market performance. | Good past performance leads to a U shaped relationship with turnover: both the very best and very worst performers trade more, but for different reasons (overconfidence vs. strategy change). | Excessive trading by overconfident managers explains why good performance often does not persist; the high turnover group fails to maintain their edge.
for_the_app: Add a 'Confidence Check' metric: if a user's portfolio has had strong recent gains, the app should flag a warning to reduce trading frequency or hold current positions to avoid overconfidence driven turnover.

title: Is the Aggregate Investor Reluctant to Realise Losses? Evidence from Taiwan
authors: Brad M. Barber, Yi‐Tsung Lee, Yu‐Jane Liu et al.
key_findings: In aggregate, investors in Taiwan are about twice as likely to sell a stock if they are holding it for a gain rather than a loss (1995–1999). | 84% of all Taiwanese investors sell winners at a faster rate than losers. | Individual investors, corporations, and dealers exhibit the disposition effect, while mutual funds and foreigners (less than 5% of trades) do not. | Short term momentum strategies in Taiwan (1981–2002) show no reliable profit: the 'winner loser' return difference is statistically insignificant (e.g., 0.0068% for 1-month formation/1-month hold, t stat 1.14). | Despite strong evidence of the disposition effect, the paper finds 'little evidence of momentum profits' in the Taiwanese market during the sample period.
for_the_app: The app should flag 'disposition effect' risks: when a user holds a stock that has dropped, the app should highlight that the user is statistically likely to hold it too long, and warn that past price momentum (winners) does not guarantee future returns in this context.

title: The probability of backtest overfitting
authors: David H. Bailey, Jonathan Michael Borwein, Marcos López de Prado et al.
key_findings: In a simulation of a random walk (no real signal), optimizing 8,800 parameter combinations produced an in sample Sharpe ratio of 1.27, but the Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBO) was 55%, meaning the 'best' strategy had a 55% chance of underperforming the average out of sample. | In a second simulation with a real seasonal effect added, the PBO dropped to 13%, correctly identifying that the strategy selection added value and was not purely overfit. | Standard 'hold out' methods (testing on a single fixed unseen dataset) are unreliable because they do not account for the total number of trials (N) attempted, leading to false positives when billions of combinations are tested. | The CSCV method requires a sufficient number of trials (N) to generate a granular distribution of performance ranks; if N is too small, the estimation of overfitting probability becomes inaccurate. | A high PBO indicates that the selection process is likely overfitting, even if the in sample Sharpe ratio looks excellent; conversely, a low PBO suggests the strategy selection is robust.
for_the_app: The app should include a 'PBO Calculator' feature that asks the user for the number of strategy variations tested and the in sample performance, then outputs the probability that the result is a false positive, warning the user if the probability of overfitting is high (e.g., >50%).

title: Pseudo-Mathematics and Financial Charlatanism: The Effects of Backtest Overfitting on Out-of-Sample Performance
authors: David H. Bailey, Jonathan Michael Borwein, Marcos López de Prado et al.
venue: Notices of the American Mathematical Society
key_findings: If a researcher tries only 10 alternative strategy configurations on random data, they are expected to find a strategy with an in sample Sharpe ratio of 1.57, even though the true out of sample Sharpe ratio is 0. | With only 5 years of data, no more than 45 independent model configurations should be tried to ensure the expected maximum in sample Sharpe ratio does not exceed 1. | In a simulation of a random walk with 1,000 daily prices, the optimal parameter combination (Entry day=11, Holding period=4, Stop loss=-1, Side=1) produced an annualized Sharpe ratio of 1.27 purely by chance. | The Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio (PSR) for the random walk example was 2.83, implying less than a 1% probability that the true Sharpe ratio is below 0.5, despite the true value being 0. | Backtests that do not report the number of trials (N) attempted to find the optimal parameters make it impossible to assess the risk of overfitting.
for_the_app: The app must implement a 'trials counter' that tracks every variation of a storyline or rule tested; it should automatically penalize the confidence score of a strategy based on the number of trials (N) used to generate it, using the Minimum Backtest Length (MinBTL) formula to warn users if the data history is too short for the number of tests performed.

title: Extreme Value Theory and Backtest Overfitting in Finance
authors: Daniel C Byrnes
key_findings: For 10 tested strategy configurations (N=10) over one year of data, a Sharpe ratio higher than 3.82 is required to be 95% confident the strategy is not skill less (pure chance). | For 10 tested strategy configurations (N=10) over one year of data, a Sharpe ratio higher than 1.53 is required to be 50% confident the strategy is not skill less. | The mathematical approximation used to calculate these thresholds converges very slowly (rate of 1/log n), meaning the formula may be inaccurate for small sample sizes or realistic numbers of trials. | The paper assumes returns follow a normal distribution, but notes that real financial data often has 'fat tails' (power law distribution), which makes extreme events more likely and the normal distribution model potentially unreliable. | The paper proposes that future work should use the Frechet distribution (for fat tailed data) instead of the Gumbel distribution (for normal data) to better model real market backtests.
for_the_app: The app should include a 'Backtest Validity' warning that calculates the number of strategy variations tested and adjusts the required performance threshold (Sharpe ratio) upward based on the Minimum Backtest Length formula to prevent users from acting on false positives.

title: How hard is it to pick the right model? MCS and backtest overfitting
authors: Diego Aparicio, Marcos López de Prado
key_findings: MCS is not robust to multiple testing. | MCS requires a very high signal to noise ratio to be usable. | Most modern finance model selection methods are subject to backtest overfitting. | Overfitting tends to produce very good results in backtests but only for the short term (as noted by citing papers).
for_the_app: The app should implement a strict penalty for testing many storylines (multiple testing correction) and warn users that a strategy passing a standard test might just be overfit noise unless the signal strength is very high.

title: PSEUDO MATHEMATICS AND FINANCIAL CHARLATANISM: BACKTEST OVERFITTING AND OUT-OF-SAMPLE PERFORMANCE
authors: David H. Bailey, Jonathan Michael Borwein, Marcos López de Prado et al.
key_findings: High performance is easily achievable after backtesting a relatively small number of alternative strategy configurations. | The higher the number of configurations tried, the greater the probability that the backtest is overfit. | Financial analysts rarely report the number of configurations tried, making it impossible for investors to evaluate the degree of overfitting. | Backtest overfitting has a detrimental effect on the future strategy's performance due to the nature of financial time series.
for_the_app: The app should track and display the 'number of strategy configurations tested' for every storyline it generates, warning the user if the number is high to indicate a high risk of overfitting.

themes: From signal to trade; Skill or luck
title: Does the Stock Market Overreact?
authors: Werner F. M. De Bondt, Richard H. Thaler
key_findings: Over a 3-year formation and 3-year test period, loser portfolios (bottom 35 stocks) outperformed the market by 19.6% over 36 months, while winner portfolios underperformed by 5.0%, resulting in a 24.6% difference (t statistic: 2.20). | The overreaction effect is asymmetric: the reversal is much larger for losers than for winners. | Most of the excess returns for loser portfolios are realized in January, with excess returns of 8.1% in the first January, 5.6% in the second, and 4.0% in the third. | For a 1-year formation period, no significant price reversal was observed (difference in cumulative average residual was -0.005 at 12 months). | The effect is strongest when the formation period is longer (3 to 5 years) and the portfolios are more extreme (top/bottom 35 stocks vs. deciles).
for_the_app: The app should flag stocks with extreme negative returns over the last 36 months as potential 'reversal candidates' and specifically highlight the month of January as a high probability entry or exit point for these storylines.

themes: Text and attention signals; From signal to trade
title: All That Glitters: The Effect of Attention and News on the Buying Behavior of Individual and Institutional Investors
authors: Brad M. Barber, Terrance Odean B
key_findings: Individual investors are net buyers on high attention days (e.g., 17.32 percent order imbalance on news days vs –2.51 percent without news at large retail brokerage) | All of the alphas reported in the last two columns of Table V are negative, most reliably so | The three factor alphas for the news sort are not significantly different from zero | Institutional investors are more likely to be net buyers on days with low abnormal trading volume than on those with high abnormal trading volume | Investors prone to engaging in attention based buying do not benefit from doing so
for_the_app: Add a warning feature when news/volume spikes occur to prevent attention based buying

themes: Events that make prices drift; From signal to trade
title: The New Issues Puzzle
authors: Tim Loughran B, Jay R. Ritter
key_findings: IPOs had an average annual return of only 5% over the five years after going public (1970-1990). | SEOs had an average annual return of only 7% over the five years after the offering (1970-1990). | An investor would have needed to invest 44% more money in issuers than in non issuers of the same size to achieve the same wealth five years later. | The median 5-year raw return for IPOs was -39%, while the median for matching firms was 16%. | Issuing firms underperformed by 38 basis points per month (approx. 4% per year) in regressions, even after adjusting for size and book to market effects.
for_the_app: Add a 'New Issue Warning' flag to the app: if a stock has issued equity in the last 60 months, the app should highlight the historical tendency for underperformance and suggest waiting or avoiding unless other strong positive storylines override this signal.

themes: News spreading to linked companies; Text and attention signals; Already priced in or not; Does it still work; From signal to trade
title: Bad News Travels Slowly: Size, Analyst Coverage, and the Profitability of Momentum Strategies
authors: Harrison G. Hong, Terence M. Lim, Jeremy C. Stein
key_findings: Momentum profitability declines sharply with firm size once past the very smallest stocks | Momentum strategies work better among stocks with low analyst coverage (Sub1 vs Sub3 differential of 0.42 percent per month) | Effect of analyst coverage is greater for stocks that are past losers than for past winners | Low coverage momentum lasts up to 2 years (19.63 percent total profit for Sub1 vs 8.90 percent for Sub3 over 24 months) | LAST strategy (short low coverage losers, long high coverage losers) earns 9.32 percent cumulative profit over 2 years
for_the_app: Flag stocks with low analyst coverage as having higher potential for delayed price reaction to news events

title: When Are Contrarian Profits Due to Stock Market Overreaction?
authors: Andrew W. Lo, A. Craig MacKinlay
key_findings: At lag 1 (1 week), positive cross autocovariances account for half of the expected profits; in the central size quintile, they account for 67 percent. | For the smallest size quintile, positive cross effects account for 66 percent of expected profits at lag 2. | The strategy yields an average profit of $1.69 per week for all stocks and $4.53 per week for the smallest quintile. | The ratio of expected profits to average long investment is 1.1 percent for all stocks and 2.2 percent for the smallest quintile. | Positive cross effects (lead lag) persist at lags 2, 3, and 4, contradicting the 'bid ask bounce' model which predicts profits should vanish after lag 1.
for_the_app: The app should prioritize linking news events to large cap 'leader' stocks and then flagging their small cap 'follower' counterparts (suppliers, peers) as potential buy targets 1-4 weeks later, rather than just flagging the stock that just dropped.

themes: News spreading to linked companies; Already priced in or not; Does it still work; From signal to trade
title: Market Frictions, Price Delay, and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns
authors: Kewei Hou, Tobias J. Moskowitz
key_findings: The most severely delayed firms (top decile) command a return premium of more than 12% per year after adjusting for size, value, and momentum factors. | The delay premium subsumes the entire size effect and a portion of the value effect; when adjusting for delay, the return spread between small and large firms drops from 57 basis points to 5 basis points (equal weighted). | Post earnings announcement drift is monotonically increasing in delay; low delay firms show no drift, while high delay firms show significant drift over the 12 months following an earnings surprise. | Idiosyncratic risk is priced (associated with higher returns) only among the most severely delayed firms, not among non delayed firms. | The delay effect is strongest among small, value, and recent loser stocks, and the top decile of delayed firms represents less than 0.02% of the total market value.
for_the_app: The app should calculate a 'Price Delay' metric for every stock in its database by analyzing how quickly its price reacts to broad market news over the past year, and flag high delay stocks that have recently experienced positive news or earnings surprises as potential 'slow burn' opportunities.

themes: News spreading to linked companies; Already priced in or not
title: Contagious Speculation and a Cure for Cancer: A Nonevent that Made Stock Prices Soar
authors: Gur Huberman, Tomer Regev
key_findings: EntreMed's stock rose from a Friday close of $12.06 to a Monday close of $51.81 (a 330% return) following a Sunday New York Times article that contained no new information, having been reported 5 months prior. | On the day of the non new news (May 4, 1998), the Nasdaq Biotechnology Index (excluding ENMD) rose 7.5% on average, with 7 stocks rising over 25% and 3 rising over 100%. | The price surge was largely permanent; EntreMed's price did not fall below $20 until late August 1998, and by late fall it was still 40% higher than its pre article price. | When the news was debunked in November 1998, EntreMed's stock fell 24% in one day but remained more than double its pre article price. | Bristol Myers Squibb (BMY), a large partner firm, saw a 3.12% return ($3.3 billion market cap increase) on the day of the non new news, whereas it showed minimal reaction to the actual scientific breakthrough 5 months earlier.
for_the_app: The app should flag when a news story about a company is a 're report' of older information (e.g., by checking dates of original scientific papers or prior articles) and warn users that a surge in linked peers might be a temporary sentiment bubble rather than a fundamental shift.

title: The "Dartboard" Column: Second-Hand Information and Price Pressure
authors: Brad M. Barber, Douglas Loeffler
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
