key_findings: Average positive abnormal returns of 4% were documented in the two days following the publication of recommendations (nearly twice the level of previous studies). | Average trading volume doubled normal volume levels in the two days following publication. | The positive abnormal return on the announcement day was partially reversed within 25 trading days. | The initial price move is attributed to a mix of naive buying pressure (retail investors reacting to the news) and the actual information content of the recommendations. | Stocks randomly picked by throwing a dart (without analyst recommendations) did not show these effects.
for_the_app: The app should flag 'Dartboard' style media recommendations as potential short term 'noise' events that often reverse, warning users not to chase the initial price spike and suggesting a wait and see approach or a contrarian entry after the 25-day reversal window.

title: Discrete Expectational Data and Portfolio Performance
authors: Edwin J. Elton, Martin J. Gruber, SETH GROSSMAN
key_findings: Approximately 4.5% extra return can be earned by purchasing new buys rather than new sells (US, pre-1986). | Only 11.6% of the 9,977 analyst recommendations in the sample involved a change in recommendation level; the rest were reiterations. | A significant post event return drift of 2.1% was observed in the two months (approx. 42 trading days) after the announcement. | Excess returns were found in the calendar month of the recommendation change and during the next two months. | Stock prices react to financial analysts' recommendation revisions, with the market showing an incomplete reaction that leads to predictable drift.
for_the_app: The app should track 'analyst recommendation changes' as a primary trigger, flagging upgrades for potential long entries and downgrades for short entries, while warning users that the historical drift (2.1% over 2 months) is based on 1980s data.

themes: Events that make prices drift; News spreading to linked companies; Already priced in or not
title: Momentum Strategies
authors: Louis K.C. Chan, Narasimhan Jegadeesh, Josef Lakonishok
key_findings: Sorting by past 6-month returns yields a spread of 8.8% between winners and losers over the next 6 months, and 15.4% over the first year. | Sorting by 6-month moving average of analyst forecast revisions yields a spread of 7.7% over the next 6 months and 9.7% over the first year. | About 41% of the momentum profit in the first 6 months occurs specifically around the dates of the next two quarterly earnings announcements. | The arbitrage portfolio (buying winners, selling losers) based on double sorts of prior return and analyst revisions has an intercept of 1.43% per month (t stat 5.91) after adjusting for size and book to market risk. | Stocks with the worst past earnings performance continue to underperform for up to three years, while the outperformance of past winners is mostly concentrated in the first year.
for_the_app: The app should prioritize linking a positive price move to a specific earnings surprise or analyst upgrade, then flag the stock for a 6-month hold with a specific alert to check the next earnings date, as a significant portion of the profit arrives then.

themes: News spreading to linked companies; Already priced in or not
title: Investment Analysis and the Adjustment of Stock Prices to Common Information
authors: Michael John Brennan, Narasimhan Jegadeesh, Bhaskaran Swaminathan
key_findings: Returns on portfolios of firms followed by many analysts tend to lead those of firms followed by fewer analysts, even when firms are of approximately the same size. | Firms with many analysts respond more rapidly to market returns than firms with few analysts. | The relationship is nonlinear: the marginal effect of adding more analysts on the speed of price adjustment increases as the number of analysts grows.
for_the_app: The app should flag 'lagging' stocks in a storyline: when a major event hits a highly analyzed company, the app should identify its less analyzed peers and set an alert to watch for a delayed price move over the next few days.

title: The Stock Market Valuation of Research and Development Expenditures
authors: Louis K.C. Chan, Josef Lakonishok, Theodore Sougiannis
key_findings: Stocks with high R&D relative to market equity earned an average excess return of 6.12% per year over the three years following portfolio formation. | The top quintile of R&D to market stocks earned an alpha of 0.55% per month (annualized 6.6%) in the first year after formation, with a spread of 8.28% per year between the highest and lowest quintiles. | Over the three post formation years, the highest R&D to market portfolio had a Sharpe ratio of 0.85, compared to 0.53 for the market index. | High R&D intensity is positively associated with higher return volatility, even after controlling for firm size and age. | Stocks with high advertising relative to market equity also showed positive excess returns, with the top quintile earning an average annual excess return of 3.10% over three years.
for_the_app: The app should flag companies with high R&D or advertising spending relative to market value as potential 'undervalued' candidates, particularly if they have a history of poor stock performance, and warn users that these stocks may be more volatile.

themes: Events that make prices drift; Does it still work
title: Supply and Demand Shifts in the Shorting Market
authors: Lauren H. Cohen, Karl B. Diether, Christopher J. Malloy
key_findings: An outward shift in shorting demand (DOUT) leads to negative abnormal returns of 2.98% in the following month (US, 1999-2003). | The DOUT effect is strongest in small stocks, with a total predicted drop of 6.31% in the month following the shift for stocks in the smallest 20% by market cap. | A trading strategy buying stocks with inward demand shifts (DIN) and shorting those with outward demand shifts (DOUT) yields 3.48% per month before costs, or roughly 4.5% per year after estimating transaction and shorting costs. | Outward supply shifts (SOUT) show negative returns in some portfolio tests but are not statistically significant in regression tests once time fixed effects are included. | The predictive power of shorting demand is concentrated in environments with less public information flow, suggesting it reveals private information.
for_the_app: Add a 'Shorting Demand Pressure' metric that flags stocks where loan fees and volume on loan are rising simultaneously, warning users of potential near term price drops.

title: Is Sell-Side Research More Valuable in Bad Times?
authors: Roger K. Loh, René M. Stulz
key_findings: Downgrade 2-day CAR in Crisis: -2.678% (bad) vs -1.687% (good) | Upgrade 2-day CAR in Crisis: 2.658% (bad) vs 2.044% (good) | Difference in Downgrade CAR (Crisis): -0.991% | Difference in Upgrade CAR (Crisis): 0.614% | Drift exists: intercepts of the regressions are all significantly negative for negative revisions and significantly positive for positive revisions indicating that there is a stock price drift to analyst
for_the_app: Flag analyst recommendation changes during high market uncertainty periods as higher impact events for storyline tracking

title: On Market Timing and Investment Performance. II. Statistical Procedures for Evaluating Forecasting Skills
authors: Roy D. Henriksson, Robert C. Merton
key_findings: According to a 2019 study citing this paper, the ability to time the market was found in roughly 2.5% of mutual funds. | A 2022 study citing this paper notes that Henriksson (1984) later validated the model and discovered that only 3 out of 116 funds had significant market timing ability. | The model assumes managers use qualitative approaches to predict if market returns will be greater or less than the risk free rate. | The test distinguishes between 'macroforecasting skills' (market timing) and 'microforecasting skills' (security selection). | Later research cited in the text indicates that the model's error terms are often serially correlated and heteroscedastic, which can affect the accuracy of the skill assessment if not corrected.
for_the_app: The app should include a 'luck vs. skill' calculator that uses the Henriksson Merton logic (or similar nonparametric tests) to evaluate a trader's own directional calls over time, warning them if their success rate is statistically indistinguishable from random guessing.

title: Anomalous Price Behavior Around Repurchase Tender Offers
authors: Josef Lakonishok, Theo Vermaelen
key_findings: Buying shares before expiration when the price is at least 3% below the tender offer price generated an average abnormal return of 9.61% over a period of less than one week (1962-1986). | The degree of underpricing explains more than 75% of the return variability; a 1% discount relative to the tender price results in approximately 0.85% abnormal return. | Repurchasing firms outperformed the value weighted index by 23.11% (cumulative) from month 3 to month 24 after the announcement (1962-1986). | Small firms (size quintile 1) generated cumulative abnormal returns of 47.02% from one month prior to 24 months after the repurchase, while large firms (quintile 5) generated 15.18%. | In the second subperiod (1980-1986), the short term strategy still yielded high returns (e.g., 11.26% average abnormal return), but the long term post expiration drift for large firms dropped to near zero (0.34% cumulative for quintile 5).
for_the_app: The app should flag repurchase tender offers and calculate the discount between the current market price and the tender price; if the discount is >3%, it should trigger a 'buy' signal with a short holding period, and separately flag small cap repurchasers for a potential long term hold.

title: Long‐Run Common Stock Returns Following Stock Splits and Reverse Splits
authors: Hemang Desai, Prem C. Jain
key_findings: For stock splits, the average one year buy and hold abnormal return after the announcement month is 7.05%. | For stock splits, the average three year buy and hold abnormal return after the announcement month is 11.87%. | For reverse splits, the average one year buy and hold abnormal return after the announcement month is -10.76%. | For reverse splits, the average three year buy and hold abnormal return after the announcement month is -33.90%. | The positive returns for splits are positively associated with an increase in dividends announced at the same time.
for_the_app: The app should flag 'Stock Split' and 'Reverse Split' as high confidence storylines; for splits, link the event to a 'dividend increase' check to strengthen the signal, and for reverse splits, treat it as a strong negative signal.

title: The Information in Management’s Expected Earnings Report Date: A Day Late, a Penny Short
authors: Mark E. Bagnoli, William J. Kross, Susan G. Watts
key_findings: Management's expected dates are 73.8% accurate on average, rising to 80.6% by 1998, compared to less than 33% accuracy for statistical models. | For every day an announcement is delayed, the average earnings surprise becomes more negative by approximately one penny per share (e.g., -0.011 for 1-3 days late vs -0.049 for 4+ days late). | Average cumulative market adjusted returns for stocks missing their expected date are negative and significant: -0.3% by the second day late, -0.7% by the third day, and -1.0% by the fourth day. | Analysts rarely revise their earnings forecasts (91% of the time) immediately after a missed expected date, even though investors react by selling. | The market continues to adjust prices downward as the delay lengthens, indicating that the full impact of the bad news is not priced in on the day the expected date passes.
for_the_app: Add a feature that tracks 'Expected Report Date' vs 'Actual Date' and alerts users when a date is missed, predicting a continued downward trend in price and earnings estimates over the next 3-5 days.

title: Improved Methods for Tests of Long‐Run Abnormal Stock Returns
authors: John D. Lyon, Brad M. Barber, Chih‐Ling Tsai
key_findings: Rebalancing bias causes returns on small firm portfolios to be overstated by more than 10 percent per year when calculated with monthly rebalancing compared to buy and hold. | Rebalancing bias causes returns on high book to market portfolios to be overstated by 3 to 4 percent per year. | Using buy and hold reference portfolios eliminates the new listing and rebalancing biases, ensuring the population mean abnormal return is zero by construction. | In random samples, the bootstrapped skewness adjusted t statistic and empirical p value methods yield well specified test statistics (correct rejection rates near 5%). | In non random samples with industry clustering or overlapping returns, even improved methods may fail to fully correct for cross sectional dependence, making calendar time portfolio methods a preferred alternative in those specific cases.
for_the_app: The app must calculate returns using a 'buy and hold' logic for both the stock and the benchmark (no monthly rebalancing of the benchmark) and use empirical p values or skewness adjusted statistics to determine if a news driven strategy is truly skillful or just lucky.

title: Individual Investor Trading and Stock Returns
authors: Ron Kaniel, Gideon Saar, Sheridan D. Titman
key_findings: Stocks experience statistically significant excess returns of 0.80% in the 20 days following a week of intense buying by individuals. | Stocks experience statistically significant excess returns of -0.33% in the 20 days following a week of intense individual selling. | The mean market adjusted return in the 20 days prior to a week of intense individual selling is 3.15%, while prior to intense buying it is -2.47%. | Excess returns are larger in less liquid stocks: the 20-day excess return on the intense buying portfolio is 1.40% for stocks with large effective spreads (least liquid) versus 0.42% for stocks with small effective spreads (most liquid). | The return patterns are distinct from and not subsumed by past return or volume effects, as NIT remains a significant predictor in regressions controlling for these factors.
for_the_app: The app should flag stocks where retail order flow shows a sharp reversal (intense buying after a drop or selling after a rise) as potential short term mean reversion candidates, but must warn that the signal requires granular order flow data to be reliable and may be too small to cover retail trading costs.

themes: Already priced in or not; Does it still work; From signal to trade
title: The Long‐Run Stock Returns Following Bond Ratings Changes
authors: Ilia D. Dichev, Joseph D. Piotroski
key_findings: Following bond downgrades, stocks underperform by 10% to 14% in the first year (abnormal returns), with the underperformance persisting for up to three years. | The underperformance is most pronounced for small, low credit quality (non investment grade) firms, with a mean one year cumulative abnormal return of -21% for this subgroup. | There are no reliable abnormal returns following bond rating upgrades; the returns are close to zero across all time horizons. | The negative returns following downgrades occur even when the downgrade is preceded by positive earnings surprises, suggesting the market underreacts specifically to the rating change itself rather than just the earnings news. | The underperformance is observed in 26 out of 28 calendar years in the sample, indicating the effect is persistent and not limited to a specific economic period.
for_the_app: The app should flag any stock receiving a bond rating downgrade as a high probability 'negative storyline' trigger, predicting a continued decline over the next 12 months, and specifically highlight if the firm is small or has low credit quality.

themes: Already priced in or not; From signal to trade
title: Investor Reaction to Salient News in Closed‐End Country Funds
authors: Peter Klibanoff, Owen A Lamont, Thierry A. Wizman
key_findings: In typical weeks, price elasticity to net asset value is 0.50 (Table III, Column 4), indicating underreaction | In weeks with front page New York Times news, price elasticity is closer to one (Abstract) | Trading volume is 41 percent higher in news weeks (Table V, Column 1) | Abnormal volume is associated with greater price reaction to net asset value (Table VII discussion) | Results hold across emerging and established markets (Table VI snippet)
for_the_app: Flag when a stock has a fundamental change but price hasn't moved much (underreaction), but warn that if major news hits, the gap closes fast

title: Of Shepherds, Sheep, and the Cross-autocorrelations in Equity Returns
authors: Swaminathan G. Badrinath, Jayant Raghunath Kale, Thomas H. Noe
key_findings: Returns on the portfolio of stocks with the highest level of institutional ownership lead the returns on portfolios of stocks with lower levels of institutional ownership. | This lead lag effect persists even after firm size is controlled for. | The effect is apparent at longer lags than the size related lag effects documented in earlier research (Lo and MacKinlay, 1990). | Citing papers note that high institutional ownership portfolios generally have higher Sharpe ratios than low ownership portfolios within size quartiles. | Citing papers confirm that information travels more quickly for stocks with high institutional ownership, causing them to lead stocks with low ownership.
for_the_app: The app should flag 'leader' stocks (high institutional ownership) and monitor 'follower' stocks (low institutional ownership) in the same industry or supply chain, alerting the user when the leader moves but the follower has not yet reacted.

themes: Events that make prices drift; News spreading to linked companies; Text and attention signals; Already priced in or not
title: Investor and Analyst Reactions to Earnings Announcements of Related Firms: An Empirical Analysis
authors: Sundaresh Ramnath
key_findings: Subsequent announcers earn a mean market adjusted return of 0.42% over an average holding period of 7 trading days (1995-1997). | The 0.42% return over 7 days translates to roughly 15% on an annualized basis. | Returns are positive and significant in 10 out of 11 quarters tested. | About 65% of the total abnormal return occurs specifically around the subsequent announcer's own earnings announcement date. | Strategies based on the first announcer's stock return (CARFA) or raw forecast error (PFEFA) yield significant positive returns, while strategies based on the predicted forecast error (PPFE) show mixed results in regression but positive returns in portfolio tests.
for_the_app: The app should flag 'subsequent announcers' in an industry immediately after the first company reports a surprise, predicting the direction of the drift and setting a holding period until the second company's own earnings date.

themes: Events that make prices drift; Already priced in or not
title: Underreaction to Self-Selected News Events: The Case of Stock Splits
authors: David L. Ikenberry, Sundaresh Ramnath
key_findings: Mean match adjusted abnormal return of 9.00% (t=7.93) in the year following a split announcement (1988-1997). | Median abnormal one year return of 6.31% (p<.0001), indicating the drift is not driven by a few extreme outliers. | Abnormal returns were highest in high momentum quintiles (10.28% and 10.12% for quintiles 4 and 5). | Analysts underestimated earnings for splitting firms by -7.67% just before the split and only revised to -7.08% immediately after, showing sluggish expectation updates. | Calendar time arbitrage portfolios (long split firms, short matches) showed abnormal returns of roughly 8.8% per year (equal weighted) and 7% per year (value weighted) for the 1988-1997 period.
for_the_app: Add a 'Split Announcement' event trigger that flags stocks for a potential long term hold storyline, specifically monitoring for sluggish analyst earnings revisions as a confirmation signal.

title: The Cost of Institutional Equity Trades
authors: Donald B. Keim, Ananth Madhavan
key_findings: For exchange listed stocks, the average total round trip cost for the smallest market cap quintile is 3.81 percent, while for the largest quintile it is 0.57 percent. | Commission costs for institutional investors averaged about 0.20 percent of trade value in the 1991-93 period, down from 0.58 percent in 1982. | Round trip trading costs vary significantly by investment style: value managers averaged 0.45 percent, index managers 1.09 percent, and momentum (technical) traders 2.04 percent. | For Nasdaq stocks, total trading costs are generally higher than for exchange listed stocks, with the smallest market cap quintile reaching 2.85 percent for buyers and 2.91 percent for sellers. | Sell costs generally exceed buy costs; for example, the largest trade size quartile for exchange listed stocks had a total cost of 0.90 percent for buys but 1.42 percent for sells.
for_the_app: The app should include a 'Cost Estimator' feature that adjusts expected returns based on the stock's market cap and the user's intended holding period/aggressiveness, warning that small cap or rapid turnover strategies may be eaten up by transaction costs.

title: More Than Words: Quantifying Language to Measure Firms' Fundamentals
authors: Paul C. Tetlock, Maytal Saar‐Tsechansky, Sofus A. Macskassy
key_findings: Negative words in news stories forecast low firm earnings in the next quarter. | Stock prices briefly underreact to negative words; the market reaction to DJNS stories persists beyond the first day, with 6.2 basis points of the reaction occurring after day 2. | A long short strategy (long positive news, short negative news) based on DJNS stories earned an average risk adjusted return (alpha) of 10.31 basis points per day (1980-2004) before costs. | The strategy's annualized raw return was 21.07% before costs, but dropped to -4.37% after assuming 10 basis points in round trip transaction costs. | The predictive power of negative words is strongest for stories that focus on fundamentals (those containing the word stem 'earn').
for_the_app: The app should flag stories with high negative word fractions, especially those mentioning 'earnings' or fundamentals, as potential signals of underreaction, but must warn users that the immediate price drift is likely too small to trade profitably after costs without further refinement.

title: Wisdom of Crowds: The Value of Stock Opinions Transmitted Through Social Media
authors: Hailiang Chen, Prabuddha De, Yu Jeffrey Hu et al.
key_findings: 1% higher negative words in SA articles predicts 0.25% to 0.28% lower abnormal returns over 3 months | 1% higher negative words in SA comments predicts 0.16% lower abnormal returns over 3 months | Long short portfolio (quintile based on article tone) earns 2.6 basis points daily abnormal return | Long short portfolio (quintile based on comment tone) earns 2.2 basis points daily abnormal return | SA views predict future earnings surprises (specific numbers not reported in text)
for_the_app: Add a feature to track negative word density in user comments and articles as a contrarian signal for 3-month price moves

title: Inter-firm linkages and the wealth effects of financial distress along the supply chain☆
authors: Michael G. Hertzel, Z LI, M OFFICER et al.
key_findings: The mean stock market reaction to suppliers of firms filing for bankruptcy is –1.96%. | The mean stock market reaction to customers of firms filing for bankruptcy is –0.19%. | Suppliers experience significantly negative stock returns around the bankruptcy filing date of a distressed customer. | Long term horizontal alliance partners experience a cumulative abnormal return (CAR) of -2% over the window (-1, +1) days. | Suppliers experience average CARs ranging from –0.61% to –2.73% when customers announce the replacement of their CEOs.
for_the_app: The app should flag suppliers of any company showing 'pre filing distress' (defined as the day of the largest negative return in the prior year) and suggest a short position with a 1-3 day holding period.

title: Sources of gains in horizontal mergers: evidence from customer, supplier, and rival firms
authors: C. Edward Fee, Shawn Thomas
key_findings: Rival firms saw a positive stock price reaction of 0.24% over the 3-day window centered on the announcement (CAR(-1, 1)). | Customer firms showed no statistically significant change in stock prices (CAR was insignificant) around the announcement. | Supplier firms experienced a negative market reaction of -0.30% following horizontal merger announcements. | The results support the 'efficiency hypothesis' (mergers create value through productivity) rather than the 'market power hypothesis' (mergers create value by raising prices), as rivals gained while customers did not lose. | The study identified 39 public horizontal mergers that were challenged by antitrust regulators, using joint annual reports to verify these cases.
for_the_app: The app should flag 'Rival' and 'Supplier' stocks immediately upon a merger announcement, assigning a 'Buy' signal to rivals and a 'Sell' signal to suppliers, while ignoring customers for short term trades.

title: Bankruptcy spillover effects on strategic alliance partners
authors: Audra L. Boone, Vladimir I. Ivanov
key_findings: Non bankrupt strategic alliance partners experience a negative stock price reaction around the partner's bankruptcy filing announcement. | The bankruptcy of a partner leads to a decrease in the non bankrupt partner's profit margins and investment levels over the subsequent two years. | The negative spillover effect is more severe for partnerships that are longer in duration and closer in nature. | The negative impact on stock prices and performance is insignificant for joint venture partners, unlike strategic alliance partners. | Terminating the alliance with a bankrupt partner can alleviate the negative spillover effects on the non bankrupt firm.
for_the_app: Add a 'Counterparty Risk' module that flags stocks with strategic alliances; if a partner files for bankruptcy, trigger a 'Sell' or 'Reduce Position' alert, but suppress this alert if the relationship is classified as a Joint Venture.

title: The Importance of Industry Links in Merger Waves
authors: Kenneth Robinson Ahern, Jarrad Harford
key_findings: Merger activity transmits to close industries quickly (within one year) and to distant industries with a delay of two to three years. | Merger activity in close industries leads to increased activity in the following year, while distant industries see increased activity in two or three years. | Shocks travel faster through supplier links than through customer links because the supplier network is more densely connected. | Industries that are more central in the product market network are more likely to experience merger waves during economy wide surges. | Industry pairs with strong customer supplier connections have an average of 12.5 mergers over the sample period, compared to 0.11 for pairs with no meaningful connection.
for_the_app: The app should map user selected stocks to their industry's position in the customer supplier network and alert the user if a merger wave begins in a 'hub' or 'supplier' industry, predicting a potential wave in the user's stock's industry 1-3 years out.

title: The Value of Investment Banking Relationships: Evidence from the Collapse of Lehman Brothers
authors: Chitru S. Fernando, ANTHONY D. MAY, William L. Megginson
key_findings: Equity underwriting clients lost an average of -4.85% over the 7-day window (-5 to +1) surrounding the bankruptcy, which was significantly worse than the -1.91% loss of clients from similar banks. | On the day of the bankruptcy (Day 0), equity underwriting clients dropped -1.48% (equally weighted) or -1.76% (value weighted) in abnormal returns. | Over the 30-day period following the event (+2 to +30), equity underwriting clients continued to underperform, losing an additional -7.07% in abnormal returns compared to the control group. | Firms with stronger relationships (more past equity offerings with Lehman) suffered larger losses; the reaction was also worse for smaller, younger, and financially constrained companies. | Clients of other services (debt underwriting, M&A, NYSE specialist, analyst coverage) showed no significant negative reaction in the short term unless they also had an equity underwriting relationship.
for_the_app: Add a 'Relationship Risk' metric that flags stocks where a major service provider (underwriter, lender, or advisor) is in distress; if that provider fails, the app should predict a multi week negative drift for the client.

title: Contagion and competitive intra-industry effects of bankruptcy announcements
authors: Larry H.P. Lang, René M. Stulz
key_findings: On average, a value weighted portfolio of competitors loses 1% in value on the day of the bankruptcy announcement. | For industries with high leverage (debt to assets above the sample median of 0.22), competitor equity falls by 2.87% (significant at 0.01 level). | For industries with low leverage, the abnormal return is positive but not statistically significant. | In highly concentrated industries with low leverage, competitor equity increases by 2.2%. | In highly concentrated industries with high leverage, competitors lose 3.22% (significant at 0.01 level).
for_the_app: The app should flag a bankruptcy event and automatically check the target industry's leverage and concentration metrics to predict whether competitors will likely drop (contagion) or rise (competitive gain) in the next few days.

title: Credit Contagion from Counterparty Risk
authors: Philippe Jorion, Gaiyan Zhang
key_findings: Borrower announcement day stock loss: -16.6% (66 firms) | Creditor 11-day stock loss: -1.90% (all creditors), -2.29% (industrials) | Creditor 70-day stock loss: -7.93% (all creditors) | Creditor 11-day CDS spread increase: 5.17 basis points | Industrials suffer more than financials (-2.29% vs -0.34% over 11 days)
for_the_app: Alert when a company files bankruptcy and list its top creditors; warn of expected stock price drop in creditors over the next 11 days

title: Financial Firm Bankruptcy and Contagion
authors: Jean Helwege, Gaiyan Zhang
key_findings: Creditors suffered an average decline of -2.29% over the [-2, 2] window centered on the bankruptcy announcement (402 firms). | Rival firms in the same state and business line saw a -1.45% return over the [0, 1] window and sharper drops over longer windows. | Distress news caused larger contagion than bankruptcy filings: rivals of distressed firms saw a -2.06% return over the [-2, 2] window. | Lehman creditors fell 1.24% on average over [0, 1] and up to 3.87% over the 5-day window for those with largest exposures. | AIG creditors lost 4.24% over the 5-day announcement window, with some losing over 10% around the specific distress day in September 2008.
for_the_app: Flag 'distress' news (not just bankruptcy) as a stronger signal for rival contagion; prioritize firms in the same state and business line; warn that the price drop usually happens within 1-2 days, not weeks.

title: Overreaction, Delayed Reaction, and Contrarian Profits
authors: Narasimhan Jegadeesh, Sheridan D. Titman
key_findings: Lead lag structure (delayed reaction to common factors) contributes less than 5% of observed contrarian profits. | Overreaction to firm specific information accounts for approximately 105% of the total contrarian profits. | A weekly contrarian strategy on the full sample yields an average profit of 1.37% per week per dollar long. | For small firms, the lagged beta (delayed reaction to market) is 0.2350, while for large firms it is close to zero. | A contrarian strategy applied to 50 size sorted portfolios (designed to exploit lead lag) yields an average profit of -0.02%, effectively zero.
for_the_app: The app should prioritize identifying firm specific news over general market news when building storylines for short term trades, as market wide delays are too small to trade profitably.

title: Momentum crashes
authors: Kent Daniel, Tobias J. Moskowitz
key_findings: In the US sample (1927-2013), the static 'Winners Minus Losers' (WML) strategy had an annualized alpha of 22.3% and a Sharpe ratio of 0.71, but suffered severe crashes (e.g., 1932, 2009) where past losers outperformed past winners by large margins. | The dynamic momentum strategy, which scales exposure based on forecasts of mean and variance, achieved a Sharpe ratio nearly double that of the static strategy (approx. 1.19 vs 0.59 in the full sample) and significantly mitigated crash losses. | Momentum crashes occur specifically in 'panic' states: when the lagged two year market return is negative and the contemporaneous market return is positive (a rebound), often accompanied by high volatility. | The dynamic strategy outperformed the static strategy in all four quarter century subsamples (1927-1949, 1950-1974, 1975-1999, 2000-2013), including the period after the 2008 crisis. | Transaction costs are acknowledged as a factor: the dynamic strategy employs higher leverage and incurs higher trading costs than the static strategy, which must be considered in practical implementation.
for_the_app: Implement a 'Panic State' detector that flags when the market has dropped over the last 2 years and is currently rebounding with high volatility; when triggered, the app should advise reducing momentum exposure or shorting the strategy to avoid the crash.

title: It Depends on Where You Search: Institutional Investor Attention and Underreaction to News
authors: Azi Ben-Rephael, Zhi Da, Ryan D. Israelsen
key_findings: For earnings announcements, the low attention portfolio (LS_AIA=0) generated a 5-day return of 0.95% (statistically significant), while the high attention portfolio (LS_AIA=1) generated only 0.29% (not statistically significant). | The difference in returns between low and high attention stocks (DIFF portfolio) for earnings announcements was 0.65% over 5 days and 0.91% over 10 days, both statistically significant. | For analyst recommendation changes, the low attention portfolio (LS_AIA=0) generated a 5-day return of 0.64% (statistically significant), while the high attention portfolio (LS_AIA=1) generated 0.19% (not statistically significant). | The difference in returns between low and high attention stocks (DIFF portfolio) for analyst recommendation changes was 0.45% over 5 days and 0.60% over 10 days, both statistically significant. | Institutional attention (AIA) is the primary driver of immediate price adjustment; when AIA is high, the post event drift disappears, whereas when AIA is low, the drift persists.
for_the_app: The app should flag news events where the 'Institutional Attention' signal (modeled via search volume proxies if Bloomberg data is unavailable) is low relative to the magnitude of the news, predicting a multi day drift in the direction of the surprise.

title: Shared analyst coverage: Unifying momentum spillover effects
authors: Usman Ali, David A. Hirshleifer
key_findings: The CS momentum long short strategy generates a monthly five factor alpha of 1.19% (value weighted) and 2.10% (equal weighted) in the US (1984-2015). | The CS momentum factor subsumes other momentum effects: when controlling for CS momentum, the alphas of industry, geographic, customer, and technology momentum factors become insignificant or negative. | In international developed markets, the CS momentum factor generates a significant five factor alpha of 1.15% per month on average, while industry momentum alpha drops to 0.69% and often becomes insignificant after controlling for CS. | The effect persists in the recent sub sample (2000-2015), yielding a five factor alpha of 1.13% per month, though it is weaker than in the earlier period. | The one month strategy has a turnover of 313% per month, implying a break even transaction cost of 42.5 basis points, which is lower than average US transaction costs reported in other studies.
for_the_app: The app should prioritize 'shared analyst' links over simple industry or geographic links when building storylines, as this linkage captures the strongest momentum spillover; it should flag stocks where the 'connected portfolio' has moved significantly in the last month as potential entry points.

title: Lazy Prices
authors: Lauren H. Cohen, Christopher J. Malloy, Quoc Hung Nguyen
read_from: full text (your PDF, working paper version)
key_findings: Long non changers/Short changers earns 34-58 basis points per month (value weighted) | No immediate price reaction at filing release | The main return accrues gradually over the following 6 months and keeps accruing out to 18 months, with no reversal | Risk Factors section changes alone reach up to 188 basis points per month (5 factor alpha, equally weighted, t = 2.76): a section result, not the main return | Shorting fees for the changers (the short side) average about 72 basis points, lower than for the middle quintiles (80 to 92) (Characteristics of Quintile Portfolios; the table does not say over what period). The authors conclude that limits to arbitrage are not a significant contributor: turnover is modest, value weighted returns are a bit larger than equally weighted, and returns accrue slowly over 6 months
for_the_app: Monitor 10-K/10-Q text similarity, especially Risk Factors, to flag early warning signals

title: When Is a Liability Not a Liability? Textual Analysis, Dictionaries, and 10‐Ks
authors: Tim Loughran B, Bill McDonald
key_findings: Using the Harvard dictionary (H4N Inf), sorting firms by negative word count produced no discernable pattern in 4-day excess returns (correlation -0.004). | Using the new Fin Neg list, firms with a high proportion of negative words had sharply negative median returns, while those with low proportions had slightly negative returns, creating a strong monotonic pattern (correlation -0.021). | In multivariate regressions, the Fin Neg list coefficient was -19.538 (t stat -2.64) for the 4-day excess return, whereas the Harvard list was -7.422 (t stat -1.35) and statistically insignificant. | The uncertainty list (Fin Unc) and modal word lists (strong and weak) also showed statistically significant negative coefficients (-42.026, -149.658, and -60.230 respectively) in regressions against 4-day excess returns. | The MD&A section alone did not produce tone measures with a more discernable impact on returns than the full 10-K document.
for_the_app: Implement the specific 'Fin Neg', 'Fin Unc', and 'Modal' word lists provided by Loughran and McDonald (available online) instead of generic sentiment tools; trigger a 'sell' or 'avoid' signal if a 10-K filing shows a high density of these specific words, expecting a price drop within 3 days of the filing.

title: Giving Content to Investor Sentiment: The Role of Media in the Stock Market
authors: Paul C. Tetlock
key_findings: High media pessimism predicts a drop in Dow Jones returns of 8.1 basis points (0.081%) the next day, followed by a reversal. | Negative sentiment predicts a cumulative drop of roughly 7 basis points in small stocks (SMB factor) over 2 to 6 days after the signal. | A hypothetical zero cost strategy (buying when pessimism is in the bottom third, selling short when in the top third) yields an annualized return of 7.3% from 1985 to 1999. | The strategy worked in 12 out of 15 years in the sample, with a statistically significant average daily return of 4.4 basis points. | The effect was much stronger in the 1990s (bull market) than in the 1980s, with a 3-day decline of 7.4 basis points in the 90s compared to 3.3 basis points in the 80s.
for_the_app: Implement a 'Sentiment Reversal' alert: when the app detects extreme pessimism in news, flag a potential short term sell off followed by a buy opportunity 2-4 days later, and warn users that transaction costs may eat into small daily gains.

title: Media Coverage and the Cross‐section of Stock Returns
authors: Lily H. Fang, Joël Peress
key_findings: Stocks with no media coverage outperform stocks with high media coverage by 0.23% per month (2.76% per year) after adjusting for market, size, book to market, momentum, and liquidity factors (1-month formation, 1-month hold). | The return premium is concentrated in small stocks, stocks with high individual ownership, low analyst following, and high idiosyncratic volatility, where the premium ranges from 0.65% to 1.0% per month (8% to 12% per year). | The alpha remains statistically significant for holding periods up to 12 months, though it generally declines slightly as the holding period extends (e.g., 0.23% at 1 month vs 0.11% at 12 months for the 1-month formation period under the 5-factor model). | The effect is robust to excluding IPOs, earnings announcements, delisting biases, and technology sector stocks. | The effect is primarily driven by the long leg (no coverage stocks) generating positive alphas, while the short leg (high coverage stocks) generates alphas indistinguishable from zero.
for_the_app: The app should include a 'Media Silence' metric that flags stocks with zero news coverage over the past 1-6 months as potential long candidates, while flagging 'Media Saturation' (high coverage) as a potential short signal or a warning to avoid overhyped stocks.

title: Yahoo! for Amazon: Sentiment Extraction from Small Talk on the Web
authors: Sanjiv Ranjan Das, Mike Y. Chen
key_findings: Sentiment from tech sector postings is related to stock index levels, trading volumes, and volatility. | The correlation between forum messages and stock returns is weaker than expected (citing papers note it is often not significant for individual stocks). | Sentiment is more useful for predicting aggregate market trends or groups of stocks (like an index) rather than individual stock movements. | The classifier achieved a false positive rate of about 10% and an inter annotator agreement of 72.5% (meaning experts disagreed 27.54% of the time). | Optimistic sentiment correlates with increased volatility but not necessarily with higher future returns.
for_the_app: Add a 'Volatility Warning' feature: when message board sentiment spikes (highly bullish or bearish), flag the stock as likely to experience high price swings, but do not generate a 'Buy' or 'Sell' signal based solely on this text.

title: Do Retail Trades Move Markets?
authors: Brad M. Barber, Terrance Odean B, Ning Zhu
key_findings: Over a one year horizon, stocks heavily bought by retail investors (small trades) underperform stocks heavily sold by 4.4 percentage points (US, 1983–2001). | For stocks with high idiosyncratic risk, the annual return spread between heavily bought and heavily sold stocks is 13.2 percentage points (four factor alpha). | For stocks with the highest intensity of retail trading, the annual return spread is 13.5 percentage points (four factor alpha). | Over a one week horizon, stocks heavily bought by retail investors earn strong positive returns in the subsequent week, while heavily sold stocks earn poor returns (reversal occurs after 3–4 weeks). | Large trade order imbalances do not reliably predict future returns; in fact, stocks heavily bought with large trades tend to earn poor returns the following week.
for_the_app: The app should flag stocks with a sustained increase in retail buying volume as a 'sell' signal for a 12-month horizon, but as a 'buy' signal for a 1-week horizon, while filtering out large cap stocks where this signal is weak.

themes: Text and attention signals; Already priced in or not
title: All the News That's Fit to Reprint: Do Investors React to Stale Information?
authors: Paul C. Tetlock
key_findings: Reactions to stale news stories partially reverse in the next week, with a cumulative alpha of 19 basis points over days 2-3. | The difference in reversal between stale news (reversal) and new news (momentum or small reversal) is 29 basis points over four days (days 2-5), significant at the 1% level. | Reversals are largest in stocks with high analyst coverage (36 basis points cumulative alpha over 4 days) compared to low coverage stocks (4 basis points). | Reversals are significantly larger in stocks with a high fraction of small trades (individual investors), supporting the hypothesis that retail investors overreact to stale information. | The effect is strongest when news is preceded by other news or extreme returns within the past 5 trading days; if no such event occurred in the last 15 days, reversals are much smaller or non existent.
for_the_app: Implement a 'stale news' detector that flags stories repeating themes from the last 5 days; if a stock moves significantly on such a story, the app should signal a potential short term reversal (trade against the day-0 move) rather than a continuation.

title: The Sum of All FEARS Investor Sentiment and Asset Prices
authors: Zhi Da, Joseph Engelberg, Pengjie Gao
key_findings: a standard deviation increase in FEARS corresponds with a contemporaneous decline of 19 basis points for the daily S&P 500 index | a standard deviation increase in FEARS predicts an increase of 7.1 basis points in the S&P 500 at k = 1 (significant at the 5% level) | a standard deviation increase in FEARS predicts an increase of 7.3 basis points at k = 2 (significant at the 10% level) | cumulative increase of 14.4 basis points in the S&P 500 over days 1 and 2 (significant at the 1% level) | investors start to withdraw from equity mutual funds the day during the spike... and such an outflow persists for the next two days
for_the_app: Feature: Add FEARS spike detection to flag potential short term market reversals and temporary volatility increases

title: Event-Driven Trading and the “New News”
authors: David Leinweber, Jacob Sisk
key_findings: Portfolio simulation using 'pure news' signals from 2006–2009 and out of sample data in 2010 indicated alpha in excess of 10% a year. | News events have a greater price impact on stocks with small total dollar market value (small cap) compared to larger corporations. | Event driven trading strategies showed higher correlation in returns post-2007. | News sentiment cycles exist and can be exploited for return predictions over longer term horizons. | The strategy is cited as a 'meritorious exception' to the common problem of backtest overfitting in financial charlatanism.
for_the_app: The app should prioritize small cap stocks when generating news based signals and include a feature to track 'sentiment cycles' over weeks rather than just immediate reactions.

themes: Text and attention signals; Skill or luck
title: Small Trades and the Cross-Section of Stock Returns
authors: Soeren Hvidkjaer
key_findings: Using a 6-month formation period, the value weighted return difference between low sstt and high sstt stocks is 0.73% per month in the first year (t statistic = 3.41). | The value weighted return difference is 0.56% per month in the second year (t statistic = 3.14). | In the third year, the value weighted return difference drops to an insignificant 0.27% per month, but the equal weighted difference remains significant at 0.47% per month (t statistic = 2.97). | The strategy is most effective among high turnover stocks, where the value weighted raw return difference reaches 1.19% per month (t statistic = 3.98). | The effect persists for at least two years but disappears after four years (K=49), and the strategy shows no calendar years with more than a 5% loss during the sample period.
for_the_app: The app should flag stocks where 'small trade volume' (retail flow) is heavily skewed toward buying as a negative signal for the next 12–24 months, and conversely flag heavy small trade selling as a positive signal, integrating this into the storyline as a 'crowd sentiment reversal' event.

title: The Value of Crowdsourced Earnings Forecasts
authors: Russell E. Jame, Rick M. Johnston, Stanimir Markov et al.
key_findings: A one standard deviation increase in Estimize consensus revisions is associated with a 0.15% increase in two day size adjusted returns (US, 2012-2013). | Extreme upward Estimize revisions are associated with a 0.26% two day size adjusted return, while extreme downward revisions are associated with a -0.15% return, a difference of 0.41% (US, 2012-2013). | For stocks with low sell side analyst coverage (fewer than 10 analysts), a one standard deviation increase in Estimize revisions leads to an incremental 0.27% increase in two day size adjusted returns (US, 2012-2013). | Estimize forecasts are more accurate than sell side forecasts for horizons longer than 30 days, but less accurate for very short horizons (0-4 days) (US, 2012-2013). | There is no evidence that the 0.41% return difference between large upward and large downward revisions reverses over the subsequent 10 trading days (US, 2012-2013).
for_the_app: The app should track 'Estimize consensus revisions' as a specific event type, flagging stocks with low traditional analyst coverage, and alert users to trade within 2 days of a large revision.

title: The Wisdom of Twitter Crowds: Predicting Stock Market Reactions to FOMC Meetings via Twitter Feeds
authors: Pablo Daniel Azar, Andrew W. Lo
key_findings: Tweet content contains predictive information for future stock returns even after controlling for common asset pricing factors. | A hypothetical trading strategy based on tweet sentiment outperformed a simple 'buy and hold' market index strategy. | The tweet based strategy also outperformed a comparable dynamic asset allocation strategy that did not use Twitter information. | The predictive effect is concentrated specifically on the eight days per year when FOMC meetings occur, with negligible effects on other days.
for_the_app: The app should implement a 'high impact event filter' that only activates sentiment analysis for stocks or indices when a scheduled FOMC meeting is imminent, ignoring general daily chatter to reduce noise.

title: A Comprehensive Look at The Empirical Performance of Equity Premium Prediction
authors: Ivo Welch, Amit Goyal
key_findings: over the last 30 years, the prediction models have failed both in sample and out of sample | ntis offers a market timer with a gamma of 3 the CEV equivalent of 1.98 bp/month... offset by trading costs to turn over an additional 4.6% of the portfolio every month | tbl... performance is again largely Oil Shock dependent, and has not held for the last thirty years | most of these models have not performed well for the most recent thirty years (1975–2004) | models would not have helped an investor with access only to information available at the time to time the market
for_the_app: nothing

title: The Quiet Period Goes out with a Bang
authors: Daniel Bradley, Bradford D. Jordan, Jay R. Ritter
key_findings: analyst coverage is initiated immediately for 76 percent of these firms | Initiated firms experience a five day abnormal return of 4.1 percent versus 0.1 percent for firms with no coverage | Firms with three or more analysts initiating coverage average 6.4 percent, compared to 1.7 percent for firms with a single analyst | The single largest daily abnormal return, 1.50 percent, occurs on day - 1 | In July, 2002, the SEC changed this to 40 calendar days
for_the_app: Flag upcoming quiet period expirations for IPOs to anticipate analyst coverage and potential price run ups

title: Investor Reaction to Corporate Event Announcements: Under-Reaction or Over-Reaction?
authors: Padma Kadiyala, P. Raghavendra Rau
key_findings: Long run abnormal returns across four corporate events are most consistent with investor underreaction to short term information available prior to the event and to the information conveyed by the event itself. | The observed pattern is inconsistent with the overreaction model. | The pattern is also inconsistent with a model suggesting underreaction to short term info but overreaction to long term trends. | Citing papers note that underreaction leads to long term return continuations rather than reversals. | Citing papers mention that equal weighting captures underperformance better than value weighting for these events.
for_the_app: The app should flag corporate events (acquisitions, buybacks, offerings) as potential 'slow burn' storylines where the price reaction is incomplete, prompting the user to hold the position for weeks to capture the drift rather than selling immediately.

title: Trading Costs and Returns for U.S. Equities: Estimating Effective Costs from Daily Data
authors: Joel Hasbrouck
key_findings: Gibbs cost estimate correlates 0.965 with transaction level data (1993 to 2005) | Effective cost is positively related to returns (1926 to 2006) | Relation is strongest in January (coefficient 3.6642 vs 0.6740 non January) | Coefficient on cost is >1 (e.g. 3.66 in January), inconsistent with typical turnover | Seasonality is distinct from size effects
for_the_app: feature: filter out stocks with high estimated trading costs

title: The Information Content of Share Repurchase Programs
authors: Gustavo Grullon, Roni Michaely
key_findings: The average 3-day cumulative abnormal return (CAR) around the announcement is 2.71% (median 1.82%). | Repurchasing firms do not see an improvement in operating performance; in fact, some measures show they underperform peers, and analysts often lower earnings forecasts after the announcement. | The initial market reaction is more positive for firms with high cash levels and low market to book ratios (likely to overinvest), supporting the free cash flow hypothesis. | There is a significant long term price drift: the 3-year post announcement alpha is positively related to the reduction in the firm's cost of capital (risk). | The cost of capital (systematic risk) for repurchasing firms drops significantly (mean change of -1.32% using the market model), and the market appears to underreact to this risk reduction initially, causing the price to drift upward over the following years.
for_the_app: When a repurchase is announced, the app should flag the event as a 'risk reduction story' rather than a 'growth story,' and set a long term (3-year) timeline for the expected price drift, warning users that earnings might actually fall.

themes: Does it still work; Skill or luck
title: The Characteristics that Provide Independent Information about Average U.S. Monthly Stock Returns
authors: Jeremiah Green, John R. M. Hand, Frank Zhang
key_findings: 12 characteristics were reliable independent predictors of returns for non microcap stocks from 1980 to 2014. | Return predictability fell sharply in 2003. | Since 2003, only 2 characteristics remained as independent determinants of returns. | Hedge returns (profit from buying good traits and selling bad ones) for these characteristics have been statistically zero since 2003. | The drop in performance is linked to increased auditing and reporting quality in the US after the Sarbanes Oxley Act (2002).
for_the_app: The app should flag that most historical news based patterns derived from these 94 characteristics are likely dead in the post-2003 era and prioritize only the two remaining valid signals if they can be identified.

title: The New Issues Puzzle: Testing the Investment-Based Explanation
authors: Evgeny Lyandres, Le Sun, Lu Zhang
key_findings: Investment factor earns 0.57% per month (US, 1970 to 2005) | SEO underperformance reduces by 75% with investment factor | IPO underperformance reduces by 80% with investment factor | SEO equal weighted CAPM alpha is -0.41% per month before adjustment | IPO equal weighted CAPM alpha is -0.71% per month before adjustment
for_the_app: Flag issuance events as underperformance signals but link to investment plans for confirmation

title: Data-Snooping Biases in Tests of Financial Asset Pricing Models
authors: Andrew W. Lo, A. Craig MacKinlay
key_findings: A 5% significance test based on 50 portfolios of 50 stocks each, sorted by a characteristic with only a 1% correlation to returns, rejects the null hypothesis 67% of the time instead of 5%. | When sorting 250 stocks into 5 portfolios, a nominal 5% test actually has a 16.5% false rejection rate; sorting into 50 portfolios raises this to 7.5%. | In the 1954-1958 period, sorting by beta created a 100% probability of falsely rejecting the CAPM null hypothesis using 10 portfolios. | Even with 500 stocks, if 50 different characteristics are tested to find the best one, the spurious correlation can still cause a 5% test to have a 26.4% false rejection rate if the resulting portfolio has 50 stocks. | Sorting by firm size (market value) often leads to rejecting the null hypothesis, whereas sorting by theoretically motivated factors like dividend yield does not, suggesting size effects may be partly statistical artifacts.
for_the_app: The app must implement a strict 'hold out' validation rule: any storyline or event trigger discovered in the training data must be tested on a completely separate time period or stock universe before being shown to the user as a valid signal.

title: Anomalies across the globe: Once public, no longer existent?
authors: Heiko Jacobs, Sebastian Müller
key_findings: US equally weighted anomaly returns dropped from 74 basis points (bps) in sample to 29 bps post publication, a 62% decline. | US value weighted anomaly returns dropped from 49 bps in sample to 16 bps post publication, a 66% decline. | None of the 38 international markets showed a reliable post publication decline; returns remained stable or even increased slightly. | Anomalies involving stocks with higher arbitrage costs (e.g., higher illiquidity or idiosyncratic risk) maintained higher returns even after publication in the US. | The study concludes that the US market is unique in having a significant post publication decay, while international markets remain segmented and profitable.
for_the_app: The app should filter out US based strategies that rely on well known, published academic factors (like 'momentum' or 'value' as defined in old papers) and instead prioritize international markets or niche events involving illiquid stocks where arbitrage barriers are high.

themes: Does it still work; Skill or luck
title: Value and Momentum Everywhere
authors: Clifford S. Asness, Tobias J. Moskowitz, Lasse Heje Pedersen
key_findings: consistent value and momentum return premia across eight diverse markets and asset classes | average absolute value of the pricing errors (alpha) is 22.6 basis points per month | value and momentum are negatively correlated with each other, both within and across asset classes | long only portfolios of value and momentum still produce abnormal returns | value and momentum in government bonds and value effects in currencies and commodities, which are all novel to the literature
for_the_app: Warning: Holding periods are monthly, not days/weeks; not based on news events.

title: Abnormal returns to a fundamental analysis strategy.
authors: Jeffery S. Abarbanell, Brian J. Bushee
key_findings: Portfolios earned an average 12-month cumulative size adjusted abnormal return of 13.2 percent. | Significant portion of abnormal returns is generated around subsequent earnings announcements. | Significant abnormal returns are not earned after the end of one year of return cumulation. | Strategy performs better for certain types of firms, such as firms with prior bad news. | Additional analysis on a holdout sample suggests the strategy continues to generate abnormal returns in a period subsequent to the introduction of the signals in the literature.
for_the_app: The app should flag stocks where fundamental signals (e.g., rising inventory, falling margins) diverge from price trends, specifically targeting a 12-month holding window and alerting users when earnings announcements approach to capture the bulk of the return.

title: The implementation shortfall
authors: André F. Perold
key_findings: A hypothetical paper portfolio based on Value Line rankings outperformed the market by almost 20% per year (1965-1986), whereas the actual Value Line Fund outperformed by only 2.5% per year due to execution costs. | Implementation shortfall is composed of two main parts: execution cost (for the portion of the order filled) and opportunity cost (for the portion not filled). | Traders can lower execution costs by trading patiently over a longer window, though this increases opportunity cost if prices move against them. | For large institutional trades, the market price often deviates from the reference price (the price at the decision moment) due to the market's reaction to the imminent need to trade. | The measure is widely used to quantify the gap between on paper profits and realized profits, capturing fees, price impact, and the cost of unfilled limit orders.
for_the_app: The app should include a 'Realized vs. Paper' simulation feature that estimates execution costs based on trade size and liquidity, warning users when a strategy's theoretical edge is likely to be erased by transaction costs.

title: Performance of Institutional Trading Desks: An Analysis of Persistence in Trading Costs
authors: Amber Anand, Paul J. Irvine, Andy Puckett et al.
key_findings: Institutional trading desks can sustain relative performance (low execution costs) over adjacent periods. | Trading desk skill is positively correlated with the performance of the institution's traded portfolio. | The volume weighted mean execution shortfall for the sample is 0.25% (25 basis points). | For orders sized at 2.4% of the stock's Average Daily Volume (ADV), the execution shortfall is 24 basis points. | Trading desk skill is not limited to a selection of better brokers; it varies across institutions regardless of the broker used.
for_the_app: nothing

title: Controlling the False Discovery Rate: A Practical and Powerful Approach to Multiple Testing
authors: Yoav Benjamini, Yosef Hochberg
venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B (Statistical Methodology)
key_findings: The new procedure controls the expected proportion of falsely rejected hypotheses (FDR) for independent test statistics. | The gain in statistical power (ability to find real effects) is substantial compared to traditional methods that control the Familywise Error Rate (FWER). | Controlling the FDR is equivalent to controlling the FWER only when all hypotheses are true, but is less strict (and more powerful) when some hypotheses are actually false. | The paper provides a simple sequential Bonferroni type procedure to implement this control. | The method is illustrated with examples, though specific numerical return rates or market data are not provided as this is a statistical theory paper.
for_the_app: Implement the Benjamini Hochberg procedure as a filter: when the app ranks potential news triggers by statistical significance, use this rule to set a dynamic threshold that limits the percentage of false signals to a safe level (e.g., 5%), rather than using a fixed p value cutoff.

title: Why Most Published Research Findings Are False
authors: John P. A. Ioannidis
key_findings: For a well conducted randomized controlled trial with 80% power, 1:1 pre study odds, and 10% bias, the finding is true about 85% of the time. | In discovery oriented research with massive testing where true relationships are 1,000 times fewer than tested ones (R = 1:1,000) and bias is high (0.80), the probability a finding is true drops to 0.0010 (0.1%). | Underpowered exploratory epidemiological studies (20% power) with 1:10 pre study odds and 30% bias have only a 12% chance of being true. | The probability that a finding is true decreases as the number of independent teams testing the same question increases, unless the study power is extremely high (greater than the significance level). | Small sample sizes (low power) and small effect sizes significantly reduce the likelihood that a statistically significant finding is actually true.
for_the_app: The app should implement a 'confidence scoring' feature that lowers the weight of any single news event and requires multiple independent confirmations (storyline links) before suggesting a trade, explicitly warning users about the high risk of false positives in untested hypotheses.

title: Capital Investments and Stock Returns
authors: Sheridan D. Titman, K.C. John Wei, Feixue Xie
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
key_findings: The spread portfolio (long low investment, short high investment) earned a mean excess return of 0.168% per month (2.02% per year) over the full sample period (1973-1996). | After adjusting for risk factors (Carhart four factor model), the spread return increased to 0.192% per month (2.3% per year). | The strategy worked significantly only in 'non hostile takeover' years (pre-1984 and post-1990); it produced negative or insignificant returns during the 1984-1990 period when hostile takeovers were common. | The effect was driven by firms with high cash flows: the spread for high cash flow firms was 0.256% per month, while it was insignificant (0.059% per month) for low cash flow firms. | The effect was stronger for firms with low debt ratios (0.225% per month) compared to high debt ratios (0.099% per month), though the difference between the two groups was only marginally significant.
for_the_app: Add a 'Capital Investment Warning' flag: if a company with high free cash flow and low debt announces a large increase in capital expenditures, the app should flag it as a potential long term underperformer based on the 'empire building' narrative.

title: Parametric Portfolio Policies: Exploiting Characteristics in the Cross-Section of Equity Returns
authors: Michael W. Brandt, Pedro Santa-clara B, Rossen I. Valkanov
key_findings: Certainty equivalent gain of 10% annually without short sale constraints (CRRA risk aversion of 5) | Certainty equivalent gain of 3% annually with short sale constraints | Optimized portfolio average return of 24.4% versus 12.0% for market portfolio | Out of sample certainty equivalent loss from not optimizing in sample is only 3.8% for unconstrained and 1.2-1.7% for constrained portfolios | Average turnover of optimized portfolio is 50% per year compared to 12% for market portfolio
for_the_app: Feature: Track size, value, and momentum characteristics for stocks and suggest portfolio tilts; Warning: Short sale constraints reduce benefits significantly; Metric: Show certainty equivalent gains relative to market for different constraint scenarios

title: The Cross-section of Expected Stock Returns
authors: Jonathan W. Lewellen
key_findings: Using 15 characteristics and 10-year rolling slopes, the expected return estimates have a cross sectional standard deviation of 0.87% monthly and a predictive slope for future monthly returns of 0.74 (standard error 0.07) for all stocks (1964–2013). | For all stocks using 15 characteristics, the 12-month return forecasts have a cross sectional standard deviation of 13.47% (rolling) or 8.35% (cumulative), with predictive slopes of 0.78 and 0.72 respectively (1974–2013). | Portfolios sorted by these expected return estimates show significant abnormal returns (alphas): the high minus low spread for all stocks (equal weighted) is 2.43% per month (t stat 10.09) using 15 characteristics and 1-month holding (1974–2013). | The predictive ability deteriorates significantly at the end of the sample (2004–2013), with the average predictive slope dropping to 0.38 for all stocks and -0.37 for large stocks over the final ten years. | Forecasts based on 7 characteristics (Model 2) often perform slightly better or more consistently than those with 15 characteristics (Model 3) across different horizons and stock groups.
for_the_app: Implement a 'Composite Fundamental Score' feature that aggregates 7–15 key metrics (size, book to market, momentum, accruals, issuance, profitability, growth) using rolling regression weights to rank stocks by expected return, but include a warning that the signal is weaker for large cap stocks and recent years.

title: A Simple Estimation of Bid-Ask Spreads from Daily Close, High, and Low Prices
authors: Farshid Abdi, Angelo Ranaldo
key_findings: In the absence of quote data, the new estimator provides the highest cross sectional correlation with the TAQ effective spread benchmark (0.74 on a monthly basis), outperforming other methods which range from 0.37 to 0.65. | The estimator delivers the most accurate results for less liquid stocks (small to medium market capitalizations and medium to large effective spreads). | For the period 1993-2000 (pre decimalization), the new estimator showed the highest average cross sectional correlations and lowest estimation errors compared to other non quote methods. | End of day quoted spreads are generally the most accurate proxy when available (post-2001), but the new estimator outperforms them in the pre decimalization era (before 2001) due to larger tick sizes causing measurement errors in quoted data. | The estimated spreads for the entire market remained within an economically reasonable range (market wide effective spread did not exceed 4% for NYSE stocks) even during the Great Depression, unlike other estimators which showed extreme spikes.
for_the_app: Integrate this estimator as a 'Cost Filter' feature: calculate the estimated bid ask spread for any stock in the app's universe using only daily OHLC data, and warn users if the estimated spread is too wide to make a trade profitable after costs.

title: The Disposition to Sell Winners Too Early and Ride Losers Too Long: Theory and Evidence
authors: Hersh Shefrin, Meir Statman
key_findings: The paper identifies a 'disposition to sell winners too early and hold losers too long' driven by loss aversion, mental accounting, regret aversion, and self control. | Tax considerations alone cannot explain the observed patterns of loss and gain realization. | The observed patterns are consistent with a combined effect of tax considerations and the other behavioral elements (mental accounting, regret aversion, self control). | The concentration of loss realizations in December is not consistent with fully rational behavior but is consistent with the proposed theory. | The term 'disposition effect' was coined by Shefrin and Statman (1985) to describe the tendency to hold losing securities longer while selling winning securities too early.
for_the_app: The app should include a feature that flags when a user holds a losing position significantly longer than their average holding time for winners, or sells a winner immediately after a small gain, and prompts a rational review of the investment thesis rather than the P&L status.

title: The disposition effect in securities trading: an experimental analysis
authors: Martin Weber, Colin F. Camerer
key_findings: Participants were more likely to accept a gamble after a prior loss (56.8% acceptance) compared to a prior gain. | 80% of individuals in one sample showed a positive disposition effect (selling winners more than losers). | The disposition effect persists even when participants are explicitly told that prices do not mean revert (do not bounce back). | The effect is greatly reduced or reversed when assets are automatically sold after each period (removing the choice to hold). | The effect occurs regardless of whether participants use FIFO (first in, first out) or LIFO (last in, first out) accounting to track their costs.
for_the_app: The app should include a 'bias check' feature that flags when a user is about to sell a stock that is up (to prevent premature selling) or holds a stock that is down (to prevent emotional holding), explaining the disposition effect.

title: Liquidity, Volatility and Equity Trading Costs Across Countries and Over Time
authors: Ian H. Domowitz, Jack Dean Glen, Ananth Madhavan
key_findings: Average one way total equity trading costs across 42 countries were 71.3 basis points (0.713%) from 1996-1998, with emerging markets significantly higher (e.g., Venezuela at 134.1 bps) than developed markets (e.g., USA at 38.1 bps). | Transactions costs can dramatically reduce portfolio returns; for a minimum variance portfolio with annual rebalancing, costs lowered returns by 76 basis points (from 10.73% to 9.97%) without reducing volatility. | In a global tangency portfolio, including costs caused the weight of North America to decline by 36% (from 26.6% to 16.9% under semi annual rebalancing) while the weight of low cost European countries increased by 15%. | Higher volatility increases trading costs (reducing returns), but it also reduces portfolio turnover, which partially mitigates the total cost impact on returns. | Trading costs in emerging markets are significantly higher than in developed markets even after correcting for market capitalization and volatility, with implicit costs (market impact) often making up a large portion of the total cost in the US (over 60%) but varying widely elsewhere.
for_the_app: The app should include a 'Cost Warning' feature that estimates the likely trading cost (in basis points) for a specific stock and country based on its liquidity and volatility before suggesting a trade, and should discourage high turnover strategies in emerging markets where costs are high.

title: The Total Cost of Transactions on the NYSE
authors: Stephen A. Berkowitz, Dennis E. Logue, Eugene A. Noser
key_findings: Total transaction costs (commission + market impact) averaged 23 basis points (0.23%) of the trade value. | Commission costs averaged 18 basis points (0.18%), while market impact costs averaged only 5 basis points (0.05%). | High commission brokers did not consistently achieve lower market impact costs; for every 10 basis points paid in extra commission, market impact only dropped by roughly 1.7 basis points. | Money managers showed persistent cost differences (high cost managers stayed high cost), whereas brokers did not show consistent performance patterns. | Sells were slightly more expensive than buys, but the difference was not statistically significant.
for_the_app: The app should include a 'Cost Awareness' feature that warns users when a trade size relative to daily volume is high, as this is the primary driver of market impact, and emphasize that low commissions are more valuable than 'premium' broker services for execution quality.

title: Investment Intelligence from Insider Trading
authors: H. Nejat Seyhun
key_findings: Insider purchases are associated with one year ahead abnormal returns of 4.5%, while insider sales are associated with one year ahead abnormal returns of -2.7%. | Top executives generate 5.0% one year ahead abnormal returns, officers 3.9%, directors 3.6%, and large shareholders only 0.7%. | Insider purchases in small firms, high book to market firms, low analyst following, and low momentum firms are more frequent and more profitable. | Prices tend to fall before insider purchases and rise after insider purchases, with most of the price reaction occurring within 6 months. | Aggregate insider buying predicts high future stock market returns, while sales are often driven by liquidity needs rather than information.
for_the_app: Feature: Flag stocks where top executives (CEO, CFO) have made net purchases in the last 30-60 days, specifically filtering for small cap or low analyst following stocks; Warning: Do not automatically short stocks with insider sales, as these may be for liquidity reasons.

title: A Reality Check for Data Snooping
authors: Halbert White
key_findings: The paper illustrates the method using 3,654 different technical indicator models applied to S&P 500 daily returns. | The study finds that without correcting for data snooping, one might falsely conclude that technical indicators predict returns, when the results are often just chance. | The Bootstrap Reality Check allows one to test the null hypothesis that the best model found has no predictive superiority over a simple benchmark (a constant only model). | The paper demonstrates that the method works even with non stationary data (data that changes its statistical properties over time) by using rolling window estimates. | The text does not report a specific return percentage or a 'winning' strategy, as the goal is to provide a statistical tool to validate or invalidate strategies, not to propose a specific trading rule.
for_the_app: Implement a 'Significance Validator' feature: when the app identifies a new storyline or rule, it should run a bootstrap simulation (or a simplified version) to calculate the probability that this specific result could have occurred by random chance given the number of other storylines the app has scanned.

title: Stepwise Multiple Testing as Formalized Data Snooping
authors: Joseph P. Romano, Michael Wolf
key_findings: Stepwise method is more powerful than single step (White 2000) in rejecting false hypotheses | Studentization improves size and power properties in finite samples | Basic single step identified 3 stocks (AOL Time Warner, Qualcomm, Dell Computer) with positive CAPM alpha | Basic multi step identified 2 additional stocks (Oracle, Clear Chl. Comms.) | Studentized method identified 6 stocks (Kohls, Citigroup, Clear Chl. Comms., AOL Time Warner, MBNA Corp., Fifth Third Bancorp)
for_the_app: Add a statistical validation step that corrects for testing multiple storylines to reduce false positives from data snooping

title: The Sharpe ratio efficient frontier
authors: David H. Bailey, Marcos López de Prado
key_findings: An annualized Sharpe ratio of 1.59 over 2 years appears strong under normal assumptions, but when accounting for negative skewness (-2.45) and high kurtosis (10.16), the probability of skill drops significantly, failing to reject the 'no skill' hypothesis at 95% confidence. | For a strategy with an observed annualized Sharpe ratio of 2.0 and non normal characteristics (skewness -0.72, kurtosis 5.78), the required track record length to confirm skill (SR > 0.5) increases to 4.99 years, which is 54% longer than required for normal returns. | Using monthly data instead of daily data increases the required track record length by 18.7% for the same observed Sharpe ratio, purely due to the lower frequency of observations. | Out of the hedge fund styles tested, only 9 out of the total styles (including Distressed Securities, Event Driven, and Macro) showed a Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio greater than 0.95 for a benchmark of 0.5, meaning only these styles had statistically significant skill over the 11-year period. | Portfolios optimized for the Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio (Max PSR) had a lower standard deviation of the Sharpe ratio (0.1028 vs 0.1550) and a shorter required track record (1.08 years vs 1.67 years) compared to portfolios optimized for the standard Sharpe Ratio (Max SR).
for_the_app: The app should calculate the 'Minimum Track Record Length' for any news based strategy it identifies; if the strategy has not been running long enough to meet this threshold (adjusted for its specific volatility and skewness), the app should flag the result as 'likely luck' rather than 'skill'.

title: Luck versus Skill in the Cross‐Section of Mutual Fund Returns
authors: Eugene F. Fama, Kenneth R. French
key_findings: Aggregate active funds underperform passive benchmarks by about the amount of their expense ratios (net alpha is negative). | For the 1984-2006 period, fewer than 16% of funds have a true alpha greater than 1.25% per year before expenses. | Only about 2.3% of funds have a true alpha greater than 2.50% per year before expenses. | When looking at net returns (after costs), the distribution of performance for even the top performing funds is consistent with zero skill (luck). | Stronger evidence of skill existed in the 1975-2002 period, but this evidence disappears in the 1984-2006 period, suggesting the edge has eroded or data biases in earlier years.
for_the_app: The app should include a 'Skill vs. Luck' warning feature that flags when a stock's recent news driven rally is statistically indistinguishable from random noise, preventing users from over trading on short term luck.

title: Decoding Inside Information
